It holds the differential in rationality between the advanced and the ordinary to be general and pervasive, not confined to specialties a layman could hire.

items.stem: Which kind of equality does the constrained vision rank above equality of condition, and on what ground?
options: Equality of potential — innate capacities differ far less than upbringings do, so policy should equalize the points where people start rather than where they finish.
Equality of opportunity — results can never be fully equalized, so the rules of the process should give every person identical prospects of reaching any given result.
Equality of discretion — no group has a superiority general enough to warrant deciding for others, so each person exercises his own, guided by widely shared experience.
Equality of esteem — the worship of rank is an unearned psychic windfall for the privileged, so honor should be detached from wealth and spread across the community.

items.stem: The chapter surveys contemptuous verdicts on what ordinary people are presently capable of — the peasant likened to an oyster, the masses to an invalid. From which quarter, on Sowell's account, have such verdicts characteristically come?
options: Only the explicitly racist and Social Darwinist writers
Writers in the constrained tradition
Both traditions in roughly equal measure
Writers in the unconstrained tradition
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Kinds of Equalities and Inequalities

items.stem: According to the chapter, leading thinkers of the constrained vision concede that many rewards in society go to people who have not personally earned them.
options: True
False

items.stem: Sowell reports that Smith and Friedman were moved by the same gross disparities of wealth that outraged Godwin and Dworkin. Why, on the chapter's account, does this shared reaction tell us nothing about which vision a thinker holds?
options: Because the visions part over causation — what produced the disparity, and what remedy is open at what risk — not over moral principles.
Because each camp reserves its indignation for a different target, inherited privilege on one side of the divide and commercial profit on the other.
Because the constrained thinkers' expressions of concern are merely rhetorical, masking a settled conviction that existing rewards are deserved.
Because only secondary figures in either tradition voiced such reactions, while each tradition's leading exponents stayed silent on inequity.

items.stem: Both visions, the chapter says, concede that people's developed capabilities are unequal. What, in its account, actually determines how strong the case for surrogate decision-makers becomes?
options: How low the average capability of the ordinary person is estimated to be, measured across the society as a whole.
How sincerely the elite is thought to have made the well-being of the ordinary masses its central concern.
Whether innate potential is believed to be spread equally across all individuals and across social groups.
How wide the capability gap between different sets of people is taken to be, rather than its average level.

items.stem: A town choral society pays small honoraria to its soloists, and the solo roster has been filled by the same dozen voices for years. Two members address the annual meeting. Mara calls several current soloists coasting beneficiaries of the society's habits, no finer than the rank and file, and wants the audition rule enforced exactly as written for every singer, with any member who wishes engaging the retired opera coach in town for lessons at their own expense and judgment. Deniz calls most of the membership unable, for now, to hear their own faults, and wants a standing board of the three conservatory-trained members to assign every singer's parts, repertoire and practice plan, granting that dues must rise and some singers will quit, a price he counts well worth paying. Which pairing correctly places the two speakers?
options: Both speakers constrained
Both speakers unconstrained
Mara unconstrained; Deniz constrained
Mara constrained; Deniz unconstrained

items.stem: A hill village's irrigation association meets after a dry summer; under rotations handed down for generations, a few households draw far more water than the rest. Four members speak. Tamsin is incensed that the largest draws water the meadows of families who have not cleared a ditch in years, wants the rotation bell rung by the book for every household, and would have disputing farmers split the cost of a hired surveyor whenever a channel's fall is doubted. Odo wants the old rotation captains stood down and every question of a draw or a ditch put to a show of hands of the full membership, each household casting one vote alike whatever its acreage, and the tally posted in the hall that same evening. Petra wants a permanent board of the two agronomy-schooled farmers and the schoolhouse engineer to set each household's draw, cropping and channel repairs season by season, conceding that the meters and a clerk's wage will cost the village dearly and counting that cost slight beside the gains. Mina wants the driest crofts carried through hard summers by a standing subscription that the better-watered households are invited, never compelled, to join, with the rotation itself left exactly as the elders set it and the next dry year met in the same way. Which speaker's position belongs to the unconstrained vision?
options: Petra
Tamsin
Odo
Mina
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Kinds of Equalities and Inequalities

items.stem: A retired master-weaver writes to her guild about the journeyman's medal, whose stipend has gone for a generation to apprentices of the same three workshops. Any child set young to a loom, she writes, could have matched most of the medalists, the difference lying in the bench and not the blood; and several recent winners she names outright as no credit to the craft, carried to the stipend on their workshop's reputation. She opposes the committee's plan to rotate the medal among the workshops by turns until each has had its share; asks instead that the judging rules be read aloud unchanged and applied alike to every bolt entered, and that the two judges who last year let a famous name sway their marks be put off the panel; and remarks that any shop wanting the medal badly can buy winters of the pattern-drawer's teaching, as two of the winning three once did. Which vision is the letter speaking from?
options: Neither vision
The constrained vision
The unconstrained vision
Both visions equally
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Kinds of Equalities and Inequalities

source.title: A Conflict of Visions: Ideological Origins of Political Struggles

learning_objectives.7.1: Explain why power carries a far larger explanatory role in the unconstrained vision than in the constrained — much of what happens being the deliberate exertion of power, versus systemic processes producing results no one planned — and what follows from that difference: more occasions for moral condemnation and more prospects for sweeping reform on one side, fewer of both on the other.
learning_objectives.7.2: Explain how the two visions invert what must be explained: war, crime, and poverty as the natural state of limited man, so that peace, order, and prosperity are what require special causes and deliberate contrivances — versus as deviations from human nature whose special causes lie in institutions, and why localizing an evil's cause is precisely what makes a solution, rather than a trade-off, possible.
learning_objectives.7.3: Explain why punishment is a painful but accepted trade-off in the constrained vision and a barbaric indulgence in the unconstrained one — rehabilitation being an available solution only if decency is man's natural condition to be restored (the broken-leg logic), not an artificial creation of childhood conditioning that cannot be re-run on an adult (the invasion of little barbarians).
learning_objectives.7.4: Explain how the two visions divide over where discretion should lie: the unconstrained vision placing it with those foremost in sincerity, knowledge, and articulated reason — spanning Godwin's anarchic individualism to totalitarianism, depending only on how far the wisdom of the few is trusted to pervade the many spontaneously — while the constrained vision places it in systemic processes (traditions, families, markets) through which ordinary people convey their experience to one another.
learning_objectives.7.5: Explain why judicial boundary-drawing is the legal equivalent of laissez-faire — courts defining the limits of discretion and refusing to second-guess its exercise within them (Holmes) — while the unconstrained vision directs courts to judge the substance and trade-offs of what others decide within those limits (Dworkin's fresh moral insight, Tribe's implicit constitutional values), so that state-action cases turn on process versus result.
learning_objectives.7.6: Given a concrete act — an offer too attractive to refuse, a refusal to confer a benefit, a prohibition — determine whether each vision's conception of power counts it as an exercise of power, deciding by whether pre-existing options were reduced or behavior merely changed, never by how bad the outcome or how irresistible the pressure.
learning_objectives.7.7: Given an unfamiliar speaker's stance on one question of power — the causes of crime, the cure for poverty, the amassing of military strength — determine the stance the same vision implies on a different one, placing the speaker by whether the evil's cause is localized and removable or diffused in human nature, never by how much the language dwells on circumstance, grip, or cost.

Chapter 7 → Visions of Power.text: Power explains far more of society's workings on the unconstrained view, where outcomes follow from someone's deliberate exertion of it. That yields more occasions for moral blame and more hope that a different exertion could remake things. On the constrained view, systemic processes produce results nobody planned, so power explains less, leaving fewer judgements to make and fewer sweeping reforms likely to succeed. The word itself carries two incompatible senses here.

Chapter 7 → Force and Violence.text: Both visions prefer reason to force and differ on how far reason reaches. One hunts the special causes of war and crime, since locating a cause makes a cure thinkable; the other treats both as what limited people do, so peace and order are what need explaining and deterrence is what is available. Punishment follows: a painful duty accepted where no cure exists, or barbarity where rehabilitation would restore a nature that was sound.

Chapter 7 → The Locus of Discretion.text: Who should decide? The constrained answer is whoever bears the consequences, with courts marking boundaries and then declining to second-guess choices inside them. The unconstrained answer gives discretion to those furthest advanced in knowledge and conscience, and asks courts to weigh the substance of what others decide. Beneath the dispute sit two meanings of power: cutting someone's existing options, or merely changing what they do.

Chapter 7 → Summary and Implications.text: Stances on armament, crime and poverty travel together because they rest on one prior question: is an evil localized and removable, or spread through human nature? The first makes solutions thinkable; the second leaves only trade-offs. The two meanings of power part here too. Cutting away someone's prior options is power on either view; merely altering what they choose counts only on the second, and a reward does that as surely as a threat.

items.stem: According to the chapter, how much of what society produces does each vision put down to the exercise of power?
options: Both visions attribute most social outcomes to impersonal processes, and differ only over whether observers may rightly pass moral judgment on those outcomes.
Both visions attribute most social outcomes to deliberate power, and differ only over whether that power is chiefly political, military, or economic in form.
The unconstrained vision traces much of social life to someone's deliberate use of power, while the constrained vision credits many outcomes to systemic processes that nobody directed.
The constrained vision traces most social outcomes to deliberate power because it distrusts human nature, while the unconstrained vision credits outcomes to the spontaneous goodness of individuals.

items.stem: Why do unhappy social circumstances draw more moral condemnation within the unconstrained vision than within the constrained one?
options: An outcome produced by someone's deliberate power has an author who can be blamed, while an outcome nobody planned gives moral judgment nothing to fasten on.
The unconstrained vision treats blame as a spur that mobilizes reform, worth assigning whether or not any exertion of power produced the circumstances.
The constrained vision denies that power is ever abused in social life, leaving it nothing in unhappy circumstances that could be an object of blame.
Adherents of the unconstrained vision hold sterner value premises, condemning uses of force that adherents of the constrained vision are prepared to endorse.

items.stem: Within the unconstrained vision, why does giving power a large role in explaining society also make sweeping reform look achievable?
options: Sweeping reform in the unconstrained vision works chiefly by adjusting incentives until behavior shifts, a lever available whatever first caused the trouble.
Reformers in the unconstrained vision are held exempt from the corrupting effects of power, so entrusting them with sweeping change carries no risk of abuse.
The constrained vision holds existing arrangements to be the best attainable, so it rejects sweeping reform on principle rather than doubting its success.
What deliberate power brought about, power aimed at different goals can remake at the root; results grown from unplanned processes give reform no handle.

items.stem: In the chapter's account, the constrained vision gives power a small share in explaining social outcomes, and two consequences follow: grim circumstances present fewer occasions for condemning anyone morally, and sweeping reforms carry less prospect of achieving their goals. Yet this vision still recognizes that power can be abused.
options: True
False

items.stem: Sowell presents the disagreement between Gunnar Myrdal and Peter Bauer over Third World development as beginning at the most fundamental level, before any dispute over policy. Where does he say the two economists part first?
options: Myrdal sets out to explain what made the industrial West so productive; Bauer sets out to explain why the poorer countries remain dependent.
Myrdal sets out to explain the masses' resistance to modernization; Bauer sets out to explain why reformers discount the burdens their plans impose.
Myrdal sets out to explain why the poorer countries remain underdeveloped; Bauer sets out to explain why any country ever becomes prosperous at all.
Myrdal sets out to explain how planning can reconcile competing interests; Bauer sets out to explain how markets deliver goods their own operators cannot account for.

items.stem: Godwin traced war to undemocratic institutions; some modern writers Sowell cites trace social evils to the capitalist economy. Sowell says the particular location chosen matters less than the localization itself. Within the unconstrained vision, what does localizing an evil's cause accomplish?
options: It turns a clash of visions into a question of evidence, letting empirical findings settle what assumptions alone could never decide.
It marks out who or what can be removed or neutralized, so the evil can be ended outright rather than merely traded against other costs.
It supplies a target for moral condemnation, and public indignation at a named culprit is what carries sweeping reform into practice.
It settles which surrogate decision-makers should hold discretion, since whoever has diagnosed an evil is best placed to direct its remedy.

items.stem: Sowell observes that both visions recognize most people as horrified by certain crimes and morally incapable of committing them; the visions divide over where that horror comes from. What does each vision say produces it?
options: The constrained vision credits an aversion born into human nature itself; the unconstrained vision credits habits of restraint that institutions deliberately instill.
The constrained vision credits conditioning by social traditions and institutions; the unconstrained vision credits a natural aversion that injustice wears down.
The constrained vision credits each person's fear of becoming a victim in turn; the unconstrained vision credits compassion that social brutality has not yet drained.
The constrained vision credits the deterrent shadow of punishment; the unconstrained vision credits the example of the morally and intellectually advanced few.

items.stem: Because the constrained vision takes war and crime to be rooted in human nature rather than in removable special causes, it presumably concludes that little can be done to reduce either.
options: True
False

items.stem: As Sowell presents him, how did Adam Smith regard the infliction of punishment on the guilty?
options: As a painful duty, accepted because crime admits of no solution
As a routine civic task that a humane man can perform without distress
As a brutalizing indulgence in vengeance left over from a crueler age
As a stopgap to be retired once the reformation of offenders proves reliable

items.stem: Sowell says believers in the unconstrained vision see punishment not as a hard necessity but as something close to barbarism. On that vision's own premises, why?
options: A genuine solution, rehabilitation, is at hand, so accepting a painful trade-off serves no purpose
Crime mirrors the character of the whole society, so loading its cost onto one offender punishes the wrong party
No court can know an offender's circumstances well enough to measure out his suffering justly
The suffering inflicted on the guilty outweighs whatever deterrence society gains from making examples of them

items.stem: Godwin granted that punishment can alter how a man behaves. Why did this concession leave his objection to punishment standing?
options: Behavior ruled by fear leaves the sentiments untouched, and for Godwin only a changed disposition is a solution
Behavior compelled by threat lapses the moment the threat is lifted, so the improvement never outlasts the sentence
The change in behavior is purchased with suffering that outweighs whatever harm the original offense inflicted
Punishing a man for circumstances he never chose embitters him against society and breeds still further crime

items.stem: According to the chapter, the two visions' split over rehabilitation follows from a prior split over decency itself: the unconstrained vision takes decency to be man's natural condition, which treatment can restore much as a set broken leg heals on its own, while the constrained vision takes decency to be an artificial product of childhood conditioning, with little prospect of being created in an adult.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, the unconstrained vision spans which political range?
options: From Smith's laissez-faire economics at one end to Godwin's anarchism at the other
From the Federalists' republicanism at one end to Mill's guided democracy at the other
From Godwin's anarchic individualism at one end to totalitarianism at the other
From the regulated welfare state at one end to fully centralized planning at the other

items.stem: Sowell notes that some holders of the unconstrained vision, Godwin among them, would leave decisions with individuals, while others would lodge them in organizations run by the wise and virtuous. In his account, what separates these two camps within the one vision?
options: Whether human nature is regarded as fixed at its core or open to deliberate improvement
How morally tolerable coercion is judged to be, apart from its practical effectiveness
How far the few's wisdom is trusted to reach the many's decisions without being imposed
How much weight is given to trade-offs as against outright solutions to social evils

items.stem: Sowell writes that neither vision would leave individuals free to act with no regard for anyone else; what differs is the kind of guidance that reaches an ordinary person, and from whom. Which pairing captures his contrast, the unconstrained vision's channel first and then the constrained vision's?
options: Rules of formally enacted law; old customs that statutes have not yet gotten around to recording
Teachings of the morally advanced; shifts in price and approval that pass on others' experience
Commands of government planners; a life left wholly free of pressure from any other person
Findings of credentialed experts; moral sermons handed down by the authorities of tradition

items.stem: The constrained vision places discretion in traditions, families, and markets presumably because it holds the pooled judgment of ordinary people to be wiser than the judgment of any elite.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, what position did Oliver Wendell Holmes take on choices made within the legal boundaries of someone's discretion?
options: Courts should weigh the sincerity and good faith of the chooser before deciding whether the choice deserves deference.
Courts should set them aside when judges find them excessive, since the law cannot have been meant to shelter foolish decisions.
Courts should review them for reasonableness whenever the choice imposes serious costs on parties who had no say in it.
Courts should leave them alone: one may deliberately go as near a legal line as one likes without crossing it.

items.stem: The chapter describes courts that mark out the limits of discretion and decline to re-examine what is chosen inside them, and calls this approach the legal equivalent of laissez-faire. Why, on its account, does the parallel hold?
options: Both aim at minimal government, treating every exercise of public power as an unwelcome intrusion into the private sphere.
Both predict that holders of discretion will usually choose sensibly, so that reviewing their choices would rarely change the outcome.
Both leave choices with those who gain or lose by them, confining the overseer to policing limits rather than reviewing merits.
Both favor market interests in substance: a restrained court is one that shields property and business from legislative interference.

items.stem: A leafleter defies a private development's rule against distributing literature, the owner calls in the state's trespass power, and the arrest reaches the courts. According to the chapter, what question separates the two visions' judges in state-action cases of this kind?
options: Whether freedom of speech or the right of property stands higher in the constitutional order when the two directly collide.
Whether the state's enforcement of the trespass law was carried out in procedurally correct and properly authorized forms.
Whether the court asks only if the enforced boundary was rightly drawn, or also judges the result produced inside it.
Whether the First Amendment's limits on abridging speech bind private landowners as directly as they bind the government.

items.stem: In the chapter's account, the unconstrained vision directs courts to judge the morality and reasonableness of what others decide within their legal boundaries because it holds that third parties are capable of making such judgments, so a court able to correct an unjust choice has little justification for holding back.
options: True
False

items.stem: Within the constrained vision, as the chapter presents it, what is power?
options: The ability to get another person to do whatever one wishes
The ability to reduce the set of choices another person already had
The exercise of discretion inside boundaries that the law has drawn
The possession of wealth great enough to sway other people's decisions

items.stem: According to the chapter, how does the constrained vision's definition of power classify one party's offer of a specific quid pro quo to another?
options: Not an exercise of power, provided the offer was made with benign intentions
Not an exercise of power, since the recipient's range of action is enlarged
An exercise of power, but only when accepting is practically guaranteed
An exercise of power, since the recipient's behavior is changed by it

items.stem: The chapter's summary observes that a threat and a reward can produce exactly the same change in a person's behavior. Why does the constrained vision nevertheless give the two acts opposite classifications?
options: A threat narrows the person's prior scope for action while a reward widens it, and scope is the vision's test
A threat springs from hostile intentions while a reward springs from benevolent ones, and intentions are the vision's test
A threat leaves its target worse off while a reward leaves its target better off, and outcomes are the vision's test
A threat applies pressure much harder for its target to withstand than a reward's, and resistibility is the vision's test

items.stem: According to the chapter, an offer so generous that acceptance is all but certain would presumably count as an exercise of power even on the constrained vision's definition, since so lopsided a choice arguably leaves its recipient no real alternative.
options: True
False

items.stem: For eleven years Nella has played the organ, unpaid, for a small village congregation every Sunday. A city oratorio society that heard a recording of her playing invites her to become its principal organist, with featured solos and broadcast concerts, and with rehearsals that fall on Sunday mornings. Friends agree that declining was unthinkable, and Nella herself says the society left her no real way to refuse. She accepts, and the congregation loses its longtime organist. How does each vision's conception of power classify the society's invitation, as an act toward Nella?
options: Unconstrained: power; constrained: power
Unconstrained: not power; constrained: power
Unconstrained: power; constrained: not power
Unconstrained: not power; constrained: not power

items.stem: A college's one travel fellowship for junior scholars can be sought only with a nomination from the candidate's department head. Dr. Okafor, who heads a small department, judges that his junior colleague Dr. Veras needs another year of fieldwork before her project can stand scrutiny, and he declines to put her name forward. Unable to apply without him, she stays on her present appointment for another year; colleagues murmur that her whole year was settled in one man's office and that she never had a say in it. How does each vision's conception of power classify Okafor's refusal, as an act toward Veras?
options: Unconstrained: not power; constrained: power
Unconstrained: not power; constrained: not power
Unconstrained: power; constrained: not power
Unconstrained: power; constrained: power

items.stem: A village footpath association looks after the trails around a small nature reserve. For years walkers have cut across a meadow where a rare orchid has begun to seed, so this spring the wardens close the meadow crossing altogether, posting signs that send everyone around by a lane that adds a few minutes to the walk. Members praise the decision, nobody is fined or even scolded, compliance is cheerful, and by summer the orchids have recovered. How does each vision's conception of power classify the wardens' closure, as an act toward the walkers?
options: Unconstrained: power; constrained: not power
Unconstrained: power; constrained: power
Unconstrained: not power; constrained: power
Unconstrained: not power; constrained: not power

items.stem: According to the chapter, what is the hallmark of how the unconstrained vision explains evils such as war and crime?
options: It attributes each evil to the personal wickedness of the individuals who commit it.
It treats each evil as the default condition of mankind, to be contained by deliberate contrivances.
It holds each evil to be beyond explanation and therefore beyond deliberate remedy.
It traces each evil to a specific, removable cause rather than to human nature in general.

items.stem: The chapter holds that where people stand on whether a peaceful nation should build up military power lines up closely with where they stand on unrelated domestic questions such as crime and punishment.
options: True
False

items.stem: Godwin located the cause of war in undemocratic political institutions; some modern writers locate it in a capitalist economy; others trace crime to poverty or discrimination. Why does the chapter treat these quite different diagnoses as expressions of one and the same vision?
options: Each places the cause somewhere narrower than human nature, so the evil can in principle be removed.
Each blames an institution its author already opposed on other grounds, so the diagnosis follows the politics.
Each concedes that some measure of war and crime must persist whatever reforms are made.
Each calls for an enlargement of government power to administer the remedy it proposes.

items.stem: Adam Smith conceded that soldiering works a loss on a man's humanity and that punishing a criminal pains every humane observer — yet the chapter counts him squarely within the constrained vision. Why do those concessions not pull him toward the unconstrained side?
options: He reckoned the costs smaller than his critics did, so they carried little weight with him.
He spoke of the costs chiefly to display sympathy, while his real case rested elsewhere.
He expected gentler institutions eventually to deliver deterrence without its painful side.
He accepts each cost as a standing trade-off, not as a stage on the way to any solution.

items.stem: A longtime officer of a village improvement association moves to abolish its maintenance rota — the roster assigning each household its weeks tending the green and verges. The rota itself, she argues, bred the shabbiness it was meant to cure: assigned weeks turned neighbors into grudging minimum-doers, and the neglect will go out with the roster that feeds it. The association now also faces a run of break-ins at its communal tool shed. On the chapter's account, which response to the break-ins does her position on the rota imply?
options: Write the losses into the budget as the price of keeping a common shed.
Fit stronger locks and set stiff penalties for anyone caught.
Hand the matter to the town constable and keep the association out of it.
Reclaim whoever is taking the tools rather than make an example of them.

items.stem: A regional sports league's disciplinary chair devotes her annual report to the players she has suspended — the family strain behind one foul, the scholarship another player lost, how heavily a season's ban lands at nineteen. A board member proposes an inquiry to find and remove the handful of coaches whose methods, he says, put dirty play into the game. She declines, asking instead that the automatic-suspension table stand as written, this season and every season after. The league's junior clubs, meanwhile, keep folding for want of money. On the chapter's account, which approach to the clubs' troubles does her choice imply?
options: Ask what keeps the solvent clubs standing, and build more of that.
Search out whatever is draining the clubs, and shut it off.
Carry the struggling clubs with subsidies from the league's gate money.
Let clubs that cannot pay their way close without league interference.

items.stem: Enrollment in a university department has slid for ten years. One professor proposes handing the overhaul to a standing committee of its three most cited members — the rest of the faculty, junior and senior alike, to take no part in the drafting — with the finished design then circulated and defended in open meetings, which he expects to carry the adoption vote on its own. The department is meanwhile feuding with a rival unit that has begun cross-listing its core courses. On the chapter's account, which stance toward the rival unit does his proposal imply?
options: Cede the contested courses and put the effort into what remains.
Ask the provost to draw a boundary between the units and enforce it.
Go straight to talks, treating the feud as a tangle to be cleared up.
Settle nothing until the department has rebuilt its bargaining position.

source.title: A Conflict of Visions: Ideological Origins of Political Struggles

learning_objectives.8.1: Contrast the status each vision gives justice: categorically paramount and uncompromising, with rights derived from justice as "trumps" that prevail over every non-trump (Rawls; Godwin's "superior claims of justice"), versus instrumental — important because society "cannot subsist" without justice "tolerably observed," and therefore subordinate at times to the preservation of order, since man suffers more from the breakdown of even an unjust order than from some injustices.
learning_objectives.8.2: Explain why, on Sowell's reading, the Holmes–Godwin conflict over individualizing punishment is a difference in empirical assumptions rather than value premises — Holmes too ranked tailoring justice to the individual as the morally higher standard, and deliberately chose the lower one as the only standard human courts can administer, while Godwin held that "every case is a rule to itself" and that punishing by category of crime confounds the qualities of men.
learning_objectives.8.3: Contrast the two accounts of where good law comes from: the codified experience of vast numbers of people over centuries — precedents followed unless "flatly absurd or unjust," judges as neutral transmitters of process principles (Holmes's life-of-the-law, Blackstone's presumption that old rules are well founded) — versus the deliberate creation of learned men and of judges who must make explicit substantive choices, because process neutrality is illusory where legal rules tilt results against particular groups (Condorcet; Tribe's "dangerous allure of proceduralism"; Dworkin's activist court).
learning_objectives.8.4: Distinguish the two conceptions of what a right is: a zone of immunity from public authority — a process conception, justified by the social processes it serves and implying no facilitating activity by the authorities (Holmes resting free speech on social expediency) — from an entitlement inhering in individuals as a recognition of their humanity, ranked by its importance to those who exercise it and judged by results, so that speech outranks property and speech priced out of reach counts as unfree (Dworkin, Tribe).
learning_objectives.8.5: Given an unfamiliar argument about rights, law, or aid to the less fortunate, determine which vision it expresses by where it grounds the claim — in process characteristics and the limits of what courts and societies can do, or in results to which people are entitled — rather than by the policy's direction, its party coloration, or how warmly it speaks of rights.
learning_objectives.8.6: Explain why the unconstrained vision demands for the less fortunate not charity but justice — every member of society entitled to some share of its wealth simply by membership, irrespective of contribution — and why, within that vision, calling the transfer charity is itself the offense, filling the rich with unearned pride and the poor with servility (Bellamy's crusts; Godwin's rich as "merely administrators"; Shaw on almsgiving).
learning_objectives.8.7: Explain why Hayek attacks social justice as a process while its advocates define it as a result — the particulars of a spontaneous order, being neither intended nor foreseen by anyone, can be neither just nor unjust, so demanding just results means organizing society to assign shares and undermines the rule of law — and why each side thereby assumes away the other's primary concern, leaving most constrained thinkers simply silent on the whole literature.

Chapter 8 → Visions of Justice.text: Rawls and Smith both called justice a society's first virtue and meant near-opposites. For Rawls it is uncompromising: no person's inviolability yields to the general welfare, and an injustice is tolerable only to avert a worse one, rights acting as trumps. For Smith it earns its place because society cannot hold together without it, needs only tolerable observance, and may give way to order — since men suffer more from disorder, even unjust, than from some wrongs.

Chapter 8 → Legal Justice.text: Holmes held that courts cannot weigh each person's temperament as heaven might, so they apply a common standard and accept the rougher justice — he thought the finer kind better, merely beyond human courts. Blackstone presumed an old rule well founded even when its reason is forgotten. Godwin held the opposite: every case is its own rule, and sentencing by category confuses men rather than distinguishing them. Condorcet and later writers wanted law deliberately built, and judges choosing openly.

Chapter 8 → Individual Rights.text: One tradition makes a right a boundary authority cannot cross: people act within it whether wisely or foolishly, the point being the processes it protects, and it obliges nobody to make exercising it easy. Holmes defended speech so, as a wager under imperfect knowledge. The other makes a right something owed to a person recognising their humanity, ranked by what it means to the holder — so speech outranks property, and speech nobody can afford is not free.

Chapter 8 → Social Justice.text: Godwin wrote perhaps the first treatise on it, and his demand was moral rather than governmental — he and Condorcet still backed property and laissez-faire. Both traditions have worked to relieve poverty; what divides them is calling it a debt, not a kindness, since members are owed a share whatever they contributed, and naming it charity leaves the giver proud and the receiver servile. Hayek answers that a spontaneous order's outcomes, intended by nobody, can be neither just nor unjust.

items.stem: The chapter identifies two claims about justice that hold consistently across the unconstrained vision, whatever else its adherents disagree about. Which option states them?
options: Justice means applying the same rules to everyone, and whatever results follow are just
Justice must be enforced by government power, and its demands override private property rights
Justice holds society together, and it need only be observed tolerably well to do that
Justice is categorically paramount, and the rights derived from it belong to individuals

items.stem: According to the passage from Rawls the chapter quotes, under what condition alone may an injustice be tolerated?
options: When justice in the society at large remains observed to a tolerable degree
When the advantages it secures for many outweigh the sacrifices borne by a few
When the order society depends on would otherwise break down entirely
When tolerating it is necessary to avoid a still greater injustice

items.stem: The chapter reports that writers in the unconstrained vision speak of rights grounded in justice as 'trumps' that prevail over every non-trump. What does the chapter say becomes of this concept in the constrained vision?
options: It survives, but with order installed as the one trump that overrides any claim of justice
It is refused because rights in that vision are absolute and need no ranking between them
It simply has no application in a vision that weighs everything as incremental trade-offs
It applies only to the core zones of immunity and is denied to broader claims of justice

items.stem: According to the chapter, the constrained vision treats justice as instrumentally important: society cannot hold together where injustice prevails, so justice takes its standing from the need to keep society in being, not society its purpose from the need to bring about justice.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter presents Holmes as recognizing two standards of justice — one that weighs each person's particular makeup, and one that holds everyone to a general standard regardless of it. On Sowell's account, what did Holmes do with these two standards?
options: He denied that a tailored standard exists even in principle, dismissing any appeal to one as a confusion of morality with law.
He granted that the tailored standard was morally higher, and chose the general one as the only standard fallible human courts can administer.
He held that the general standard was morally higher, because holding all men to one common measure is itself the fullest form of equal justice.
He endorsed the tailored standard for civil liability judgments while reserving the general standard for the punishment of crimes alone.

items.stem: Godwin held that no two crimes are ever alike and that justice must weigh the circumstances of each case; Holmes defended punishing by the general category of the crime. According to Sowell, what kind of disagreement is this?
options: A difference in theories of human nature: Godwin believed criminals can be remade by scientific treatment, while Holmes held men's passions essentially unchanging.
A difference in moral priorities: Holmes prized the deterrence of crime as punishment's purpose, while Godwin prized giving each offender his individual desert.
A difference in empirical assumptions: both ranked individualized justice as morally higher, but Holmes judged it beyond the reach of human courts.
A difference in value premises: Holmes held that tailoring punishment to the individual offender would itself be a morally inferior form of justice.

items.stem: On Sowell's reading, Holmes shared Godwin's view that tailoring punishment to the individual offender, rather than to the general category of the crime, would be the morally higher standard of justice.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, Godwin held punishment to be inimical to the improvement of the mind. What reasoning does the chapter report for this claim?
options: Human courts lack the knowledge to weigh every circumstance of a case, so punishment inevitably falls on men who could not have acted otherwise.
Being punished breeds resentment against society in the offender, hardening him against the very lessons the punishment was meant to impress on him.
No two crimes are ever alike, so punishing by the general category of the crime treats offenders of very different qualities as if the same.
Incentives distract a person from the genuine reasons that make one kind of conduct preferable, and those reasons are what ought to govern behavior.

items.stem: According to the chapter, when no one can any longer state the reason behind a standing rule of law, what did Blackstone say the law will do?
options: Presume the rule well founded, so long as nothing in it is flatly contrary to reason
Treat the rule as lapsed, since a rule whose reason cannot be stated is not truly law
Refer the rule to the legislature, which alone can re-enact it on freshly stated grounds
Leave the rule's force to each judge's assessment of its usefulness in the case at hand

items.stem: The chapter presents two opposed accounts of how good law comes into being. Which contrast between them does Sowell draw?
options: Law as principles fixed in human nature and open to discovery by any careful mind, versus law as convention that varies arbitrarily from one society to the next
Law as the legacy of the great minds of earlier ages, whose wisdom today's judges cannot equal, versus law as the ongoing work of the best minds of the present
Law as each judge's settled sense of what is fair in the case at hand, versus law as the strict letter of whatever statutes a legislature has enacted
Law as the distilled experience of vast numbers of people across many generations, versus law as the deliberate work of a few minds of exceptional learning

items.stem: The chapter reports that thinkers in the unconstrained vision reject the ideal of the judge as a neutral transmitter of process principles. On the account Sowell presents, why?
options: Since no interpretation of a text can ever be neutral, a court is free to reach whatever result its members would prefer the law to produce, there being nothing left to constrain the choice
Those who framed long-standing rules of process meant them to burden the groups they disfavor, so a judge who applies such rules today knowingly renews a deliberate original wrong
Written constitutions and statutes carry no genuine authority over a present-day court, so the enacted text deserves nothing more than a respectful nod while results are selected
Where rules of process fall unevenly on different groups, the neutrality of principles and judge alike is held illusory, so the substantive choices a ruling makes should be faced openly

items.stem: According to the chapter, in locating the life of the law in experience rather than logic, Holmes largely denied that law contains any logic and that the great minds of the past contributed anything of substance to it.
options: True
False

items.stem: In the constrained vision as the chapter describes it, what is a right?
options: An entitlement belonging to each person as an acknowledgment of that person's humanity, held for the holder's own benefit
A legal boundary within which people decide for themselves, exempt from official second-guessing of their choices
A guarantee that public authorities will furnish whatever assistance the exercise of the right requires
A claim whose standing depends on how much it matters to the particular person who asserts it

items.stem: On the constrained conception of rights as the chapter presents it, a right of free speech is an exemption from public authority, and it implies no duty on the authorities to make speaking possible.
options: True
False

items.stem: In the unconstrained vision as the chapter describes it, freedom of speech stands far above property among rights. What, on the chapter's account, gives speech that standing?
options: That vision declines to count property as a right at all, leaving speech without a rival claim to stand above
Speech does more than property to keep the process of testing truth alive, so protecting it benefits society most
The ranking flips the constrained vision's own, which puts property first for the economic process it keeps running
A right's weight is its worth to those who exercise it, and speech is universal where property is unevenly spread

items.stem: The chapter describes a conception of rights on which a person's speech can be unfree even though nothing the person might say is forbidden or penalized by government. What makes that judgment possible, according to the chapter?
options: A refusal by the authorities to supply a forum counts, on this conception, as itself an act of public authority against speech
The right is judged by what its holder can actually do with it, so speech priced beyond the speaker's means fails the test
An exemption nobody can afford to use fails as an exemption, so even the process conception registers the unfreedom
Rights on this conception are absolute, so any practical hindrance to exercising one, public or private, violates it outright

items.stem: According to the chapter, Godwin and Condorcet held the unconstrained vision and yet supported property rights and laissez-faire. What pitfall does Sowell say their case illustrates?
options: Confusing the moral duties a vision prescribes with the political duties it would enforce
Assuming that every thinker must fit cleanly into one of the two visions
Mechanically mapping the two visions onto the political left and right
Reading a thinker's vision off the warmth of their language about rights

items.stem: According to the chapter, which statement about rights holds in both visions alike?
options: Rights derive from justice and prevail as trumps over every competing consideration
Rights are ranked by their relative importance to the individuals who exercise them
Rights are affirmed, and in neither tradition are they treated as absolute
Rights are zones of immunity from public authority, differing between the visions only in scope

items.stem: On Sowell's account, a writer who defends property rights and rejects any government direction of the economy presumably holds the constrained vision.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter notes that twentieth-century schemes of transfer to the poor came from Milton Friedman as well as from George Bernard Shaw. On Sowell's account, why does the direction of such a proposal fail to reveal its proposer's vision?
options: Because the visions differ only over means, one preferring voluntary almsgiving where the other prefers transfers organized through the machinery of government
Because the two visions take no position on transfers to the poor, dividing instead over individual rights and the historical development of the law
Because humane provision comes from both visions; what marks the unconstrained case is grounding the transfer in justice, a share owed rather than given
Because both men combined elements of the two visions, so that the chapter declines to place either of them cleanly within one tradition

items.stem: After a blight ruins a third of the plots in a growers' cooperative, two officers address the winter meeting. The stores officer moves to double the winter issue of seed and meal to every grower whose plot failed, though the store can bear such an issue for one season only. The officer wants the amount set by a published schedule, so much per plot lost and nothing weighed beyond that, holds that no grower has a claim on the common store — the blight was nobody's doing — and finishes on the shame of a prosperous cooperative watching its neighbors go under. The rounds clerk votes against the motion while allowing that the sums are about right. What a failed grower receives, the clerk argues, is already that grower's portion, held by membership in the common work, and the ledger should show a debt discharged rather than a gift made; sacks handed over under the name of relief, the clerk warns, teach receivers to bow and givers to preen. The motion carries, and the minutes record the clerk as the only officer against it. On Sowell's account of the two visions, which placement fits the two officers?
options: Both officers from the unconstrained vision
Both officers from the constrained vision
The stores officer from the unconstrained vision; the rounds clerk from the constrained
The stores officer from the constrained vision; the rounds clerk from the unconstrained

items.stem: A federation of village reading rooms promises in its charter that any member may borrow from any room's shelves with no custodian to question the choice. At the annual conclave, two trustees speak for a proposed courier round to carry books to members in the hill villages, where the nearest room is a day's walk. The first trustee, a bookbinder, allows that the round would be the costliest line in the federation's accounts, then puts the case plainly: for hill members the borrowing clause stands on paper only, a member who cannot reach a shelf has been denied the thing itself, and the federation owes them the round — and should any custodian grudge the shelf space the carrier takes, the members' borrowing matters more than a custodian's arrangement of a room. The second trustee, a mill clerk, seconds the round as a kindness well worth its cost in a good year, though nothing owed is at stake: the clause promises only that no custodian may question or refuse a member at the shelf, a line never to be crossed, under which books no committee would have picked have found their readers and quarrels have died in the open air. The mill clerk closes by reading the borrowing clause aloud and calling it the finest sentence the founders ever wrote. On Sowell's account of the two visions, which placement fits the two trustees?
options: Both trustees from the unconstrained vision
The bookbinder from the unconstrained vision; the mill clerk from the constrained
The bookbinder from the constrained vision; the mill clerk from the unconstrained
Both trustees from the constrained vision

items.stem: A carters' lodge debates provision for members laid up by injuries taken on the road. The tally keeper moves a compulsory levy: a fixed cut of every member's haulage earnings, pooled and assigned by the trustees so that an injured carter draws a settled share. A member hurt in the common work, the keeper argues, holds a claim on the lodge's earnings by membership itself, and leaving that claim to whatever a collection plate gathers wrongs the injured twice — though the keeper admits the first year's rate would be guesswork. The gate warden rises against the levy and against any trustee reaching into a member's purse, while not holding that the injured are owed less: everything a carter earns on the lodge's common roads, the warden says, is held in trust for the rest, and a laid-up member's portion is as real as any debt — but members brought to reason on the matter will pay that portion unasked, and compulsion only keeps them paying for the wrong reason while putting off the day they pay for the right one. The levy fails on a show of hands, and the warden moves that no motion touching a member's purse be brought again that year. On Sowell's account of the two visions, which placement fits the two speakers?
options: The tally keeper from the constrained vision; the gate warden from the unconstrained
Both speakers from the constrained vision
Both speakers from the unconstrained vision
The tally keeper from the unconstrained vision; the gate warden from the constrained

items.stem: Which notion does the chapter place at the core of social justice, as the unconstrained vision conceives it?
options: That every member of a society is owed a share of its wealth proportioned to what that member contributed to producing it
That every member of a society is owed some share of the wealth it produces, whether or not the member helped produce it
That every member of a society is owed a decent minimum of its wealth, provided the member contributes what work he or she can
That every member of a society is owed an identical share of its wealth, full equality being the whole tradition's demand

items.stem: Smith and Mill, the chapter notes, took part in efforts to help the poor, and Burke and Smith joined Godwin and Condorcet in the campaign against slavery. On Sowell's account, what then distinguishes the unconstrained vision's position toward the less fortunate?
options: It holds that a transfer to the poor pays a debt owed in justice, rather than answering a call of humanity alone
It grounds the poor's claim in the labor they themselves spent producing the wealth of their society
It urges that voluntary almsgiving be enlarged until the poor receive full shares rather than crusts
It calls for relief of the poor to be organized through the machinery of government rather than left to individual conscience

items.stem: The chapter reports that Bellamy's Looking Backward objected not only that the poor received crusts but that the crusts arrived under the name of charity. Within the unconstrained vision as Sowell presents it, why was the name itself an offense?
options: It presented as voluntary a transfer that, in this vision, only the compulsion of law could make into an act of justice
It denied the poor the credit for producing the wealth, when their own labor was what entitled them to far more
It recast a debt as a gift, the rich showing generosity with what was not theirs, the poor taking their due as a favor
It advertised how little was being given; full shares handed over under the very same name would have carried no offense

items.stem: According to the chapter, schemes for transferring income to the poor have presumably come from the unconstrained tradition alone, since that is the vision which makes relief of the less fortunate a matter of justice rather than of charity.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, what do the advocates of 'social justice' and Hayek each understand that term to name?
options: Its advocates understand it as a result, which they favor; Hayek reads it as a process, which he rejects.
Both sides understand it as a result; the advocates hold that result reachable, while Hayek holds it unreachable and so not worth pursuing.
Both sides understand it as a process; the two camps divide over which features a process must have to count as just.
Its advocates understand it as a process, which they favor; Hayek reads it as a result, which he rejects.

items.stem: The chapter quotes Hayek calling it absurd to demand justice of a spontaneous order. As the chapter presents his argument, what grounds that charge?
options: Meeting the demand would oblige government to make discretionary awards inside domains once fenced off from its power, eroding the rule of law.
The shares such an order hands out come, over time, to track what each participant has contributed, so its results already meet the only workable test of justice.
Whatever hardships the order leaves some people with are outweighed by the general prosperity it generates, which empties the demand of any practical force.
No one intends or foresees who ends up with what under such an order, so there is no agent whose dealings could be just or unjust, only a personified 'society'.

items.stem: On the chapter's reading, Hayek's objection to the demand for social justice falls on the process that meeting the demand would require, not on the pattern of results its advocates hope to see.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter sets Hayek's case against social justice beside Rawls's case for it. According to Sowell, how do the two arguments stand to each other?
options: Neither answers the other, but the silence is tactical: each side judged that engaging the rival literature head-on would lend it a standing it had not yet earned.
Each abstracts away what the other treats as primary: Rawls the processes, to reason about goals; Hayek the goals, to reason about processes. Neither takes up the other's question.
They meet on one shared question, whether freedom or justice ranks higher, and give opposite answers: Hayek puts freedom ahead of justice, and Rawls puts justice ahead of freedom.
Hayek concedes the results Rawls wants would be just but denies they can be reached, while Rawls concedes the dangers Hayek names but counts justice worth the risk of them.

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.1.1: Identify the kinds of evidence Flynn offers for his claim that Singapore delivers the world's best healthcare at the world's lowest cost — published outcome rankings, per-person spending comparisons, and a week of first-hand observation undertaken because the numbers seemed too good to be true to a self-described cynical economist.
learning_objectives.1.2: Explain what Flynn's pairing of outcome rankings with spending comparisons is meant to establish: that the United States pays far more per person than Singapore and still trails it on every outcome he cites, so the gap is a failure on both axes rather than a price-for-quality trade-off — and that the countries usually offered as US models, Canada and the United Kingdom, also spend far more than Singapore.
learning_objectives.1.3: Explain how, on Flynn's reading, the cabbie's complaint that he has to go to the gym because he would bear much of the cost of developing diabetes is evidence the system works rather than a flaw: personal cost exposure, explicitly not a government mandate, produces the sustained preventive effort US professionals mostly just talk about.
learning_objectives.1.4: Explain why Flynn treats the US origin of Singapore's components — price tags and health savings accounts, developed in America decades earlier — together with their use by Whole Foods and by Indiana, as answering his opening question of whether the approach could work back home: the US merely invented, while Singapore implemented.
learning_objectives.1.5: Explain why Flynn expects reform on Singapore's model to be thankless but not fruitless: beneficiaries stop perceiving a good system and complain about the very incentives that make it work, while the payoff he claims accrues whether or not anyone notices.

Chapter 1 → The Cabbie's Tale.text: A sceptical economist flew out for a week because the reported pairing of top results with the lowest spending seemed implausible. He found a well-run neighbourhood clinic whose staff saw nothing remarkable in it, and a driver who resented exercising because he would meet much of the cost of falling ill — pressure no rule imposed. The components, he notes, were American inventions that another country merely applied. Reform, he predicts, would go uncredited without going unrewarded.

items.stem: According to the chapter, why did Flynn fly to Singapore to examine its healthcare system in person?
options: No published figures on Singapore's system existed, so he had to gather the basic data himself.
He was convinced the statistics were false and went to document the system's hidden flaws.
The statistics he had read seemed too good to be true, and he wanted to confirm they were not lying.
Singapore's health ministry had invited him on an official visit to evaluate its neighborhood polyclinics.

items.stem: According to the chapter, on what kinds of evidence does Flynn rest his claim that Singapore delivers the world's best healthcare at the world's lowest cost?
options: Published outcome rankings, a week of observing the system himself, and cost projections from his own economic model.
Published outcome rankings, per-person spending comparisons, and the results of Whole Foods' and Indiana's programs.
Published outcome rankings, per-person spending comparisons, and a week of observing the system himself.
A week of observing the system himself, per-person spending comparisons, and an official evaluation by its health ministry.

items.stem: Flynn reports gathering first-hand evidence during his week in Singapore. According to the chapter, which of the following was part of that effort?
options: Meeting the health ministry's leadership to review the government's own official outcome statistics.
Comparing the annual budgets of several polyclinics with those of comparable clinics in the United States.
Touring the country's leading private hospitals rather than its government-run neighborhood clinics.
Asking doctors, former public health officials, cabbies, and shop clerks what they thought of the system.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the Bloomberg Businessweek ranking Flynn cites is presumably a measure of per-person healthcare spending rather than of health outcomes.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, how does per-person healthcare spending in the United States compare with Singapore's?
options: The US spends about one and a half times as much per person as Singapore.
The US and Singapore spend about the same amount per person on healthcare.
The US spends somewhat less per person than Singapore does.
The US spends nearly three times as much per person as Singapore.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the United States edges out Singapore on at least one of the three measures of healthcare effectiveness that Flynn calls most important, even though it trails on the others.
options: True
False

items.stem: Flynn presents Singapore's outcome rankings alongside per-person spending comparisons. According to the chapter, what is that pairing meant to establish about the United States?
options: That its extra spending buys strengths the three headline measures miss and only a broader index can reveal.
That its results would rise to Singapore's level if it were willing to spend more per person on healthcare.
That Singapore's low spending is offset by weaker results on some measures, so each country trades price against quality.
That it pays far more than Singapore yet gets worse results, so the gap is not a matter of paying more for better care.

items.stem: Suppose Flynn had reported only the outcome rankings, with the United States trailing Singapore on each measure, and said nothing about spending. According to the chapter's line of argument, which reply to Flynn's case would that leave open?
options: That the outcome statistics are too good to be true and cannot be taken at face value.
That the US is simply spending less than Singapore and getting the level of care it pays for.
That Singapore's results rest on policies foreign to the US that could not be transplanted here.
That the three measures are too narrow to judge a whole system, so the ranking proves little on its own.

items.stem: According to the chapter, why does Flynn extend the spending comparison beyond the United States to Canada and the United Kingdom?
options: They spend about what Singapore spends per person, which leaves the United States as the lone high-cost outlier.
They rank ahead of Singapore on Bloomberg's broader index, which makes them the fairer benchmark for outcomes.
They, rather than the United States, developed the price tags and savings accounts Singapore later implemented.
They are the usual models offered for US reform, and even they spend far more per person than Singapore.

items.stem: According to the chapter, how did Flynn react once the cabbie explained why he hated Singapore's healthcare system?
options: He pressed the cabbie for other flaws that outsiders might have missed
He smiled, taking what the cabbie called a problem to be an answer
He told the cabbie that regular exercise was a small price for his health
He noted the complaint as his first sign that the statistics had been oversold

items.stem: According to the chapter, when Flynn asked whether the government forced him to go to the gym, the cabbie said no; he went because he would have to pay much of the cost himself if he got fat and developed diabetes.
options: True
False

items.stem: On Flynn's reading, why does the cabbie's complaint count as evidence that Singapore's system is working rather than as a report of a flaw in it?
options: What he resents is an exercise rule that the government applies evenly to every citizen
What he resents is trivial next to the treatment costs he would otherwise face
What he resents is the sort of thing people find to complain about under any arrangement
What he resents is the sustained preventive effort the system exists to produce

items.stem: According to the chapter, what struck Flynn about the cabbie's habit was that Singapore had found a way to get an ordinary citizen to comply with a government exercise requirement, something US healthcare professionals had only talked about doing.
options: True
False

items.stem: A delivery company changes one thing about breakdowns: when a van fails on its route from a fault the driver could have caught on a morning walkaround, the tow and the lost day come out of that driver's quarterly bonus. Six months in, a consultant asks four drivers what they think of it. Ben: 'I hate it. Since the bonus thing my supervisor has us sign a twenty-point sheet every morning, and I do every line, because he is at the gate checking twice a week.' Cal: 'I hate it. In March a fuel pump quit on me halfway through my route, no warning at all, and the tow and the lost day came out of my bonus anyway.' Ana: 'I hate it. Belts, hoses, tires, my own routine now, every day before I pull out. It beats paying for a tow, but I have been late to my first stop twice.' Dee: 'It's fine. The shop fixes things properly now instead of patching them, my van has not been off the road once all year, and it has never cost me a cent.' Which driver's response is the counterpart of the cabbie's in Flynn's chapter?
options: Cal
Ana
Dee
Ben

items.stem: A housing co-op has long paid for burst-pipe repairs out of its shared reserve and has run a well-attended winterizing workshop every October. Two years ago the board changed one thing about billing: a unit now pays for repairs to its own frozen pipes. The workshop continues. At this year's annual meeting a resident who says she has no interest in home maintenance tells the board she hates the change, because every October she now has to crawl under her deck to shut off the outside tap and drain the line. She adds that the workshop taught her how years ago. Several neighbors nod. The board asks what to do. If the board reasons about her the way Flynn reasons about the cabbie, what does it do?
options: Drop the billing change and expand the workshop
Leave the billing change and the workshop as they are
Make the October shutoff a bylaw with a fine for missing it
Return frozen-pipe repairs to the shared reserve

items.stem: Four colleges at one university want final grades submitted on time. At Ashby a late grade sheet costs the instructor a hundred dollars a day, itemized as a line on the next pay stub, and instructors grumble that they now drop everything in exam week. At Bell nothing is deducted; the registrar no longer covers for late grades, so a late instructor sorts out every resulting enrollment hold, and instructors grumble that they now drop everything in exam week. At Cole the dean circulates a memo every term on the importance of timeliness and presents a plaque to the most punctual department at the faculty meeting, and instructors grumble about the memo. At Dunn a staff member in the records office quietly handles whatever late grades produce, as she has for years; nobody is charged and nothing is said, and instructors do not grumble at all. A visiting economist who reasons as Flynn does about the cabbie is asked which college has built what the cabbie was describing. Which does she name?
options: Cole
Ashby
Bell
Dunn

items.stem: According to the chapter, where does Flynn say the major components of Singapore's healthcare system, such as price tags and health savings accounts, were originally developed?
options: In Canada and the United Kingdom, the countries often proposed as models for US reform
In the United States, in many cases decades before Singapore made use of them
In the United States, but only recently and in response to Singapore's results
In Singapore, by officials designing a system to suit its own population

items.stem: According to the chapter, when Flynn says the United States 'merely invented, while Singapore implemented,' the inventions he has in mind are mainly medical technologies, such as drugs and devices, that Singapore then adopted.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, Flynn went to Singapore wanting to know, among other things, whether what it was doing 'might also work back home.' After returning, he discovered that Singapore's major components had originally been developed in the United States. How does Flynn treat that discovery in relation to his question?
options: As answering it yes: the ideas are already American and should have produced the result here first, so all that is missing is implementation
As answering it no: Singapore succeeded only by reworking American ideas that had already failed at home, so re-importing them would repeat that failure
As changing it: since the ideas were American, Flynn argues the United States deserves the credit for Singapore's results rather than needing to copy them
As leaving it open: who invented a policy says nothing about whether it works, so Flynn falls back on the outcome statistics to settle the question

items.stem: According to the chapter, having argued that Singapore's components were invented in America, Flynn then points to Whole Foods Market and to former Indiana governors as Americans who, he says, have already implemented such policies. What work does this citation do in his argument?
options: It supplies his main evidence: detailed cost and outcome figures from these programmes, which replace the Singapore statistics as proof
It concedes a limit: private firms and state governments can adopt such policies, but Flynn doubts a national system could
It names the inventors: Flynn credits Mackey, Daniels and Pence with originally developing price tags and health savings accounts
It moves the claim from 'could work here' to 'has already been done here': Americans can implement, not only invent

items.stem: According to the chapter, Flynn writes that the United States 'merely invented, while Singapore implemented.' Which reading best captures the contrast he is drawing?
options: The policies were developed in America as voluntary options, while Singapore made them work by having the government compel their use
The policies were developed in America but never used to build its healthcare system, while Singapore built its system on them
The policies were developed in America in rough form, and only Singapore's later refinements turned them into something that could work
The policies were developed in America and adopted in both countries, but Singapore has run them more effectively than the United States

items.stem: At the close of the chapter, Flynn tells anyone who signs on to implement Singapore-style reform in the United States what to expect. According to the chapter, what does he predict?
options: Reform will probably be fruitless, but reformers would still be thanked.
Reform will probably be thankless, but it won't be fruitless.
Reform will be appreciated once Americans notice how much better it is.
Reform will be resisted until the government mandates regular exercise.

items.stem: According to the chapter, Flynn expects that a few years after a Singapore-style reform took effect, most Americans would probably remember how bad the old system had been and thank the reformers for the change.
options: True
False

items.stem: Flynn closes the chapter by predicting that reform on Singapore's model would probably be 'thankless' but would not be 'fruitless.' According to the chapter, what distinction is he drawing?
options: Whether Americans invent the components is separate from whether they implement them.
Whether the reform pays off depends on whether people notice and appreciate it.
Whether people complain about the reform shows whether it has failed to deliver.
Whether people credit the reform is separate from whether it delivers its benefits.

items.stem: Flynn writes that 'a fish doesn't know that it's living in water,' and earlier he describes a senior polyclinic nurse who could not understand why anybody would be impressed by her clinic. According to the chapter, what point do these two illustrations make?
options: People complain about a system's incentives even when the incentives work.
People who benefit from a well-run system stop noticing how good it is.
People resent being photographed or studied by outsiders.
People in poor neighborhoods have access to modern, well-run public clinics.

items.stem: In his closing prediction, Flynn writes that, 'as with my cabbie in Singapore, people will find things to complain about.' According to the chapter, what does invoking the cabbie add to his prediction that reform would be thankless?
options: Some beneficiaries would find genuine flaws in the system that outsiders cannot see.
Some beneficiaries would need a government mandate before they changed their habits.
Some beneficiaries would resent the very incentives that make the system work.
Some beneficiaries would stop noticing the system because they were used to it.

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.2.1: Explain how the chapter establishes that Singapore's rise since independence was exceptional: the reversal of its standing relative to the United States, matched by comparable gains in health and environment, and its ranking as the richest nation once oil, banking and gambling economies are set aside.
learning_objectives.2.2: Explain how the chapter makes the PAP's electoral dominance the enabling condition for Lee's long-horizon policymaking, including the feedback loop by which policy success extended that dominance.
learning_objectives.2.3: Explain how meritocratic schooling and integrated, owner-occupied public housing were designed to give every ethnic and religious group an equal chance at advancement and a real stake in the economy.
learning_objectives.2.4: Apply Lee's carrot-and-stick logic for escaping the middle-income trap to a novel case, predicting whether a proposed policy pairing would make low-productivity production unprofitable enough to push firms to upgrade.
learning_objectives.2.5: Explain the role of the Central Provident Fund in Singapore's development: how compulsory saving at high combined rates supplied domestic capital in place of borrowing from foreign investors, and why Lee put its investment under engineers and technocrats rather than bankers.
learning_objectives.2.6: Explain how Singapore's tax design — low, flat, almost no deductions, with credits only for research and development, training, high-efficiency equipment and intellectual property — makes innovation, investment and entrepreneurship the only route by which a firm can reduce its taxable income.

Chapter 2 → The Colony of Singapore.text: A trading settlement founded under a British company in the early nineteenth century, drawing labourers from China and elsewhere, it prospered by sitting at the narrow point every east-west voyage through the region must pass. Independence arrived late and poor, with income per head roughly a fifth of the American figure. Within half a century that relationship had inverted, and among countries with varied economies none was richer.

Chapter 2 → Rich, Green, and Prosperous.text: Gains were not confined to income. Where cholera and typhoid once circulated and waste ran untreated into the water, the city is now unusually clean and densely planted, topping assessments of urban greenery. Most residents own their homes, a far larger share than in America, and a tenth of households hold wealth above a million dollars, behind only an oil state and a banking centre.

Chapter 2 → How Did Things Get So Good?.text: The explanation offered is governance. The governing party won by margins wide enough, on this account, to free the first prime minister from bargaining with rivals, factions or interest groups, leaving him to pick whichever policies he judged best. Success then made that party more popular still and secured further terms — a loop the chapter credits with letting ministers spend their time solving problems rather than campaigning, and so plan further ahead.

Chapter 2 → Policies for Prosperity?.text: Schooling was made excellent and advancement made to follow measured achievement, so every community shared one route upward. Flats were built with subsidy and then sold rather than let, with quotas keeping each block mixed, which gave residents both an asset and a stake. To escape stalling at low-wage manufacturing, owners were offered generous help buying better machinery and training staff, while a charge on wages made staying cheap unprofitable.

Chapter 2 → Savings and Wealth.text: A compulsory savings scheme, the Central Provident Fund, was inherited from the colonial administration and expanded until worker and employer each put in a quarter of pay — an extraordinary rate by rich-world standards.
