bank_meta.chapter_title: Why Is the US Healthcare System Doing So Badly?

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.6.1: Identify the three parties in the chapter's framework and the payment flow that defines third-party payment: the patient as first party, the provider as second, and the payer -- Medicare, Medicaid or private insurance, involved in neither providing nor receiving care -- as third, with payments flowing from third parties to second parties for services delivered to first parties, rather than directly from consumer to producer as when hiring a lawyer or a mechanic.
learning_objectives.6.2: Explain how, on the chapter's account, the route a payment takes determines whether a provider must care about the customer: in a two-party market first parties spending their own money take their business elsewhere, so competition forces a retailer to deliver value rather than poor service at inflated prices, and routing healthcare payment through third parties removes exactly that pressure.
learning_objectives.6.3: Explain how the chapter's motorised-wheelchair example shows that free to individuals does not mean free to society: because a third party -- the taxpayer -- foots the bill, the user gets the benefits while bearing none of the costs, so costs and benefits become isolated from one another and people acquire more equipment than anyone facing the true cost would.
learning_objectives.6.4: Explain why the chapter calls physicians pushovers on requests like wheelchairs and antibiotics: approval costs the doctor nothing while denial is time-consuming under patient-volume pressure and risks losing the patient, complaints, or a malpractice suit -- an asymmetry whose large-scale form is defensive medicine, with unnecessary imaging, blood panels, biopsies and prescriptions whose costs are dumped onto third parties.
learning_objectives.6.5: Apply the chapter's analysis of share-of-volume compensation to a novel case, predicting whether an intermediary paid a roughly fixed share of the spending it processes will police that spending or grow it -- the reasoning by which the chapter rejects as short-term thinking the obvious expectation that insurers profit by denying claims.
learning_objectives.6.6: Explain why, on the chapter's account, government insurers cannot control costs even without a profit motive: as legal entitlements they must lean in favour of paying claims, and their one lever -- cutting reimbursement rates -- is offset by providers who respond by billing a larger number of procedures, or a different set, extracting as much as before.
learning_objectives.6.7: Given a novel payment arrangement, determine which party is positioned to restrain wasteful spending, by locating where the incentive to economise and the information to judge necessity coincide, as against the party that merely holds payment authority -- the chapter's diagnosis being a system that entrusts payment decisions to those with the least information while the two informed parties have no incentive to restrain.

Chapter 6 → Why Is the US Healthcare Sys.text: The chapter blames the route money travels. Patient, provider and payer are numbered first, second and third; in healthcare the payment runs from the third to the second for something the first received. Where a buyer pays directly, a seller who offers poor value loses that buyer, and competition disciplines it. Insert a payer who neither receives nor provides the service and that discipline disappears, which the chapter says is the road American healthcare took.

Chapter 6 → The False Promise of \"Free\.text: Advertising for subsidised medical equipment leads with what it costs the user rather than with what it does, because almost nothing is as persuasive as nothing. The claim is accurate and the conclusion still wrong: costless to the person is not costless to everyone, since a payer absorbs the difference, and here that payer is the public. What looks like a gift is a transfer whose price nobody at the counter sees.

Chapter 6 → First-Party Incentives.text: Take the price away from the person choosing and you take away the comparison. Someone weighing a purchase against a short remaining need would decline it at full price and accept it at none, so the equipment is ordered and the public billed. The chapter's point is not extravagance but severance: benefits accrue to the chooser while costs land elsewhere, and once the two are detached there is nothing left to weigh.

Chapter 6 → Second- and Third-Party Ince.text: Saying yes costs a clinician nothing; saying no costs time, goodwill, possibly the patient, possibly a lawsuit. That asymmetry, the chapter argues, produces agreement rather than scrutiny, and at scale becomes tests and prescriptions ordered to be safe. Nor will the payers restrain it: one earns a share of whatever volume it handles, so shrinking the volume shrinks the earnings, and the other is an entitlement that must lean toward paying.

Chapter 6 → Who's in the Know?.text: Authority and knowledge sit in different places. The patient and the clinician know the case; the distant payer decides. Cutting what it pays per procedure does not help, because providers answer a lower rate with more procedures or different ones. So judgement rests with the party least able to judge, while the two who could judge have no reason to economise, and the waste survives everyone's good intentions.

items.stem: In the chapter's framework, when a patient visits a doctor, who is the 'third party'?
options: The patient, who requests the visit and receives the services that are ultimately being paid for
A payer such as Medicare, Medicaid, or private insurance, which neither provides nor receives the care
A regulator that inspects providers and certifies the quality of the services they deliver
The provider, such as a doctor, hospital, imaging center, or lab, that delivers the services being billed
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Why Is the US Healthcare System Doing So Badly?

items.stem: According to the chapter, under the third-party payment arrangement that dominates US healthcare, how does the money flow?
options: From first parties directly to second parties, as when a customer hires a lawyer or a mechanic
From first parties to third parties, which then provide the services the first parties have paid for
From second parties to third parties, to reimburse the claims that the third parties have approved
From third parties to second parties, for services provided by second parties to first parties
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Why Is the US Healthcare System Doing So Badly?

items.stem: According to the chapter, hiring a lawyer or a mechanic presumably works the same way as US healthcare: in both cases, the payment reaches the producer by way of a third party rather than directly from the consumer.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Why Is the US Healthcare System Doing So Badly?

items.stem: According to the chapter, what forces second parties in a competitive two-party market to care about the interests of first parties?
options: Government oversight, since regulators step in against any seller that delivers poor service at inflated prices.
Competition among second parties, since dissatisfied first parties spending their own money go elsewhere.
Professional ethics, since sellers who mistreat their customers face censure from others in their own industry.
The threat of lawsuits, since first parties can recover damages from sellers who overcharge or underdeliver.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Why Is the US Healthcare System Doing So Badly?

items.stem: The chapter observes that Walmart did not become the world's biggest retailer by delivering lousy service at massively inflated prices -- had it gone that route, it would quickly have gone bankrupt. Within the chapter's argument, what is this observation meant to establish?
options: When buyers spend their own money, competition forces sellers to deliver value, a pressure the third-party payment route removes.
Retailing is simply better managed than medicine, so the remedy is recruiting proven business executives into hospital administration.
Large scale is what disciplines prices, so consolidating providers into national chains would lower healthcare costs as retailing's fell.
Providers are unusually greedy compared with retailers, whose thin margins leave no room for exploiting their own customers.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Why Is the US Healthcare System Doing So Badly?

items.stem: The chapter claims a retailer that delivered lousy service at massively inflated prices would quickly go bankrupt, yet says the US healthcare system has gone exactly that route and survived. On the chapter's account, what explains the difference?
options: Healthcare's money flows from third parties to providers, so the customer's ability to walk away no longer disciplines the seller.
Licensing keeps would-be competitors out of medicine, so dissatisfied patients have no rival providers to turn to.
Demand for care is a matter of life and death, so patients must accept whatever terms providers set no matter how they are treated.
Patients cannot judge the quality of care the way shoppers judge merchandise, so poor service goes undetected rather than unpunished.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Why Is the US Healthcare System Doing So Badly?

items.stem: According to the chapter, healthcare providers can get away with lousy service at inflated prices presumably because, unlike retailers, they face no competing second parties for their patients to choose from.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 6 → Why Is the US Healthcare System Doing So Badly?

items.stem: The chapter reports that Hoveround's motorized wheelchairs really are free or nearly free to the elderly customers who receive them. On its account, who actually bears the cost of those machines?
options: The customer, who repays the cost gradually through higher out-of-pocket charges on later medical care
Hoveround itself, which absorbs the cost of the machines as a marketing expense to grow its customer base
The taxpayer, the third party that ends up paying for the machines by way of Medicare
Mostly the customers themselves, since the chapter dismisses the promise of 'free' as advertising hyperbole

items.stem: The chapter argues that people end up buying more Hoverounds than they ever would if they faced the machines' true cost. On its account, what produces that extra buying?
options: Costs and benefits are severed: the user keeps all the gains while the taxpayer covers the bill, so nothing prompts the buyer to weigh the two
Physicians steer their patients toward the machines in order to enlarge the volume of services they are able to bill to Medicare
The advertising overstates what the machines can actually deliver, leading customers to expect benefits the product cannot really provide
Medicare's payments reduce the real resources it takes to produce each machine, so the equipment genuinely becomes cheaper for society as a whole

items.stem: Since the chapter reports that nine out of ten Hoveround customers get their machines for little or nothing, those machines are presumably close to costless to society as well.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter describes a machine that would have seen only about four weeks' use, yet would have been billed to Medicare at its full cost. What is this instance meant to establish?
options: That elderly customers usually misjudge how much use they will get from mobility equipment, so demand is inflated by honest error
That a buyer facing the full price and knowing their own situation would decline a purchase that sails through when a third party pays
That advertising the equipment as free is deceptive, since the machines are in fact billed to Medicare at their full price
That Medicare ought to prorate what it pays to the period of actual use rather than reimbursing the full purchase price of the equipment

items.stem: According to the chapter, doctors are incentivized to be 'pushovers' when patients request items such as motorized wheelchairs. Which of the following states a reason the chapter gives?
options: Doctors genuinely believe that nearly every patient who asks for such a device has a lasting medical need for it.
Verifying that a patient truly needs the device takes time the doctor does not have, while approving the request takes none.
Doctors earn a commission from the device maker on each motorized wheelchair they prescribe, so approvals raise their income.
Insurers direct doctors to approve such requests because processing a denial creates more paperwork than paying the claim.

items.stem: The chapter supposes, for the sake of argument, that a detailed mobility exam could be done quickly and at low cost - and argues that a doctor would still lean toward approving a wheelchair request. According to the chapter, why?
options: Hospital administrators push doctors to keep approval rates high so that the facility's overall billing volume keeps growing.
A refused patient will probably seek approval from another doctor, and the refusing physician may lose that patient for good.
State regulators can sanction a physician whose denial is later judged to have blocked medically necessary equipment.
Medicare rules treat mobility devices as entitlements, leaving the physician no legal authority to refuse a qualifying request.

items.stem: According to the chapter, physicians go along with patients' demands for antibiotics to treat colds because acquiescing is easier than dealing with complaints to hospital administrators or the threat of baseless but costly malpractice lawsuits.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter calls a physician's decision to practice defensive medicine - ordering extra imaging, blood panels, biopsies, and prescriptions - 'understandable.' According to the chapter, what calculation makes it understandable?
options: Extra tests raise a practice's billing revenue, and under fee-for-service payment more procedures mean more physician income.
Upsetting a patient could cost the physician dearly, while the whole cost of the useless care is passed along to a third party.
Medical training drills physicians to exhaust every diagnostic avenue, so ordering everything reflects professional thoroughness.
The extra tests sometimes catch dangerous conditions early, so their medical benefit outweighs the annoyance and expense involved.

items.stem: According to the chapter, how do private health insurance companies actually make their profit?
options: Fees collected from providers for handling their billing paperwork
About five percent of the gross medical billing they process
Investment earnings on premiums held until claims come due
Whatever remains of the premiums after the year's claims are paid

items.stem: According to the chapter, what do private insurers mostly rely on for larger profits year after year?
options: Drawing customers away from rival insurers
Cutting what they spend on their own operations
Raising premiums year after year
Denying a larger share of claims each year

items.stem: According to the chapter, why is it short-term thinking to expect private insurers to boost their profits by ruthlessly denying claims?
options: Because they lack the information to tell valid claims from invalid ones
Because larger profits require the billing they handle to keep growing
Because regulators oblige them to pay every claim that is medically valid
Because denied patients would defect to rival insurers that approve more freely

items.stem: According to the chapter, a private insurer's surest route to larger profits is presumably to deny as many claims as it can.
options: True
False

items.stem: A manufacturing group hands all of its employee travel to Traverline, an outside firm that books every flight and hotel and reviews each trip against the group's travel rules. Traverline is paid a small fixed share of every travel dollar it books. The board brought Traverline in after shareholders complained loudly about travel waste, its contract renews each year unless the board ends it, and each autumn Traverline proposes the size of the coming year's travel programme for the board to approve. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what should the board expect Traverline to do over the next several years?
options: Propose bigger programmes each autumn
Cut travel until the waste is gone
Refuse every doubtful trip request
Keep the programme at its present size

items.stem: The city of Ardenmoor repairs its streets and bridges from a fund whose annual size is fixed for the next ten years by the covenants of a bond issue, which no official can amend. Contractors bill the fund as repairs arise; in some years their invoices fall short of its limit and in others press against it. Kelbrook Associates reviews the invoices and pays the approved ones, earning a small fixed share of every dollar it pays out, and it won the contract on its record of rooting padded invoices out of client accounts. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what should the city expect Kelbrook to do?
options: Pay almost every invoice it gets
Slow payments to make the fund last
Strip the padding from the invoices
Push the fund's size up over time

items.stem: When the farm-equipment maker Drummond wound up its extended-service plans, the regulator required it to leave behind an escrowed fund to cover the plans' remaining claims, with anything unspent at closure returning to Drummond. Hartley Clearing, an outside firm appointed by the regulator, processes those final claims and is paid a small fixed share of every dollar it pays out of the fund. Once the last claim closes, the programme ends for good and Hartley's appointment ends with it; no claimant will ever deal with Hartley again. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what should be expected of Hartley?
options: Pay out most of what remains
Deny most of what remains
Settle each claim for less than billed
Approve small claims, fight large ones

items.stem: According to the chapter, why must government insurers such as Medicaid and Medicare 'always lean in favor of paying claims'?
options: Because their benefits are entitlements established in law
Because they can grow only by approving ever more claims
Because they employ no adjustors or investigators of claims
Because they earn a profit on the billing volume they process

items.stem: The chapter says Medicaid and Medicare try to keep a lid on costs by repeatedly cutting their reimbursement rates for specific procedures — yet it argues this tool cannot hold spending down. Why not, on its account?
options: Patients respond to the lower rates by seeking more visits, since their share of the bill shrinks
The cut lowers the price per procedure, while providers choose the number and mix billed
Congress soon restores the old rates once providers and patient groups lobby against the cuts
The cuts reach so few procedures that most of what providers bill stays at the old rates

items.stem: Flynn argues that Medicare and Medicaid are worse positioned than private insurers to say no to wasteful claims: they lack even the short-term profit motive to deny them, and as legal entitlements they must lean in favor of paying.
options: True
False

items.stem: In its discussion of reimbursement-rate cuts, the chapter remarks that 'second parties are not potted plants.' What point is the remark making?
options: Providers outnumber the field investigators that insurers can afford to send out
Providers, unlike distant insurers, see each patient's actual condition firsthand
Providers adjust what and how much they bill when their payment terms change
Providers abandon any payer whose rates stop covering the costs of their practice

items.stem: According to the chapter, who has the most information about a patient's actual condition, and where does the ultimate authority for payment approval and cost control sit?
options: The claims adjustors in the field have the most information, while approval authority sits with the treating physician
The hospital billing departments have the most information, while approval authority sits with the patient and the doctor jointly
The patient and the doctor have the most information, while approval authority sits with insurers and government payers
The government payers have the most information, while approval authority sits with the patient selecting among competing providers

items.stem: According to the chapter, even with claims adjustors in the field and lawsuits against those caught in fraud, the more than $2 trillion in claims handled each year leaves Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurers unable to discover whether most of the claims they pay are medically valid.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter's 'Who's in the Know?' discussion grants that third parties hold the ultimate authority to approve payments and control costs. Why, on its account, is that authority not enough to stop wasteful claims?
options: Operating under entitlement law, they are barred from refusing any claim that a licensed physician has signed, whatever their investigators find
Operating far from the patient, they cannot affordably gather the facts that separate needed care from waste, so they largely pay on trust
Handling too few claims to see patterns across providers, they cannot tell which second parties are systematically inflating their bills
Collecting a share of every claim they approve, they would see each denial they issue come straight out of their own annual revenue

items.stem: According to the chapter, the patient and the doctor are the two people with the most information about whether a treatment is really needed. Why does it conclude that neither of them will act as a brake on spending?
options: Because the payer's reviewers see thousands of similar cases a year, both defer to its judgment about what a condition requires
Because legal restrictions on patients' medical information keep both of them from passing what they know to the payer
Because neither can predict what the insurer will finally reimburse, both order generously while the approval window stays open
Because the bill lands on neither of them, the knowledge to judge necessity sits with parties who gain nothing by refusing

items.stem: Kestrel Parcel runs its delivery vans under the following arrangement. The drivers note what is wrong with the vans they take out each morning, and repair charges never touch their pay. Ostrander Garage determines what work each van that reaches it needs, and it invoices Kestrel's account for every job performed. Halloway Fleet Services approves or rejects every repair invoice from its office two states away, and it draws one flat yearly fee. The depot manager picks which vans go in as she works the yard, and repair charges come out of her fixed budget. Lately, invoices have been arriving for brake overhauls on vans barely a year old. Applying the chapter's analysis of payment arrangements, which party is positioned to restrain wasteful repair spending?
options: The depot manager
Ostrander Garage
Halloway Fleet Services
The drivers

items.stem: A private foundation is funding a three-year study at Ellsworth College under the following terms. The bench technicians run and calibrate every instrument daily, and the equipment budget is not theirs to keep or lose. Veridian Instruments advises the lab on what each experiment could use, and it is paid for each machine it places. The foundation's program officer must countersign every purchase before funds release, and she reviews each request against the approved category list from another city. The lab director set the study's methods at the start, and funds left at close-out stay with her lab for its next projects. Midway through, a proposal circulates to order a second imaging unit like the one already installed. On the chapter's analysis of spending restraint, which party can be relied on to turn down equipment the study does not need?
options: The bench technicians
Veridian Instruments
The lab director
The foundation's program officer

items.stem: Hartwell Corporation moves about forty employees a year under the following arrangement. The transferring employees choose services from a set menu before each move, and none of the charges appears on their side of the ledger. Copeland Movers performs the packing and hauling it has listed for each household, and it bills for every service line it enters. Crestline Relocation clears each mover invoice for payment from Hartwell's funds, and its reviewers judge the paperwork from a processing center out of state. Hartwell's finance office has ordered two across-the-board cuts to the moving allowance, and it examines the program's total spending every year. Invoices routinely list full-service packing for lightly furnished apartments, and the program's total has not fallen. On the chapter's diagnosis, which party's position explains why the waste persists?
options: Crestline Relocation
Hartwell's finance office
Copeland Movers
The transferring employees

bank_meta.chapter_title: Provoking Profligacy with Low Out-of-Pocket Costs

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.7.1: Identify the paired long-run trends the chapter presents as its central exhibit: the out-of-pocket share of US healthcare spending falling from nearly half in 1960 to about 11 percent in 2017, leaving third parties paying nearly 90 percent, while the share of US GDP devoted to healthcare rose from about 5 percent to nearly 18 percent.
learning_objectives.7.2: Apply the chapter's super-luxury-car thought experiment to a novel deeply subsidised market: a third party covering most of the price relieves buyers from weighing all costs against all benefits so demand rises; supply rises too, because producers collect the full price however it is split between buyer and subsidiser; and the induced consumption is waste wherever the premium good's only advantage over the practical one is status.
learning_objectives.7.3: Explain what the chapter's cross-country comparison is meant to establish: the United States was among the highest spenders in 1970 but still comparable to its peers, other nations have held healthcare spending near or below a common ceiling while only the United States went above it, and the relentless pulling-away since about 1980 means the cause must be something happening only in the United States.
learning_objectives.7.4: Given a spending surge, or a divergence between comparable cases, and several candidate explanations with facts about how each behaved over the relevant period, determine which candidates the chapter's method eliminates and on what ground: a factor that did not change cannot explain a change, and a factor shared or static across cases cannot explain a divergence.
learning_objectives.7.5: Explain why, on the chapter's account, the dominance of third-party payment made US spending grow beyond both reason and benefit -- spending decisions migrated to third parties possessing neither the incentive nor the information to make them well -- and why any alternative system must therefore be able to handle the surge in demand that low out-of-pocket costs create.

Chapter 7 → Provoking Profligacy with Lo.text: Two lines move in opposite directions across six decades: the fraction of American medical bills paid directly by patients falls from about half to roughly a tenth, while the fraction of national income going to healthcare more than triples. The chapter reads the first as the cause of the second. Subsidise most of a luxury's price and buyers stop weighing it; sellers do not mind who pays, so both demand and supply swell.

Chapter 7 → The US and the Rest of the W.text: Compared across wealthy nations over five decades, one line separates from the rest. The chapter's point is not the size of the gap but what explaining it requires: a divergence between otherwise comparable cases must be caused by something present in the diverging case alone. Since the United States was unremarkable in 1970 and pulled away afterwards, whatever did it has to be something that changed here and not elsewhere.

Chapter 7 → Why We Spend So Much.text: Rival explanations are dismissed not as false but as static: imaging machines cost much the same everywhere, and doctors ordering procedures they profit from is real and well documented yet no more common than before. A cause that held steady cannot account for a change. What moved was how little patients paid directly, shifting decisions to payers with neither the motive nor the knowledge to make them well.

items.stem: According to the chapter, Figure 7.1 tracks the share of US healthcare spending that patients paid directly out of pocket over the past two generations. What does Flynn say the figure shows?
options: It rose steadily as deductibles and copayments grew, leaving patients directly covering most of their own care.
It fell from nearly half of all spending to about 11 percent, with third parties covering nearly 90 percent.
It held at roughly a third of all spending, with government programs and private insurers splitting the rest.
It fell modestly from about half to about a third, leaving patients still the largest single class of payer.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → Provoking Profligacy with Low Out-of-Pocket Costs

items.stem: Flynn closes his spending argument with a single figure that carries two lines on two vertical axes. According to the chapter, which pairing of long-run US trends does that figure display?
options: A steep fall in the out-of-pocket share of spending paired with a steep rise in healthcare's share of GDP.
A steep rise in the out-of-pocket share of spending paired with a steep fall in healthcare's share of GDP.
A steep fall in the out-of-pocket share of spending paired with a steep fall in healthcare's share of GDP.
A steep rise in the out-of-pocket share of spending paired with a steep rise in healthcare's share of GDP.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → Why We Spend So Much

items.stem: According to the chapter, the decades in which third-party payments became overwhelmingly dominant in US healthcare also saw healthcare absorb a far larger share of the economy: between 1960 and 2016, while the out-of-pocket share of spending fell from nearly 50 percent to about 11 percent, the share of US GDP devoted to healthcare rose from about 5 percent to nearly 18 percent.
options: True
False

items.stem: In the chapter's super-luxury-car thought experiment, Flynn grants that a Honda or Ford can do nearly everything a Ferrari or Rolls-Royce can, from getting groceries to taking the kids to soccer practice. According to the chapter, what is the one thing the super-luxury car does better?
options: Conveying its owner's social status
Lasting longer before needing replacement
Protecting its occupants in a collision
Holding its value over years of ownership
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → Provoking Profligacy with Low Out-of-Pocket Costs

items.stem: According to the chapter, the 90 percent subsidy in its thought experiment would make a $300,000 Ferrari cost its buyer less than an average Honda or Ford.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → Provoking Profligacy with Low Out-of-Pocket Costs

items.stem: In the thought experiment, Flynn predicts that the supply of super-luxury cars would skyrocket along with demand. According to the chapter, why would manufacturers gladly build as many cars as the subsidised buyers want?
options: The subsidiser contracts for a guaranteed number of cars, so expansion carries no sales risk
They collect the full price however it is split between the buyer and the subsidising third party
Building at far higher volume would let them spread their costs and profit on every additional car
Booming demand would let them raise the sticker price well above what they charge today
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → Provoking Profligacy with Low Out-of-Pocket Costs

items.stem: According to the chapter, why does the thought experiment count the subsidised rush into super-luxury cars as "pure waste"?
options: Buyers who bear only a small share of the price have little reason to take care of what they acquire
The third party's outlay on the subsidy exceeds what all the buyers together would have paid on their own
A practical car already does nearly everything the luxury car can, so the upgrade buys only status
Factories shift away from practical models, creating shortages of the cars people actually need
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → Provoking Profligacy with Low Out-of-Pocket Costs

items.stem: A restaurant trade association begins paying most of the invoice whenever a member cafe upgrades its kitchen equipment, and four cafes respond that year. Marta's uses the program to order cooking ranges that match her current ones on speed and output but carry a storied nameplate her trade journal profiles. Osei's uses the program to order high-capacity fryers that cut his ticket times in half during the crush of his packed lunch rushes. Lin's uses the program to order the same standard ovens she already runs, replacing them two years before her worn units would have failed. Dario's spends his own savings, taking no program money, on a gleaming imported range whose famous badge he shows off to every food critic in town. According to the reasoning of the chapter's thought experiment, which cafe's purchase is the kind of spending the chapter calls pure waste?
options: Marta's
Dario's
Lin's
Osei's
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → Provoking Profligacy with Low Out-of-Pocket Costs

items.stem: For a decade, a conservatory endowment has paid the region's violin workshops most of the price whenever a student commissions a hand-carved concert instrument instead of buying a factory student model. Commissions have multiplied, and the workshops have added benches and apprentices. The trustees now vote to change only the payment route: a student must first pay the workshop the entire price from her own funds, and the endowment then reimburses her for all but the same small share she paid before. One trustee predicts this will finally cool the boom, because students will confront the whole price and workshops will once again face customers spending their own money. Applying the chapter's thought-experiment reasoning, what is the most likely result of the change?
options: Workshops slow their expansion once the endowment stops paying them directly
The boom in commissions and workshop hiring carries on much as before
Commissions fall sharply as students face the whole price up front
Workshop prices drop as students start bargaining with their own money
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → Provoking Profligacy with Low Out-of-Pocket Costs

items.stem: A national arts ministry has for years paid most of the invoice when a public library commissions a hand-illuminated display edition of a classic rather than buying standard reading copies. Ateliers of illuminators sprang up across the country, and most libraries now hold shelves of the editions, displayed as marks of a branch's standing while patrons check out the ordinary reading copies for actual use. When the ministry winds the program down, new commissions almost vanish within two years and most of the ateliers close. Applying the chapter's thought-experiment reasoning, which reading of the collapse follows?
options: Ateliers raised their prices so far under the program that demand died
A craft economy that had found its footing was undone by the funding change
Libraries exhausted their acquisition budgets during the boom years
The editions were never worth their whole price to the libraries
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → Provoking Profligacy with Low Out-of-Pocket Costs

items.stem: The chapter presents a figure comparing the percentage of GDP spent on healthcare by each OECD nation from 1970 to 2017. According to the chapter, what does that figure show?
options: One line — the United States — pulls up and away from all the other nations' lines over time.
A handful of the wealthiest nations break away from the rest as a group, with the United States among them.
The United States sits far above the other nations across the entire period, from the very first year shown.
Every nation's line climbs at roughly the same rate, leaving the gaps between countries unchanged.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → The US and the Rest of the World

items.stem: The chapter notes that in 1970 the United States, though already among the highest spenders, was 'still somewhat comparable' to the other OECD nations. In Flynn's argument, why does that starting point matter?
options: It concedes a weak point: if the United States was already the top spender, its problem predates the trends Flynn blames.
It shows the gap opened later, so whatever caused it must have arisen after the years when the nations were close.
It shows American healthcare was once affordable, setting the spending level the United States should aim to restore.
It establishes that all wealthy nations face the same rising costs, with the United States simply furthest along a shared path.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → The US and the Rest of the World

items.stem: According to the chapter, other OECD nations' healthcare spending has also risen since 1970, yet they have all held it near or below a common ceiling, and only the United States has ever gone above it. What does Flynn take this pattern to establish?
options: Whatever is driving the surge must be at work in the United States but not in the other wealthy nations.
That rising healthcare spending is universal among wealthy economies, so no single country's arrangements can be blamed.
That the United States spends more because it is richer, since wealthier nations devote larger GDP shares to healthcare.
That other nations imposed legal caps on healthcare budgets, a limit the United States has so far refused to adopt.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → The US and the Rest of the World

items.stem: The chapter concedes that healthcare spending trended upward in every OECD nation after 1970 — so its cross-country comparison presumably supports blaming forces common to all wealthy nations for the growth in US spending.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → The US and the Rest of the World

items.stem: According to the chapter, one candidate explanation for the great rise in US healthcare spending is conceded to be real and well documented — doctors are likelier to recommend procedures, such as X-rays, when they profit from providing them — yet it is eliminated anyway. Which candidate is this?
options: Supplier-induced demand
Expensive new medical technologies
The growth of third-party payment
Medical malpractice costs
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → Provoking Profligacy with Low Out-of-Pocket Costs

items.stem: According to the chapter, the only candidate factor that changed enough over the past two generations to account for the massive rise in US healthcare spending was the share of costs patients pay out of pocket, which fell from nearly half of all medical spending to roughly a tenth.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → Provoking Profligacy with Low Out-of-Pocket Costs

items.stem: The chapter concedes that supplier-induced demand — doctors ordering more procedures when they profit from them — genuinely raises healthcare spending and is well documented. According to the chapter, why does that concession not rescue it as an explanation of the enormous rise in US healthcare spending since the 1960s?
options: The studies behind the effect were later found to have overstated its size, leaving the documentation too weak to rely on
The evidence covers mainly physicians who own their own equipment, a group too small to move national spending totals
Supplier-induced demand raises the volume of procedures rather than their prices, and the spending rise was driven by prices
A factor can raise spending's level yet not its growth, and nothing suggests this factor intensified over the period
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → Provoking Profligacy with Low Out-of-Pocket Costs

items.stem: Figure 7.2, as the chapter reads it, shows US healthcare spending pulling up and away from every other OECD nation's after about 1980. The chapter notes that most of those nations ran single-payer systems with continuously low out-of-pocket rates through the whole period, and concludes that those nations' rates 'couldn't have had anything to do with' the US divergence. Why, according to the chapter?
options: Their low rates were offset by heavier taxes, leaving households' true exposure to costs about the same as in the United States
Those rates stayed put throughout, and a factor that held still over the period cannot produce a gap that opened during it
Out-of-pocket shares are measured differently under single-payer systems, so the rates cannot be compared across countries
Low out-of-pocket shares restrain spending under single-payer systems even though they inflate it under insurance-based ones
items.source_anchor: Chapter 7 → Why We Spend So Much

items.stem: A county's spending on bridge repair has climbed steeply for two decades, and an outside analyst sorts the candidate explanations the way the chapter sorts the candidate culprits behind the US healthcare surge. Overweight trucks grind down the decks; weigh-station studies leave no doubt about it, and loads have run at much the same pitch since logging began. The on-call contractor's invoices draw persistent complaints; its billed rates were renegotiated sharply upward midway through the period and have climbed steadily ever since. Road salt corrodes the rebar; the county has spread it in much the usual quantities every winter for as long as records run. items.stem: Kestrel and Bayline run bus networks of similar size through similar country, and for years their overtime outlays tracked each other closely. The regional driver shortage fills the trade press; both agencies chase the same scarce applicants and have run comparably short-handed through the whole decade. The fleets are of a similar vintage, and breakdowns that force covering runs at overtime have held near their long-run rate at each agency. New certification rules pull drivers into paid refresher training at overtime, and both agencies phased those rules in on the same statewide schedule. bank_meta.chapter_title: How “Single-Payer” Systems Spend Less Than We Do

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.8.1: Explain why, in the chapter's analysis, offering universal free care does not eliminate rationing but only replaces it: a zero price confronts people with benefits alone while shielding them from all costs, so demand balloons and the limited supply must be allocated by some non-price mechanism instead of the market price that would otherwise ration it to buyers willing and able to pay.
learning_objectives.8.2: Explain how the chapter resolves its opening puzzle -- why nations charging nothing out of pocket spend less than a United States whose patients do pay a small share -- namely that single-payer systems suppress the demand free care creates through centrally planned non-price rationing, while the US has none of those constraints, so its demand goes unchecked and its spending runs higher.
learning_objectives.8.3: Apply the chapter's account of the NICE guidelines to a novel treatment request, determining from a treatment's cost and its expected life extension the cost per additional year of life and which decision the guideline bands lead to.
learning_objectives.8.4: Explain how each of the NHS's additional rationing methods suppresses treatment volume without any price: bonuses that pay general practitioners to keep referral rates low, waiting lists that shed demand three distinct ways, and capital limits on beds and equipment that both excuse seeing fewer patients and create queues that dissuade the rest.
learning_objectives.8.5: Explain why, on the chapter's account, special-interest groups lobby state insurance commissioners for coverage mandates -- once coverage is mandatory, demand for the group's services rises sharply because workers face only copays and deductibles rather than the full price -- and why commissioners, whether elected or appointed, are open to it.
learning_objectives.8.6: Predict, for a novel mandate case, who the chapter's compensation logic says ultimately bears the resulting premium increase: not the employer who nominally pays, but workers, through reduced take-home pay or withheld raises.
learning_objectives.8.7: Determine, for a novel case in which a system reports that its waiting list has grown shorter, whether the chapter's account supports treating that as more care delivered or as demand shed, and what further information would distinguish the two.

Chapter 8 → How “Single-Payer” Systems S.text: Free care does not abolish rationing; it changes the instrument. A market price allocates scarce supply to those able and willing to pay it, and that is rationing. Promise care at no charge and the price is effectively zero, so people see only benefits and demand swells. Something else must then do the allocating, typically a committee weighing what a year of added life is worth against its cost, approving cheaply bought years and refusing dear ones.

Chapter 8 → Other Not-So-Nice Ways to Ra.text: Beyond the cost-per-life-year ceiling, several levers hold volume down without any price. Family doctors earn bonuses for referring fewer patients, and with no referral there is no specialist visit. Those referred join queues, which shed demand three ways: some never join on seeing the wait, some give up partway, some die first. Capping beds and scanners does double work, justifying fewer appointments and lengthening the queues that deter the rest. America has none of these.

Chapter 8 → What about Insurance?.text: State insurance regulators are political figures, and provider groups lobby them steadily to make coverage of their own services compulsory. Once it is, patients meet only a small charge rather than the full fee, so use of that service climbs and premiums follow. Employers appear to absorb this, but a firm has only so much for total pay: what goes to premiums cannot go to wages. Rising costs then breed support for further mandates.

items.stem: The chapter states that price mechanisms are themselves 'a form of rationing.' According to the chapter, what do market prices ration, and how?
options: They divide the available supply evenly, so every buyer who wants the product at the going price receives a small share of it.
They allocate the limited quantity sellers offer to the buyers willing and able to pay the market price; the rest get nothing.
They let a panel of experts decide which buyers receive the product by weighing each purchase's costs against its benefits.
They hold total demand down by placing would-be buyers on long waiting lists until more of the product becomes available.

options: Without posted prices to compare, patients cannot tell cheap treatments from costly ones and default to requesting the most advanced care.
Patients reason that their taxes have already paid for the system, so they set out to recover that value in services.
People weigh only the potential benefits of any treatment, since a price of zero shields them completely from its costs.
Providers who are guaranteed payment recommend more treatment than patients would ever have sought out on their own.

Its budget is set too low by the government, forcing it to deny treatments that a properly funded service could have covered.

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.9.1: Identify the historical comparison the chapter opens with -- the price paths of procedures insurance does not cover against those it does -- and the divergence it reports: cosmetic-services prices rose far less than overall inflation, falling in real terms even as quality improved, while medical-care and physician-services prices rose far faster than inflation.
learning_objectives.9.2: Explain how the chapter's myopia-surgery history -- radial keratotomy giving way to LASIK and then to a refined version of it -- shows price and quality improving together under first-party payment: the newcomer debuted below the incumbent's price and fell further as competition arose and better variants appeared, while the cost of each date's best available surgery fell in real terms even as that best kept improving.
learning_objectives.9.3: Explain how the three self-reinforcing factors the chapter credits for the divergent price paths -- consumers weighing costs against benefits when spending their own money, producers forced to compete on both price and quality, and advertising that pushes service and price information to potential patients -- each holds prices down where first parties pay, and why the chapter says all three go missing when third parties pay.
learning_objectives.9.4: Explain why the chapter argues the availability of expensive new technologies cannot be the cause of exploding US healthcare costs: the same technologies are available in other rich nations, yet one of them delivers better outcomes while spending far less.
learning_objectives.9.5: Apply the chapter's cause-and-effect reversal to a novel case, determining whether heavy use of costly options is the driver of overspending or instead a symptom of a payment arrangement in which the chooser bears none of the cost.
learning_objectives.9.6: Explain how, on the chapter's account, insuring proven and time-tested treatments while leaving bleeding-edge technologies to the patient's own purse restores prudent choice, so that a patient opts for a costly new treatment only when its benefits clearly outweigh its costs.

Chapter 9 → Empowering Prudence with Fir.text: The natural experiment is coverage itself. Procedures insurers never pay for leave patients spending their own money, and there prices behaved unlike the rest of medicine across two decades: they rose more slowly than prices generally, so in real terms they fell, while medical care overall outran inflation. Quality improved at the same time. Eye surgery tells the same story -- a newer technique arrived cheaper than the one it replaced and kept improving.

Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned.text: Three forces reinforce one another where patients pay directly: they weigh cost against benefit, sellers must compete on price and quality together, and advertising carries prices and options to people who would otherwise never hear of them. None operates when a third party pays. This also disposes of blaming new machines. They exist in countries spending far less, so availability cannot be the cause; heavy use is a symptom of costs nobody at the decision bears.
