Both sets of prices tracked overall inflation closely, so the chapter locates the real difference in quality rather than in price
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → Empowering Prudence with First-Party Payments

items.stem: According to the chapter, over the roughly two decades it examines, the quality of cosmetic procedures increased dramatically even as their real price fell: techniques became less invasive, required less time in the hospital, and involved much shorter recovery times at home.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → Empowering Prudence with First-Party Payments

items.stem: According to the chapter, when LASIK won approval as an alternative to radial keratotomy, how did the newcomer's price compare with the incumbent procedure's?
options: It debuted below radial keratotomy in per-eye terms only; because it treated both eyes at once, the total bill exceeded the older surgery's.
It debuted at roughly the same price as radial keratotomy, and the two procedures' prices then declined together in parallel.
It debuted well above what radial keratotomy then cost, as cutting-edge procedures usually do, and undercut the older surgery only years later.
It debuted substantially below what radial keratotomy then cost, and it fell further as competition arose among providers.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → Empowering Prudence with First-Party Payments

items.stem: The chapter contrasts what myopia patients experienced under radial keratotomy with what they experienced under LASIK. Which pairing best captures the contrast Flynn draws?
options: Radial keratotomy required an overnight hospital stay and weeks of bandaged recovery for each treated eye; LASIK was a same-visit outpatient procedure, though patients still needed several weeks at home before returning to work.

Radial keratotomy was quick to perform but left patients dependent on glasses for months while the reshaped eye settled; LASIK took longer in the operating room but freed patients from their glasses the moment the procedure was finished.

Radial keratotomy treated one eye at a time with a long wait before the second, and someone else had to drive the patient home; LASIK treated both eyes the same day, and most patients drove themselves home immediately.

Radial keratotomy reliably brought nearly every patient to full correction but carried real surgical risk; LASIK traded a somewhat lower rate of full correction for a procedure that was far safer and easier to undergo.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → Empowering Prudence with First-Party Payments

items.stem: Flynn compares what it cost to buy the best available LASIK surgery when the original version was new with what the best available version cost years later, and finds the nominal price almost unchanged. According to the chapter, why does this count as a price decline?
options: Because the newer version takes only minutes of operating time, the implied charge per minute of a surgeon's attention fell steeply even though the quoted charge for the whole procedure did not.
Because prices across the economy rose substantially in between, a roughly flat nominal price means the inflation-adjusted cost of the best available surgery fell, even as that best kept improving.
Because the original version's own price had fallen sharply by the later date, the average charge across the old and the new versions together sat well below what either had commanded at its debut.
Because the newer version handles both eyes in one visit rather than two, its effective price per treated eye works out to roughly half of what the earlier state-of-the-art surgery had commanded.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → Empowering Prudence with First-Party Payments

items.stem: Flynn presents the myopia-surgery history as a second instance of the pattern he draws from cosmetic surgery: as eye surgery moved from radial keratotomy to LASIK and its successors, quality improved dramatically while the real price of the surgery fell.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → Empowering Prudence with First-Party Payments

items.stem: In the section titled 'The Lesson to Be Learned,' Flynn attributes the massively divergent price trajectories of first-party-paid and third-party-paid procedures to three self-reinforcing factors. According to the chapter, which of the following is one of the three?
options: Insurance companies that negotiate discounted rates with providers in their networks
New medical technologies that steadily lower the cost of delivering each procedure
Government agencies that publish standardized price schedules for elective procedures
Advertising that pushes service and price information out to potential patients
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: A commentator concedes that cosmetic-surgery prices have fallen but calls the industry's aggressive advertising wasteful - money that could instead have gone to further price cuts. What role does the chapter itself assign to that advertising in markets where first parties pay?
options: Signaling financial strength, since only providers with healthy margins can afford sustained campaigns
Pushing service and price information to patients who would otherwise never learn their options
Persuading hesitant patients to buy procedures, so higher volume lets clinics spread costs and cut prices
Building brand loyalty that shields established clinics from having to match their rivals' prices
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: The chapter claims that where third parties pay there is 'no competitive pressure to improve' - even though such markets can contain just as many providers as the cosmetic-surgery market. According to the chapter's account of the three self-reinforcing factors, why does having many providers fail to generate that pressure when third parties pay?
options: Third-party payers negotiate uniform rates in advance, which makes it illegal for providers to undercut one another on price
Providers face pressure only because patients shop and compare, and patients stop shopping when the money is not their own
Providers in insured markets cluster inside hospital systems, which coordinate their prices rather than competing on them
Insurers steer patients toward the cheapest providers, which pushes prices down but removes any reward for improving quality
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: According to the chapter, patients under third-party payment presumably continue to weigh costs against benefits just as carefully as first-party payers do, but their prudent choices are largely overridden by insurers who control which treatments get approved.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: The chapter says the idea that expensive new technologies are driving up the cost of US healthcare can be disposed of. What evidence does it offer for dismissing that idea?
options: For most lower back pain, a low-cost X-ray is all the imaging a patient needs, making the costlier scan medically unnecessary
The same technologies are available in other rich nations, yet one of them delivers better outcomes while spending far less
The real price of cosmetic procedures fell over two decades even as the quality of those procedures dramatically improved
Hospitals feature their newest equipment in advertising to attract patients rather than to improve the care they deliver
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: Flynn argues that the availability of expensive new technologies — linear accelerators, PET scanners, image-guided surgical robots — cannot be the cause of exploding US healthcare costs. According to the chapter, why does comparing the United States with other rich nations establish this?
options: Hospitals acquire much of the costly equipment to advertise and to recruit physicians, so the machines are bought for show and see relatively little use
The prices of new procedures fall steeply once competitors arrive, as the myopia-surgery history shows, so the technologies do not stay expensive for long
New technologies make up only a small fraction of total medical spending, so even lavish purchases of them could not move a nation's overall costs far
A nation where the same technologies are available spends far less while delivering better outcomes, so the supposed cause is present without the effect
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: Right after stating that the technology explanation can be disposed of, the chapter reports that the United States has far more MRI machines per person than any other OECD country. According to the chapter, what work does this passage do in Flynn's argument?
options: It credits American hospitals with leading the world in adopting new technology, a lead the chapter presents as the real benefit bought by high US spending
It concedes the fact that makes the technology explanation tempting, letting the chapter state that case at its strongest before explaining why it still fails
It implies that Canada and the United Kingdom equip themselves too thinly, a sacrifice the chapter treats as the price their systems pay to restrain spending
It supplies the dispelling comparison itself, since counting scanners per person across rich countries is how the chapter shows availability cannot be the cause
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: According to the chapter, the fact that the same expensive technologies — PET scanners, linear accelerators, surgical robots — are available in other rich nations arguably demonstrates that such machines contribute little to the quality of a nation's care.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: The chapter takes up a common explanation for high American healthcare spending - that expensive new technologies are driving up its cost. According to Flynn, what is wrong with that explanation?
options: It goes too far: new technology genuinely explains part of the spending growth, though third-party payment explains the larger share.
It treats two unrelated trends as connected: technology adoption and total spending merely happen to have been rising over the same years.
It relies on the wrong comparison: American hospitals actually adopt costly new equipment more slowly than hospitals in peer nations.
It gets cause and effect backward: heavy use of costly technology is an effect of third-party payment, not the cause.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: According to the chapter, MRIs are often ordered for routine lower back pain presumably because the older, low-cost X-ray can no longer detect what such cases require, so the costlier scan has become the medically necessary choice.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: To dispel the idea that expensive new technologies are what drive up healthcare costs, the chapter observes that linear accelerators, PET scanners, and image-guided surgical robots are available in Singapore and other rich nations too, even though Singapore spends far less on healthcare while getting better outcomes. According to Flynn, what is this observation meant to establish?
options: Other rich nations keep spending down chiefly by rationing how often their advanced machines may actually be used.
Advanced equipment has grown cheap enough that buying it no longer moves any wealthy nation's spending totals.
A technology available in low-spending nations as well cannot be the cause of uniquely high American spending.
The United States buys far more advanced machines than any comparison with its peers would lead one to expect.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: The chapter calls hospitals 'complicit' in the spending that flows toward expensive new technologies: new equipment is featured in advertising to attract patients, and it helps recruit doctors who love the newest machines. According to Flynn, what lets hospitals make these purchases without worrying much about whether the technology improves care enough to justify its price?
options: Doctors' eagerness to use the newest machines guarantees the equipment will see enough cases to earn its keep.
The advertising value of new equipment reliably brings in enough extra patients to cover its price.
Most of the cost ends up being paid by third parties rather than by the hospital's own patients.
Accreditation standards oblige hospitals to keep their equipment at the current state of the art regardless of cost.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: A repertory theater lets each production's designers order sets, costumes, and stage machinery as they see fit, with every invoice billed to a patrons' endowment; no production pays from its own box-office take. In recent seasons designers have specified automated moving scenery more and more often, and the endowment's outlays have climbed steeply. Concluding that the costliest item on the invoices must be what is breaking the budget, the board bars automated scenery from all future productions. According to the chapter's cause-and-effect reasoning, what is the most likely result?
options: Designers begin trimming their other orders in the ban's wake
Outlays come back in line with the costliest item gone
Outlays swing with each season's repertoire rather than the ban
Outlays keep climbing, shifting into other elaborate stagecraft
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: Project teams at a structural-engineering consultancy run their simulations on whatever cloud machines they choose, and the bills settle into a firmwide overhead account that no project ever sees. Top-of-the-line processor clusters have become the default choice even on small jobs, and the overhead account has swollen year after year. The partners change one thing: from next quarter, compute is paid out of each project's own fixed budget, whose unspent remainder becomes that team's year-end bonus pool, while the full catalogue of machines stays available at unchanged rates. One partner objects that nothing will improve so long as the expensive clusters remain on the menu. Applying the chapter's cause-and-effect reasoning, what is the most likely result?
options: Spending stays swollen while the costliest clusters remain available
Spending falls only if the partners also cap cluster hours
Heavy cluster use recedes though the menu is unchanged
Teams abandon the top clusters even on jobs that need them
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: Owner-operator truckers buy their tires out of their own operating money; no carrier, insurer, or fund shares the bill. Across the region the premium long-haul brand outsells every mid-range rival, tire outlays sit among the larger lines in an owner-operator's books, and drivers who have run several brands tend to come back to the premium one set after set. A trade columnist argues that relentless brand marketing has truckers overspending on rubber and urges the owners' association to steer members toward mid-range tires. By the chapter's cause-and-effect reasoning, which verdict on the columnist's diagnosis follows?
options: It spots genuine overuse but prescribes too gentle a remedy
It cannot be settled either way without both brands' prices
It rightly reads brand dominance as marketing-driven overuse
It mistakes prudent purchasing for runaway overspending
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: According to the chapter, which coverage design would restore prudent decision-making about costly new treatments?
options: Insurance pays for nothing at all, so that every treatment, whether old or new, is paid for out of the patient's own savings.
Insurance pays for every treatment a physician orders, while the patient contributes a modest copayment scaled to the price of the care.
Insurance pays for proven, time-tested treatments, while any bleeding-edge new technology is paid for out of the patient's own pocket.
Insurance pays for costly new technologies, while routine, well-established treatments are paid for out of the patient's own pocket.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: The chapter imagines health insurance that covers proven, time-tested treatments but not bleeding-edge new technologies. On its account, how would that split change a patient's decision about whether to have a costly new treatment?
options: Denied any insurance reimbursement for them, physicians would simply stop offering new technologies, so the choice would never reach the patient at all.
Freed from paying anything for covered care, the patient could put the money saved toward newer treatments, making them easier to afford than before.
Bearing the full price of any new technology, the patient would weigh its benefits against its cost and choose it only when the benefits clearly won out.
Priced beyond the reach of nearly all patients, the newest technologies would effectively vanish from the market, leaving only the covered treatments available to choose.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: The chapter illustrates its argument with lower back pain: absent neurological problems, it says, a very low-cost X-ray is the only imaging needed, yet MRIs are often ordered instead. According to the chapter, why are the costlier scans ordered in these cases?
options: Because new scanners help hospitals advertise for patients and recruit physicians, hospitals channel imaging work toward their newest machines.
Because a third party picks up all or most of the cost, patients have no serious financial reason to veto the more expensive imaging.
Because insurers insist on the most thorough scan available before approving treatment, protecting themselves against a missed diagnosis.
Because physicians judge the MRI's sharper image to be worth having in back-pain cases regardless of who ends up paying for the scan.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

items.stem: According to the chapter, Singapore's system makes costly new treatments available but confronts patients with their actual costs and real prices, so a patient opts for a bleeding-edge treatment only when its benefits clearly outweigh its costs.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 9 → The Lesson to Be Learned

bank_meta.chapter_title: The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.10.1: Distinguish the three coverage arrangements the chapter lays out: the US pattern of insurance obtained through and paid mostly by employers, which the chapter says exists nowhere else; mandatory portable insurance that workers help pay for themselves, which survives unemployment and is tied to no employer; and tax-funded national services provided free of charge to all citizens.
learning_objectives.10.2: Explain how the chapter derives the wartime price and wage controls from an inflation problem: with industrial output redirected to war materiel there were few civilian goods, while full employment left workers holding abundant cash, so high demand against low supply meant rising prices, and the government fixed nearly all prices including wages and rationed what civilian goods existed.
learning_objectives.10.3: Explain how offering free healthcare let a wartime industrialist recruit tens of thousands of workers to lightly populated shipyards when raising wages was illegal: health benefits were defined as fringe benefits, neither wages nor salaries, and so sat outside the controls -- an end-run other major corporations copied to compete for scarce labour, leaving the practice in place out of habit once controls ended.
learning_objectives.10.4: Apply the chapter's account of the 1954 tax exemption to a novel compensation choice, predicting which form of pay leaves an employee better off once taxes are counted, given that employer-paid premiums are exempt while wages and other fringe benefits are taxed.
learning_objectives.10.5: Given a novel case of a firm's hiring choice or a worker's career decision, determine whether the chapter's employment-tie mechanisms -- the premium as a substantial fixed cost per employee on the firm side, loss of coverage on leaving a job on the worker side -- explain it, or whether an adjacent motive is doing the work.
learning_objectives.10.6: Explain why the chapter insists the employer-based system is a historical accident rather than a design, and why that framing carries its advocacy weight: the arrangement feels natural only because nearly everyone alive grew up after the exemption was enacted, and what an accident built rather than a design chose, a country is free to replace.

Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Em.text: Nowhere else does a job supply health coverage. The arrangement was an accident of war: with pay frozen to curb inflation, an industrialist who could not outbid rivals for scarce labour offered medical care instead, which the rules classed as a fringe benefit rather than wages. Competitors copied it and habit outlasted the controls. A 1954 tax change fixed it permanently, since benefits escape tax while an equivalent raise does not. An accident can be replaced.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what makes the United States' health insurance arrangement unique among the world's healthcare systems?
options: It is the only country that declines to provide free, tax-funded care to all of its citizens.
It is the only country where workers must pay their health insurance premiums out of their own money.
It is the only country where residents are required by law to purchase a health insurance policy.
It is the only country where health insurance is tied to employment and paid for mostly by employers.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: The chapter groups Germany, France, and Japan under one coverage arrangement and the United Kingdom and Canada under another. According to the chapter, what separates the two groups?
options: The first has employers pay most of each worker's premium; the second has individuals buy policies from a single government insurer.
The first ties each person's coverage to one particular employer; the second keeps coverage portable across job changes and job losses.
The first requires people to buy insurance that workers help pay for; the second funds free care for all citizens from general taxes.
The first leaves workers uninsured during spells of unemployment; the second covers citizens whether or not they are employed.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: The chapter notes that part of the Affordable Care Act created a convenient marketplace where individuals could contract directly with insurance companies. What point is Flynn making with this example?
options: The provision aimed to reinforce the employment-insurance relationship by obliging employers to keep offering coverage.
Even with a direct way to buy coverage available, Americans kept expecting insurance to come from their employers.
The marketplace finally broke the link between employment and insurance by letting individuals bypass their employers.
Americans hold on to employer coverage mainly because buying a policy on one's own remains too difficult to manage.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: The chapter says German workers must help pay their health insurance premiums with their own money. Even so, on the chapter's account, a German worker who loses their job still has health insurance.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: According to the chapter, what did the US government do to forestall inflation during World War II?
options: It imposed a wartime surtax on factory pay so that workers would have less cash to spend on scarce goods.
It urged households to place their extra earnings in war bonds until civilian production could resume.
It ordered manufacturers to shift part of their productive capacity back to civilian cars and household goods.
It fixed nearly all prices, including wages and salaries, and rationed the limited civilian consumer goods.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: The chapter says the wartime government was worried about inflation. According to its account, why was inflation likely?
options: With labor scarce, employers were bidding wages steadily upward, and the rising cost of pay was forcing sellers to charge more.
The government was financing the war by expanding the money supply faster than the economy's output of goods could grow.
Wartime goods were far more expensive to produce than civilian ones, and manufacturers passed those higher costs through into the prices they charged.
Fully employed workers held plenty of cash while few civilian goods were being made, so heavy demand pressed against a small supply.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: According to the chapter, the government fixed prices throughout the economy and simultaneously instituted a rationing program. What role did rationing play in that pairing?
options: It soaked up workers' surplus cash so that less purchasing power chased the scarce goods.
It kept wages and salaries from rising along with the prices of the goods still available.
It divided the small stock of civilian consumer goods among individual households.
It steered raw materials and factory capacity away from civilian production and into war materiel.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: In the chapter's account, the wartime shortage of civilian consumer goods was arguably a product of the government's price controls, which largely discouraged manufacturers from producing for the civilian market.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: According to the chapter, wartime controls made it illegal for Henry J. Kaiser to offer higher wages to attract workers to his shipyards. What inducement did he offer instead?
options: Extra rations of scarce civilian consumer goods.
A guaranteed job at the yards after the war.
Company-built housing near the shipyards.
Free healthcare for everyone he employed.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: According to the chapter, why was it legal for Kaiser to offer workers free healthcare as a recruiting inducement when offering them higher wages was illegal?
options: The government issued war contractors a special waiver allowing employee welfare programs, so long as no extra cash wages were paid.
Health benefits were defined as fringe benefits, neither wages nor salaries, so the controls that fixed pay never reached them.
Regulators counted a healthcare plan's cash value as too small a share of a shipyard wage to amount to prohibited extra pay.
Price schedules under the controls covered goods and cash wages, but services such as medical care were never brought within them.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: According to the chapter, why did the legal freeze on wages make it especially hard for Kaiser to staff his Pacific Coast shipyards?
options: His yards sat on a lightly populated coast, so the tens of thousands of workers he needed had to be drawn from back East, and a better wage was exactly the inducement the law now forbade.
His Liberty ship contract fixed what the government paid per vessel, so even had raises been lawful, matching the wage levels on offer back East would soon have pushed the whole contract into loss.

His weld-based production methods demanded seasoned shipwrights, and the freeze held those specialists at the Eastern yards that had set their higher pay scales before the controls took hold, rates his yards could now never top.

Rationing kept civilian goods scarce in the shipyard towns, and with prices fixed the shops could not stock for newcomers, so workers saw little point in moving for wages they would be unable to spend.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: The chapter says that by the war's end many major US corporations had copied Kaiser's free-healthcare offer to compete for scarce labor. Presumably, the practice then survived the end of the controls chiefly because the tax exemption for employer-sponsored insurance was already in place.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: According to the chapter, what did the 1954 update to the Internal Revenue Code do?
options: It required employers above a certain size to offer health insurance to their workers.
It extended the wartime rule placing fringe benefits outside wage and price controls.
It made fringe benefits of every kind, from cars to bonuses, free of income tax.
It exempted employer-paid health insurance premiums from the employee's income tax.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: According to the chapter, the 1954 exemption covered employer-sponsored health insurance specifically, so an employee would still owe income tax on a car received from their employer as a gift.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: The chapter says the 1954 tax exemption 'guaranteed' that employees would thenceforth prefer getting health insurance through their employers rather than buying it directly from insurers. According to the chapter, why?
options: Employers can negotiate group rates for identical coverage that no individual buyer is ever offered.
Wage rules carried over from the war still barred employers from turning benefit spending into raises.
Premiums an employer pays are deductible as a business expense, while money paid out as raises is not.
Money routed through wages is taxed before it can buy a policy; an employer-paid premium is not.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: The chapter notes that an employee would owe income tax on a car given by their employer as a gift, or on a shopping-spree bonus, though not on an employer-paid health insurance premium. What is this contrast meant to show?
options: Employers turned to cars and travel to reward workers once the postwar boom began.
Non-cash compensation is harder to value and so gets taxed more heavily than wages.
Fringe benefits of every kind sat outside the wartime wage and price controls.
The exemption singles out health insurance, not fringe benefits generally.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: Maya, a CNC machinist, is weighing two job offers she has worked out to cost each employer about the same in total. Harbor Fabrication offers a lower salary and pays the full premium on a family health policy. Datum Tool offers a higher salary and leaves each hire to arrange family coverage independently. The policy Harbor pays for is the one Maya would pick out on her own anyway. Datum's recruiter keeps returning to a single point: salary is money Maya controls, to spend, bank, or insure with exactly as she likes. Applying the chapter's account of compensation, which offer should Maya expect to leave her family with more to live on once they are insured?
options: Either — the two come out about the same
It depends on how large the premium is
Harbor Fabrication's offer
Datum Tool's offer
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: The owner of a landscaping firm has budgeted for one new benefit next season and has two candidate uses of the same money per crew member. One is paying the premium on each worker's family health policy; crew members currently buy coverage out of their own pay. The other is providing each worker a late-model pickup for personal use, replacing whatever they drive now. Since word got out, the pickups are all the crew talks about at lunch. On Flynn's account of compensation, which choice leaves each crew member better off?
options: Either — the same money delivers the same value
Providing the pickups
Neither — a plain raise of the same size would beat both
Paying the premiums
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: A retail chain let each of its three regional managers spend the same amount per employee on a year-end reward, with each manager choosing the form. Northeast staff received a straightforward cash bonus in their December pay. Midwest staff picked a travel package from a catalog their manager arranged. Southern staff received store credit to spend at a partner department store. The Midwest's choice drew the loudest reception, with staff trading itineraries for weeks, while some in the Northeast shrugged at what looked like an ordinary payday. On Flynn's account of compensation, which region's employees, if any, ended up ahead of the others?
options: The South staff with store credit
None — the three came out about even
The Northeast staff with cash bonuses
The Midwest staff with travel packages
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: According to the chapter, what do many Americans do out of worry over their employer-provided health benefits?
options: They stay in jobs they hate and delay retiring until they qualify for Medicare.
They retire early to lock in the retiree coverage their employers have promised.
They switch employers frequently in search of more generous benefit packages.
They buy individual marketplace policies to supplement what employers provide.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: According to the chapter, because workers expected employers to pay most or all of their health insurance premiums, an American business traditionally took on a substantial fixed cost for every employee it hired.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: According to the chapter, the American rise of freelancers and independent contractors rests on an exchange between firm and worker. Which statement captures that exchange as the chapter describes it?
options: The firm turns the cost of a benefit into higher cash pay, and the worker uses the added pay to buy an individual policy.
The firm moves its premium share onto the worker's invoice, and the worker recovers that share as a deduction at tax time.
The firm secures identical work at lower hourly rates, and the worker gains full control over scheduling and choice of projects.
The firm escapes buying coverage for the role, and a young, healthy worker accepts working without employer-provided insurance.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: According to the chapter, America's employer-based arrangement burdens the two sides of the labor market in characteristic ways. Which pairing states the burdens the chapter actually describes?
options: Employers are legally required to insure all full-time workers, and employees must enroll in whichever plan their employer selects.
Employers take on a sizable fixed cost with every person they hire, and employees risk their coverage whenever they leave a job.
Employers must match every raise with added benefit spending, and employees forfeit their premium history when they switch insurers.
Employers owe premiums that climb with each worker's salary, and employees owe income tax on the value of the coverage they receive.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: Four accountants recently faced a fork in their careers. Lukas (Stuttgart, Germany) turned down steady contract work from two former clients and stayed at a firm where he feels he has stopped learning. Tessa (Columbus, United States) turned down steady contract work from three former clients and stayed at a firm she has often thought of leaving. Priya (Toronto, Canada) turned down steady contract work from a longtime client and stayed at a firm whose commute she has long complained about. Marcus (Denver, United States) left his firm for a rival offering a bigger title, a corner office, and a signing bonus he bragged about for weeks. Flynn's argument in this chapter explains one of these decisions. Whose?
options: Lukas's
Priya's
Tessa's
Marcus's
items.source_anchor: Chapter 10 → The Origins of America’s Employment-Based Health Insurance System

items.stem: Consider four firms' staffing habits. An American ski lodge in Vermont staffs each winter with independent contractors, bringing many of the same cooks and guides back season after season. An American software firm in Boise keeps its year-round product work with independent contractors, re-engaging the same programmers contract after contract. A German engineering firm in Hamburg has kept its year-round design work with independent contractors for a decade, bringing back the same drafters project after project. An American retailer in Memphis answers a long slump by cutting pay, ending travel, and canceling perks, while keeping its full staff on the payroll. The retailer

The ski lodge

bank_meta.chapter_title: How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.11.1: Identify the parts of a private insurance contract as the chapter defines them: the premium paid for the right to compensation when a pre-specified event occurs, the claim filed when one does and usually paid to a second party on the insured's behalf, the deductible as the monetary limit below which no claim can be filed, and zero-deductible first-dollar coverage.
learning_objectives.11.2: Distinguish the US meanings of copay, a fixed dollar charge to access a service that is the same whatever the service costs, and coinsurance, a fixed percentage of bills above the deductible sometimes capped by an annual limit, from the usage the book adopts, under which copay means the percentage form.
learning_objectives.11.3: Explain how deductibles and percentage copays each restore first-party payment inside an insurance contract: below the deductible the insured pays everything and so comparison-shops, while a percentage copay above it keeps the insured sharing every bill, so any savings the insured finds also cut the insurer's payout.
learning_objectives.11.4: Explain how, on the chapter's account, employer-paid coverage makes health insurance seem free and steers workers toward first-dollar, cover-anything policies, and how confronting people with the full premium instead leads them to weigh what a policy is worth.
learning_objectives.11.5: Explain how the chapter maps health insurance onto the common-pool problem: a claims pool limited by the premiums collected stands in for the commons' limited grass, free or nearly free care invites the same race to consume before others do, and unfettered access privatizes benefits while socializing costs.
learning_objectives.11.6: Given a novel shared-resource arrangement and a proposed fix, determine which of the chapter's three responses to a commons dynamic the fix instantiates -- external rationing by access rules, self-rationing through a positive price at the point of use, or expanding the pool while access stays free -- and hence the outcome the chapter's logic predicts.

Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost He.text: A deductible is the floor below which no claim exists, so spending under it is the patient's own and gets shopped for. Above it, paying a share of each bill keeps that pressure on, and a cheaper bill shrinks the insurer's payment too, which is how premiums can fall. Hidden premiums and coverage of everything remove the restraint. A limited claims pool that anyone may draw on freely invites the same ruin as a common pasture.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what does an individual obtain by paying a premium under a private insurance contract?
options: The right to receive monetary compensation if one or more pre-specified events comes to pass, usually paid to a second party on the insured's behalf.
A guarantee that every expense of repair or treatment the insured incurs during the policy year will be reimbursed, paid directly to the insured as each bill arrives.
A refundable stake in the pool of premiums the company collects, paid back in proportion to contributions if no pre-specified event occurs.
A promise that the company will cover any event the insured reports, paid to whichever provider or person the insured designates in the claim.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: The chapter's insurance primer describes several contract features that adjust how much of a claim's total cost is paid by the insurance company rather than by the insured. According to the chapter, which of the following is the deductible?
options: An annual ceiling on the insured's cumulative payments, beyond which the company pays all further claims in full.
A monetary limit below which the policyholder can file no claims and so pays every cost as a first party.
A fixed dollar charge the insured must pay to access a service, identical whatever the service turns out to cost.
A fixed percentage of each bill that the insured must pay, with the insurance company covering the remaining share.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, 'first-dollar coverage' presumably refers to policies under which the insured covers the first dollars of each year's costs out of pocket, with the insurance company stepping in only after that early spending.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, in the terminology used in the United States, what does the word 'copay' refer to?
options: A fixed percentage of each bill that the insured owes on claims filed above the annual deductible
A recurring fee paid to the insurer for the right to compensation when a pre-specified event occurs
A monetary limit below which the insured cannot file any claims with the insurance company
A fixed dollar charge the insured pays to access a service, the same whatever the service costs
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: Flynn announces that the book will adopt the Singaporean terminology for cost sharing. According to the chapter, when the rest of the book says an insured person owes a 'copay', what arrangement is it describing?
options: The insured and the insurer owe a jointly shared premium, having enrolled in the coverage as partners
The insured owes the entire cost of covered events until cumulative spending moves past the deductible
The insured owes a fixed percentage of each bill above the deductible, the insurer paying the rest
The insured owes a set dollar amount every time a covered service is used, whatever that service costs
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: Flynn explains why the book will use the word 'copay' in its Singaporean sense rather than keeping the US term 'coinsurance'. According to the chapter, which of the following is one of his stated reasons?
options: Singapore's usage names forms of cost sharing for which American terminology has no word at all
Percentage charges give the insured a stronger incentive to shop around than fixed dollar charges do
The arrangement US usage calls a copay has largely disappeared from American insurance contracts
The word 'coinsurance' misleadingly suggests the two parties are enrolling for insurance together
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, US-style coinsurance does not attach to every dollar of medical spending: the insured's percentage share is owed only on claims filed once the deductible has been reached, and some policies cap the arrangement at an annual limit, past which the insurer pays all further claims in full.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, John holds a car insurance policy with an annual deductible he has not yet come close to reaching. When a covered event occurs while his cumulative costs are still below that deductible, how does Flynn say the bill gets paid?
options: John pays a set dollar charge to access the service and the insurer picks up the rest of the bill.
John pays a fixed percentage of the bill while the insurance company covers the remaining share.
John pays the entire bill out of his own pocket as a first party; no third-party payment occurs.
The insurer pays the whole bill, then recovers the amount by raising John's premium at renewal.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: Flynn illustrates percentage copays with John, who faces a repair bill well above his annual deductible and hunts down a cheaper shop that can do the same work. According to the chapter, why does the percentage form of the copay make John's bargain-hunting matter to the insurance system as a whole, and not just to John?
options: Since a percentage charge stings on every claim, John is deterred from filing small claims at all, which keeps routine events off the insurer's books entirely.
Since fewer dollars change hands on a cheaper repair, the insurer processes less paperwork per claim, and lighter overhead is what lets it lower the premiums it charges.
Since the percentage is capped at an annual maximum, John's careful shopping protects the insurer from ever facing the catastrophic bills that drive premiums upward.
Since John owes a share of whatever the bill turns out to be, a cheaper bill cuts the insurer's payout along with John's own share, so the savings are shared.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, a deductible serves the insurance arrangement in two distinct ways at once. Which pairing states both of the effects Flynn attributes to it?
options: It caps the insured's cumulative payments at an annual maximum, and it commits the insurer to paying every further claim in full once that annual maximum has been passed.
It sets a fixed dollar charge the insured pays to access each covered service, and it steadies insurer costs because that charge stays the same whatever the visit turns out to cost.
It splits each covered bill between insured and insurer in a fixed proportion, and it passes any savings the insured negotiates on a repair through to the insurance company as well.
It turns the insured into a comparison shopper on bills below the threshold, and it keeps paperwork light because no claim can be filed until spending reaches that level.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: Flynn's example has John filing a claim for a repair well above his annual deductible, subject to a percentage copay. According to the chapter, if John shops around and gets the work done more cheaply, the benefit presumably accrues to John alone, since the insurer's payout is set by the policy rather than by what the repair actually costs.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, what does the term 'moral hazard' refer to?
options: A tendency for people to change their behavior when somebody else is picking up the tab
A temptation for insured people to file claims for pre-specified events that never actually occurred
An arrangement in which the insurer pays a second party, such as a body shop, on the insured's behalf
A monetary limit below which people holding insurance policies cannot file any claims
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: The chapter claims that workers in the United States tend to want first-dollar coverage and policies that cover anything and everything. On its account, what produces that preference?
options: Workers know precisely what their employers spend on coverage and conclude that the broadest possible policy is the only way to capture the full value of that spending
Workers rarely see what their employer pays, so the coverage seems free, and a worker weighing seemingly free policies has no reason to favor one that covers less
First-dollar policies generate less claims paperwork for insurers, and those overhead savings come back to workers as longer and longer lists of covered services
Employers place only generous, first-dollar plans on the benefits menu, so a worker who might have preferred a leaner, cheaper policy never encounters one to choose
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: The chapter asks readers to imagine automobile insurance that covered car washes, oil changes, and unlimited gasoline. According to the chapter, what is this comparison meant to show?
options: That covering items people could pay for directly leads them to consume far more of those items than they would if the money came out of their own pockets
That routine, predictable purchases are not genuine insurable risks, since a pre-specified event must be uncertain before an insurer can price it into a premium
That adding routine services to a policy raises premiums chiefly through the cost of processing countless small claims, not through any change in driver behavior
That expanding the list of covered events mainly serves the insurer, which can justify charging a higher premium for every service added to the contract
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, a person who must pay the full cost of a health insurance premium out of their own pocket will presumably gravitate toward first-dollar, cover-anything policies, since seeing the full price makes the value of maximum protection obvious.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, what did Garrett Hardin's famous article 'The Tragedy of the Commons' give as its primary historical example of the common-pool problem?
options: The coastal fishing grounds that were stripped bare because any boat could take as large a catch as it pleased.
The free national healthcare systems that had to be fenced in with rationing rules to survive.
The publicly owned grazing pastures that many English communities maintained during the Middle Ages.
The village water wells that ran dry because no one could be charged for drawing water from them.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: When the chapter maps health insurance onto the medieval commons, what does Flynn say plays the part of the plot's limited supply of grass?
options: The yearly cap on copays, beyond which an insurer is obliged to pay every further claim entirely on its own.
The supply of physicians, hospital beds, and appointment slots available to policyholders at any moment.
The annual deductible, a monetary limit that each policyholder uses up as the year's medical bills accumulate.
The pool of money an insurer has for claims, since claims payments can never exceed the premiums collected.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, why does offering the insured free or nearly free care set off the same race to consume that ruined the medieval commons?
options: Each insured person knows the claims money is limited and that nothing stops anyone else from claiming it first, so all rush to consume before others do.
People from outside the plan hear that care is free and pour in as new claimants, swelling the number of users far beyond what the collected premiums had anticipated.
With a guaranteed payer behind every visit, providers rather than patients drive the race, ordering as many billable treatments as their schedules can accommodate.
Costless care makes people relaxed about protecting their own health, so they suffer more of the covered events and end up filing claims far more often than before.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter's account of the medieval commons, unfettered free access arguably socialized the plots' benefits while privatizing their costs — everyone shared in the gains from the open land, while the losses fell on whichever families arrived too late to graze.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: The chapter describes how the United States has responded to the commons dynamic Flynn sees in American healthcare. According to the chapter, what has that response been?
options: Fencing off access to the system with queuing rules and denial-of-care thresholds
Narrowing the set of pre-specified events that insurance policies agree to cover
Adding more money to the system each year while leaving its incentives unchanged
Confronting consumers with substantial deductibles as well as meaningful copays
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: According to the chapter, the United Kingdom keeps its free-at-use healthcare system from being overwhelmed by rationing access, through rules, queues, and care-denial thresholds, rather than by charging patients at the point of care.
options: True
False
