items.stem: Flynn writes that America has answered healthcare overuse by throwing more money at the system each year, which he compares to setting up additional commons plots. According to the chapter, why does that response fail to end the overuse?
options: Access still costs users nothing, so the race to consume the enlarged pool goes on
Providers simply raise their prices to capture whatever new money enters the system
Claims payments can never exceed premiums, so the extra money cannot reach patients
Insurer paperwork and overhead absorb the new money before it buys any added care
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: The chapter contrasts how the United Kingdom and Singapore each keep a limited healthcare pool from being overrun by a race to consume. According to Flynn, what distinguishes the two responses?
options: The UK expands its care budget yearly; Singapore holds its pool fixed as demand adjusts
The UK covers only core services; Singapore's policies cover anything and everything
The UK charges patients at the point of care; Singapore screens access by eligibility rule
The UK limits use by rule and queue; Singapore's users limit themselves against prices
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: A member-run ceramics studio keeps open shelves of clay and glazes from which any member may take materials while working. Most months the shelves are bare within two weeks, and members have taken to arriving at opening time on delivery days to move a month's supplies into their own lockers. At the annual meeting the studio votes to expand the materials budget, sizing it to the previous year's total usage plus a wide margin, with restocking twice as frequent. The treasurer calls it the largest materials commitment in the studio's history. Applying the chapter's commons logic, what should be expected?
options: Hoarding stops once the studio's spending becomes visible to members
The shortages end once supply is matched to what members actually use
The larger stock is consumed as before and the shortages return
Members weigh each use against its cost, taking only what their work needs
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: A flying club owns two light aircraft that members book on a shared calendar and fly as often as they wish, with the club's maintenance fund keeping both airworthy. The calendar is chronically overbooked, the engines are wearing toward overhaul years early, and the fund is running down. Concluding that members have been shielded from what their flying really costs, the board approves a steep increase in the flat annual dues so that, in its words, every member finally feels the cost of keeping these aircraft flying. Applying the chapter's commons logic, what should be expected?
options: Members fly less, each hour now weighed against what it costs them
Flying falls at first, then rebounds as the higher dues come to feel normal
The scramble for aircraft time and the rapid wear continue unabated
Members fly more, determined to get their money's worth from the higher dues
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

items.stem: A regional foundation maintains an emergency repair fund that any of its ninety member nonprofits may draw on when a roof leaks or a furnace fails. Requests are honored in the order received, and for three years running the fund has been empty by May, with directors filing for borderline repairs in January to get ahead of one another. A new administrator, hired from a bank's compliance office, answers with paperwork: a three-page application, a certified inspection before any request, a yearly cap of one award per organization, and committee sign-off on every grant. Drawing on the fund still requires no contribution from the nonprofit. Applying the chapter's commons logic, what should be expected?
options: Directors begin weighing each request against its cost and file only for true emergencies
The new rules hold only until directors learn to schedule inspections each winter in advance
The scramble to file first subsides, and the fund now lasts within its yearly means
The fund is drained as fast as before, since drawing on it still costs members nothing
items.source_anchor: Chapter 11 → How to Engineer Low-Cost Health Insurance

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.12.1: Explain why, on the chapter's account, giving primary care its own accessible delivery channel — eighteen subsidized polyclinics plus private clinics "practically on every block" — keeps Singapore's hospitals and their A&Es free to concentrate on acute care, and why the counterexample of a US free-care hospital whose emergency room absorbs the primary care of patients with no other access shows the cost of lacking that separation: each facility type concentrating on its intended purpose is what the chapter credits for short waits and high quality.
learning_objectives.12.2: Classify a described patient into the right tier of Singapore's delivery system — polyclinic or private clinic, acute general hospital, specialty center, community hospital, chronic sick hospital, nursing home — by the kind of care each exists to deliver, using the distinctions the chapter itself models: acute versus primary, well enough to leave acute care but not to go home, long-term dependence versus too sick for home care but short of hospitalization.
learning_objectives.12.3: Explain how Singapore General's two visibility devices are claimed to keep patients moving: the patient-number screens that lead each person through the hospital "like a trail of breadcrumbs" (and let the doctor confirm the right patient by number), and the public display of A&E wait times for the non-critical triage groups, which pressures staff by making their speed visible to the waiting room.
learning_objectives.12.4: Explain why the government assigned chronic sick hospitals, nursing homes and home hospice to Voluntary Welfare Organizations rather than running them directly — its stated belief in Aristotle's nation as a "community of communities", that people naturally form groups to help their neighbors — and how the funding mix, private giving plus government grants covering about a fifth of operating budgets, keeps that role viable without absorbing the VWOs into the state.
learning_objectives.12.5: Explain how the eldercare catalogue — house calls, home nursing, meals-on-wheels, escort and even maid services, plus senior care, dementia day care and day rehabilitation centers — all serves the one stated goal of letting the elderly live at home as long as possible, and why the chapter counts that goal a gain on both of its own measures: home care is less expensive and more humane than institutional care.
learning_objectives.12.6: Explain what the placement of the government's dental clinics — nearly all of them located in schools — is offered to show: it is the "very telling statistic" answering the worry that Singapore attends to the elderly at the young's expense, evidence of a cradle-to-grave approach that runs from childhood immunizations through adult screening programs to neighborhood gyms and affordable produce.
learning_objectives.12.7: Given a proposed public-hospital reform, determine whether it would reproduce the discipline the chapter credits to Singapore's arrangement — managerial autonomy over staff, wages, organization and prices; patients free to choose among many hospitals; and no recourse to taxpayer money, so a hospital that cannot attract enough patients to break even fails and its non-civil-service managers can be fired — or which of those elements its design removes.
learning_objectives.12.8: Given a described delivery system or a proposed consolidation, determine where everyday-care demand will land and what follows for the facility that absorbs it, judging by whether primary care has its own accessible channel rather than by whether the congested facility is adequately resourced.

Chapter 12 → What I Saw.text: Public hospitals deliver over four fifths of time-critical care; private practices deliver over four fifths of routine care. The public share of everyday care runs through eighteen neighbourhood clinics acting as one-stop shops, with subsidised consultations, screenings and dispensaries on site. Greeters and medical social workers meet patients at the door, the latter advising which public subsidies a person may claim. Anyone affluent using a public facility pays substantially more than someone of lesser means.

Chapter 12 → Freeing Hospital Emergency.text: Neighbourhood clinics were created deliberately so hospitals could concentrate on time-critical work. Where no such channel exists the emergency department absorbs everyday care instead: at one large American public hospital, waits have exceeded a full day because people with nowhere else to go arrive there for routine needs, and its resources were never meant for that. The claim concerns role rather than funding — give each facility one purpose and waits shorten.

Chapter 12 → Singapore’s Tiered Hospital.text: Hospitals are arranged in tiers, each specialising. General acute hospitals treat any severe illness or injury and carry emergency departments and major surgery. Specialty centres do comparable work inside a single field such as cardiology or oncology. Separate public institutions serve women and children, and psychiatric inpatients. Most acute beds sit in the public sector, because public hospitals are far larger than private ones even though private hospitals are the more numerous.

Chapter 12 → Visiting Singapore General.text: The oldest and largest public hospital runs near, but not at, full capacity and is staffed for service: porters who may not be tipped, a greeting desk with receptionists and social workers. Each arriving patient takes a number, and screens through the building show which numbers should move where, leading a person onward and letting a doctor confirm the right patient. Screens in the emergency waiting area post current waits, which pressures staff visibly.

Chapter 12 → Community Hospitals and Chr.text: Two kinds of facility handle hospitalisation that is not acute. One takes patients well enough to leave intensive treatment but not to go home, offering supervision and therapy aimed at return. The other gives long-term nursing to people left highly dependent by advanced illness. Both are run by non-profit philanthropic bodies, religious and secular, rather than by the state — a role government assigned on the view that a nation is a community of communities.

Chapter 12 → Singapore’s Elderly.text: The same philanthropic bodies run hospice services and nursing homes for those too unwell for care at home yet not ill enough for hospital. Beside them sits a catalogue of services delivered at home — visits by doctors, nursing, meals, transport, even help with housekeeping — and day centres offering therapy, supervision and activity. Every piece serves one goal: keeping people in their own homes as long as possible, which the author counts cheaper and kinder than institutions.

Chapter 12 → Singapore’s Cradle-to-Grave.text: Asked whether attention to the old comes at the young's expense, the author answers with where public dental clinics sit: nearly all of them inside schools. He reads this as evidence of a span from birth to death — childhood immunisation and vision checks, adult education and prevention, screening urged at set ages for blood pressure, diabetes and cancer. Supporting it are parkland, publicly funded neighbourhood gyms, and a push to keep produce affordable.

Chapter 12 → Why We Need Accountability.text: Each public hospital was turned into its own non-profit corporation: loosely supervised, but free to organise care, hire and dismiss staff, set pay and set its own prices. It competes for patients who may choose among many hospitals, so it must break even without needing to maximise profit. Crucially it cannot request public money if it fails, sitting outside the government's budget, and its managers hold no civil-service protection.

items.stem: According to the chapter, who delivers most of Singapore's primary care — the non-emergency walk-in appointments with general practitioners for things like checkups, sore throats, and the management of chronic conditions?
options: Public hospitals, whose outpatient departments deliver most routine checkups alongside the acute medicine they dominate.
The eighteen neighborhood polyclinics, which deliver over 80 percent of it, with private clinics taking the remainder.
Hospital A&E departments, which take non-emergency walk-ins for everything from sore throats to annual checkups.
Private clinics, which deliver over 80 percent of it; eighteen neighborhood polyclinics handle the public share.

items.stem: The chapter describes Los Angeles County Hospital as a large, government-funded facility that delivers free care — and reports that its emergency room nonetheless becomes swamped every day, with waits known to exceed twenty-four hours. According to the chapter, why?
options: The hospital's budget and staffing are too small for the volume of genuinely acute cases arriving from across the county.
Free treatment invites patients to use the emergency room for minor complaints they would otherwise pay a clinic to handle.
Its arrangement with a university medical school pulls physicians away from patient care and toward their teaching duties.
Its indigent patients have no other way to get primary care, so they bring those needs to the emergency room.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 12 → Freeing Hospital Emergency Rooms from Having to Provide Primary and Urgent Care

items.stem: Flynn observes that acute-care hospitals in the United States are forced to deliver a large volume of primary care as well, especially through their emergency rooms. According to the chapter, why do Singapore's hospitals not end up in the same position?
options: The public hospitals are built with enough beds and staff to absorb everyday complaints alongside acute cases without strain.
Steep emergency-room charges discourage patients from bringing routine complaints to a hospital in the first place.
Everyday care has accessible outlets of its own, so each type of facility is left to concentrate on its intended purpose.
Hospital A&Es screen arriving walk-ins and redirect the non-urgent ones to polyclinics, keeping their own queues for true emergencies.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 12 → Freeing Hospital Emergency Rooms from Having to Provide Primary and Urgent Care

items.stem: According to the chapter, the lesson of Los Angeles County Hospital is that making hospital care free does not by itself keep an emergency room uncrowded: patients with no other accessible source of primary care will bring those needs to the emergency room anyway.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 12 → Freeing Hospital Emergency Rooms from Having to Provide Primary and Urgent Care

items.stem: According to the chapter's description of Singapore's tiered hospital system, what are the specialty centers set up to deliver?
options: Subsidized one-stop outpatient care, health screenings, and pharmacy services
Inpatient convalescent care and therapy for patients preparing to return home
Acute care confined to a single field, such as cardiology, oncology, or dermatology
Long-term inpatient nursing care for patients left highly dependent by advanced illness

items.stem: According to the chapter's account of Singapore's delivery system, consider a seventy-year-old who broke her hip in a fall and had surgery at an acute general hospital. Her surgeons now judge her condition stable, but she cannot yet walk unaided or look after herself, and her care team expects several weeks of inpatient therapy before she can live in her own flat again. Which facility type exists to deliver the care she now needs?
options: A community hospital
A chronic sick hospital
A nursing home
An acute general hospital
items.source_anchor: Chapter 12 → Community Hospitals and Chronic Sick Hospitals

items.stem: The chapter describes the range of care Singapore arranges for its elderly. Consider an elderly widower who has grown too frail for his daughter to look after him safely at home, even with home nursing visits; he needs help with bathing, medication, and getting around at all hours, while his ailments remain the routine ones of old age, managed with regular pills rather than intensive treatment. According to the chapter, which facility type exists to serve someone in his situation?
options: A community hospital
A chronic sick hospital
An inpatient nursing home
A neighborhood senior care center

items.stem: According to the chapter, each part of Singapore's delivery system concentrates on the kind of care it exists to deliver. A middle-aged office worker has lived with diabetes for years; he needs periodic appointments to review his blood-sugar readings, adjust his medication, and get advice on his diet. Where does the chapter's account place this kind of care?
options: At a polyclinic or private clinic
At one of the public specialty centers
At an acute general hospital's A&E
At a chronic sick hospital

items.stem: According to the chapter, what do the large computer screens in Singapore General's waiting rooms (and the smaller ones above its examination rooms) do with the patient numbers assigned at check-in?
options: They show the numbers of patients due at each department at that moment, leading each person through the hospital stop by stop.
They show the current wait time at each department, so patients can pick whichever part of the hospital is moving fastest at the moment.
They show each patient's place in the order of arrival, so everyone waiting can count how many people are ahead of them before being seen.
They page each patient by name the moment an examination room opens, so nobody has to keep track of an assigned number at all.

items.stem: According to the chapter, how does the public display of wait times in Singapore General's A&E waiting room keep things moving?
options: Patients who see a long wait can head to another hospital instead, so the display spreads demand across Singapore's many competing A&Es.
Patients who can see that things are moving stay settled and quiet, so the display works on the waiting room's mood rather than on the staff.
The Ministry of Health watches the posted times in real time and steps in to redirect hospital staff whenever one triage group's queue grows.
Staff know the whole waiting room can see how quickly patients are being processed, and that visibility presses them to keep things moving.

items.stem: The chapter likens the patient numbers assigned at check-in at Singapore General to the numbers taken at certain American fast-food restaurants. According to the chapter, how does Singapore General's use of its numbers differ?
options: Fast-food numbers follow the order of arrival, while Singapore General orders its numbers by urgency so the sickest patients are called first.
Fast-food numbers settle who gets served next, while Singapore General uses its numbers to send each patient wherever they need to go next.
Fast-food numbers are good for a single transaction, while Singapore General issues each patient a fresh number at every department they visit.
Fast-food numbers are called out loud, while Singapore General shows numbers on screens to keep each patient's identity private from the room.

items.stem: According to the chapter, Singapore General's check-in numbers work like the take-a-number tickets at American fast-food restaurants — their job is to show who is next in line — and when doctor and patient finally meet, the doctor still needs the patient's name or chart to be sure the right person is in the room.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, who runs Singapore's chronic sick hospitals?
options: For-profit private hospital companies, which operate them under management contracts awarded by the Ministry of Health.
The Ministry of Health, which staffs and operates them directly as the long-term nursing arm of the public hospital system.
Voluntary Welfare Organizations, private non-profit philanthropic groups, which manage the facilities and hire their own staff.
The public acute general hospitals, which run them as attached step-down wards for patients finished with time-critical care.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 12 → Community Hospitals and Chronic Sick Hospitals

items.stem: Singapore's chronic sick hospitals are managed by religious and secular charities rather than by the Ministry of Health. According to the chapter, why does the government leave these facilities in the VWOs' hands instead of running them directly?
options: It wants intermediate care to face the same break-even discipline as the public hospitals, which cannot ask for more taxpayer money.
It aims to keep the cost of long-term care off the public budget, by leaving these facilities to be financed by private charitable donors.
It believes a nation is a community of communities — people naturally form groups to make a positive difference for their neighbors.
It inherited facilities the charities had already built, and has simply chosen not to disturb an arrangement that predates the state.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 12 → Community Hospitals and Chronic Sick Hospitals

items.stem: According to the chapter, how do the VWOs that run Singapore's chronic sick hospitals stay financially viable?
options: They depend on private charitable giving alone, keeping government money at arm's length to preserve their independence from the state.
They charge patients enough to break even, competing for intermediate-care patients just as the public hospitals compete for acute ones.
They are funded mostly by government grants, with private donations topping up the remaining share of their operating budgets.
They rely on a mix of private charitable giving and government grants that cover about a fifth of their annual operating budgets.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 12 → Community Hospitals and Chronic Sick Hospitals

items.stem: According to the chapter, the government's grants keep the VWOs financially able to run chronic sick hospitals, inpatient nursing homes, and home-based hospice services without making the organizations part of the state: the VWOs themselves still manage the facilities and hire and fire their own staff.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter describes a wide set of eldercare services in Singapore, from home-based help to neighborhood day centers. According to the chapter, what is 'the whole point' of this entire catalogue of services?
options: To concentrate long-term eldercare in inpatient nursing homes staffed by gerontologists and eldercare specialists.
To allow as many elderly people as possible to continue living at home for as long as possible.
To shift the burden of eldercare from government programs onto the Voluntary Welfare Organizations.
To free younger family members from daily eldercare duties so that they can remain in the workforce full-time.

items.stem: The chapter's eldercare catalogue ranges from doctors' house calls, home nursing, and meals-on-wheels to escort services, maid services, dementia day care, and day rehabilitation centers. According to the chapter, what makes this assortment a single strategy rather than a miscellaneous list of benefits?
options: Each service takes over a hospital function, so acute wards can discharge elderly patients earlier and keep beds available.
Each service is run by the same Voluntary Welfare Organizations, so one community group coordinates a person's entire eldercare.
Each service removes a different obstacle to staying at home, so together they keep that arrangement workable as long as possible.
Each service marks one stage of decline, moving the elderly in planned steps from independent living toward nursing-home placement.

items.stem: According to the chapter, Singapore's effort to keep the elderly living at home as long as possible is at bottom a budget measure: home care saves the system money compared with institutional care, but the saving comes at a cost to the elderly person, since institutional care remains the more humane arrangement.
options: True
False

items.stem: Senior care centers, dementia day care centers, and day rehabilitation centers are facilities outside the home, yet the chapter presents them as serving its stated goal of keeping the elderly living at home. According to the chapter, how do these centers serve that goal?
options: They take the work of caregiving off relatives permanently, so families never have to provide eldercare at home themselves.
They cover the working hours when relatives cannot provide care and rebuild the ability to manage everyday tasks at home.
They screen elderly applicants and decide who qualifies for house calls, home nursing, and the other home-based services.
They postpone nursing-home placement by giving families overnight respite stays whenever caregiving becomes too much.

items.stem: According to the chapter, nearly all of the dental clinics run by Singapore's government are located in which setting?
options: In the neighborhood polyclinics
In the public specialty centers
In the country's schools
In the neighborhood senior care centers

items.stem: The chapter raises the worry that Singapore may be paying too much attention to the elderly at the expense of the young, then answers it with what it calls a 'very telling statistic': of the 235 dental clinics the government runs, 221 are in schools. According to the chapter, what is this statistic offered to show?
options: That Singapore delivers dental care mainly through the public sector, unlike most primary care
That government attention to healthy living spans every stage of life, childhood included
That responsibility for children's healthcare rests with the school system, not the ministry
That Singapore has moved health spending away from eldercare programs and toward the young

items.stem: The dental-clinic statistic appears immediately after the chapter's long description of Singapore's eldercare services. According to the chapter, what question is the statistic meant to settle at that point?
options: Whether Singapore's attention to the elderly comes at the expense of its young
Whether the Voluntary Welfare Organizations can keep their nursing homes funded
Whether Singapore's dental care is as affordable as the rest of its medical care
Whether elderly patients can get dental treatment without going to a hospital

items.stem: According to the chapter, the approach evidenced by the school dental clinics extends well beyond childhood: adults are encouraged into screening programs for conditions like high blood pressure and breast cancer, and neighborhoods receive publicly funded gyms and markets stocked with affordable fruits and vegetables.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, what did Singapore's government do to each public hospital in order to force the public sector to be competitive?
options: Placed it under the direct operational command of the health ministry
Merged it with the private hospitals serving the same region
Sold it outright to a private hospital-management company
Converted it into a legally independent nonprofit corporation

items.stem: According to the chapter, because Singapore's public hospitals remain government institutions, their managers are civil servants: if a hospital runs in the red, the shortfall is the ministry's problem to cover, and the managers' own jobs are protected.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter says Singapore's public hospitals are under no pressure to maximize profits. Why, on its account, must they nonetheless work at being competitive?
options: Patients have their choice of many hospitals, so each must attract enough patients to break even
Government grants are renewed only for the hospitals that outperform their private competitors
The Ministry of Health audits each hospital annually and replaces boards that miss its benchmarks
Their charters require them to match whatever prices the nearby private hospitals set

items.stem: According to the chapter, why can't a Singapore public hospital that fails to break even simply ask for more taxpayer money, the way the chapter says US public hospitals do when they operate in the red?
options: The health ministry's funds are reserved by statute for the polyclinics and specialty centers
A balanced-budget clause in the constitution bars the ministry from covering hospital deficits
As a legally independent nonprofit, it sits outside the government and its budgeting process
Its charter makes it close any shortfall by charging its wealthier patients substantially more

items.stem: A province reorganizes its public secondary schools on what it calls the self-reliant model. The education ministry names each school trust's founding governors, approves its charter, audits its accounts every year, and the schools keep their state crests and official titles. Within that frame, each trust engages and dismisses its own teachers, sets their pay, arranges its own timetable, and prices its own term fees. Those fees are the trust's whole income; a trust that cannot cover its costs is wound up, and its head, serving on an ordinary employment contract, loses the post. Pupils are enrolled at the school serving their home district. Judged against the chapter's account of Singapore's public hospitals, which part of that arrangement does this design fail to reproduce?
options: Managers with real control over operations
No part — the design reproduces all of them
A failure that falls on the institution itself
Users able to take their business elsewhere

items.stem: A port city dissolves its ferry division and charters several route-based operator cooperatives in its place. Each cooperative is a nonprofit, barred from paying out any surplus to anyone. Each engages its own crews, sets their wages, fixes its own fares, and arranges its own sailings. Commuters may board any cooperative's boats on the overlapping routes, and several private water-taxi firms work the same harbor. The city pays no subsidy: a cooperative whose fares cannot cover its costs is deregistered, and its managers, employed by the cooperative rather than the city, are out of work. Whenever that happens, the city promptly licenses a replacement operator for the vacant landings so that crossings never lapse. Judged against the chapter's account of Singapore's public hospitals, what does this design do?
options: Reproduces the whole arrangement
Removes the users' power to leave
Removes the managers' operating freedom
Removes the penalty for failing

items.stem: A country breaks its state broadcaster into six regional companies, each a separate corporation outside the public service. Viewers subscribe to whichever of the six they like, or to private channels instead. A company that cannot cover its costs from subscriptions is liquidated — two have already closed, their directors dismissed with no public-sector post to fall back on — and the reform is celebrated as the end of the broadcasting bailout. Each company's journalists and technicians come to it by posting from a single national staffing corps, which grades and pays them on its uniform scale, and the monthly subscription price is set countrywide by the communications ministry. Judged against the chapter's account of Singapore's public hospitals, which part of that arrangement does this design fail to reproduce?
options: Viewers free to switch to a rival
Operating freedom for the managers
No part — all of it is reproduced
Failure borne by the company and its chiefs

items.stem: According to the chapter, why did Singapore intentionally create its polyclinics?
options: To put the country's specialist services within reach of every neighborhood
To take primary care over from the private clinics that had dominated the field
To manage primary care so that hospitals could be freed up to handle acute care
To give public hospitals overflow wards for use during stretches of peak demand
items.source_anchor: Chapter 12 → Freeing Hospital Emergency Rooms from Having to Provide Primary and Urgent Care

items.stem: Flynn describes Los Angeles County Hospital, the large government-funded free-care facility where his mother worked. According to the chapter, what swamps its emergency room every day?
options: Acute patients transferred in from nearby private hospitals
Staffing shortages that leave each shift short of physicians
Indigent patients with no other way to reach primary care
Severe trauma cases funneled to it from across the county
items.source_anchor: Chapter 12 → Freeing Hospital Emergency Rooms from Having to Provide Primary and Urgent Care

items.stem: The chapter reports that in Singapore wait times are short and service quality is high. What explanation does it give?
options: Funding runs generous enough that no facility is ever left short of staff
Each kind of facility can concentrate on the care it exists to deliver
Patients must obtain a polyclinic referral before a hospital will see them
Private hospitals absorb the overflow whenever public ones become crowded
items.source_anchor: Chapter 12 → Freeing Hospital Emergency Rooms from Having to Provide Primary and Urgent Care

items.stem: The chapter presents Los Angeles County Hospital - large, government-funded, and swamped daily - to show that what overwhelms such a facility is everyday demand from patients who lack any other way of getting primary care, not a shortfall in the facility's own resources.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 12 → Freeing Hospital Emergency Rooms from Having to Provide Primary and Urgent Care

items.stem: A city runs a flagship research library downtown - rare-manuscript vaults, subject specialists, a conservation lab - whose floor space, staffing, and open hours each exceed all eleven of its storefront branches combined. The branches are where residents of neighborhoods in which few homes have computers or printers do their everyday borrowing, printing, and homework help. To fund a new archive wing at the flagship, the council votes to close every branch. Applying the reasoning Flynn's chapter models, what should the city expect at the flagship?
options: Its specialist patrons decamp before everyday traffic arrives
Most former branch users simply stop using the system
Everyday demand floods it, and its specialist work degrades
It carries the combined traffic with capacity to spare
items.source_anchor: Chapter 12 → Freeing Hospital Emergency Rooms from Having to Provide Primary and Urgent Care

items.stem: For years a county's trial court - which hears everything from felony cases to civil suits of any size - has run a long backlog, and a review panel is weighing four features of the county. Its scheduling software, bought in the nineties, books hearings one courtroom at a time and is prone to double-booking. A nine-week clerks' strike two winters ago left a full season's filings stacked in boxes, hundreds reportedly still unlogged. The court's budget has risen twice this decade while its incoming docket has climbed steadily year over year. And the magistrate window where residents once settled small disputes without a lawyer now opens two mornings a month at the county's far edge. By the chapter's reasoning, which feature is doing the most to keep the trial court clogged?
options: The obsolete scheduling software
The shrunken magistrate window
A budget outpaced by the docket
The strike's unlogged filings
items.source_anchor: Chapter 12 → Freeing Hospital Emergency Rooms from Having to Provide Primary and Urgent Care

items.stem: At a metal-parts plant, the breakdown crew - the machinists who respond when a production line stops - has been slow for years, and complaints about it paper the crew room walls. Ever since the tool cribs closed in an old cost cut, operators have also brought the crew their routine work: blade sharpening, gauge calibration, fixture tweaks. A new plant manager reopens a walk-up tool crib on every floor, each staffed by apprentices, while the breakdown crew itself gets nothing - no added machinists, no new equipment, and a budget frozen at last year's figure. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what should be expected of breakdown response?
options: Nothing improves until the crew itself gets resources
Operators keep hauling routine jobs to the crew regardless
Breakdown calls start getting answered faster
The apprentice cribs clog and push work back onto the crew

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.13.1: Identify the funding sources the chapter says Singapore's system blends — automatic savings, public and private insurance, a fully endowed safety net, and direct government subsidies for the poor — and the three integrated programs at its heart, the 3Ms: MediSave (mandatory savings for future healthcare expenses), MediShield (a very affordable high-deductible insurance plan), and MediFund (a safety net paying the healthcare costs of the indigent).
learning_objectives.13.2: Explain why Flynn opens the financing discussion by asking readers to set aside their presuppositions: Singapore mixes market-based and central-planning incentives, which looks contradictory only from inside a theory, and his announced standard — theories usually fail in the real world — is what works in practice, which Singapore is running.
learning_objectives.13.3: Explain how, according to the chapter, the public-hospital ward-class design delivers "quality and affordable basic medical services for all": every class of ward receives the same medical care from the same physicians and nurses, the classes differ only in amenities, and richer patients are encouraged to pay much more for their accommodations so that their payments — together with massive direct subsidies — hold poorer patients' bills far lower.
learning_objectives.13.4: Apply the CPF's account earmarks and age rules to a novel case, determining which account — Ordinary, Special, MediSave, or Retirement — can fund a given expense for a person of a given age, or whether the rules block it.
learning_objectives.13.5: Explain how the chapter links Ordinary Account accumulation to transformation beyond healthcare: accumulated purchasing power at a young age means nearly everyone can fund a down payment — the world's highest homeownership rate against America's roughly 65 percent — and workers can pay to retrain when industries die, where the average American, forty percent of whom cannot cover an unexpected 400-dollar expense, must forgo retraining or borrow.
learning_objectives.13.6: Explain why Flynn presents the ceiling on MediSave balances as the system's crowning evidence rather than a retrenchment: balances accumulate across roughly three healthy decades until the national stock could fund Singapore's entire healthcare system for nearly four and a half years, the government capped balances only because collective savings were outgrowing likely future medical expenses, and no other country, he claims, has ever had to worry about over-saving for healthcare — set against America's underfunded trust funds.
learning_objectives.13.7: Explain the causal chain the chapter draws from MediSave balances to system-wide quality and low costs: accumulated purchasing power lets citizens shop around, and because they can take their MediSave money elsewhere, second parties are forced to relentlessly innovate to improve quality and reduce costs.
learning_objectives.13.8: Given a novel system that imposes a ceiling on an accumulating earmarked fund, determine what the need for that ceiling indicates about the fund's condition, judging by what circumstance makes a cap necessary at all rather than by whether a cap reads as retrenchment.

Chapter 13 → MediSave and the Miraculous.text: The financing chapters open by inviting the reader to set theory aside. The system mixes market incentives with central planning, which looks inconsistent only from inside a doctrine, and the author's declared test is what works in practice. Funding blends compulsory saving, insurance both public and private, an endowed safety net, and direct subsidy for the poor. Public wards differ in amenity but not in medical care, wealthier patients paying far more to subsidise poorer ones.

Chapter 13 → Introducing the 3Ms.text: Three linked programmes sit at the centre of the financing system. The first is compulsory saving whose balances are reserved for future medical costs. The second is insurance carrying a high deductible and a very low premium. The third is a safety net paying for the care of those who cannot. They are designed to work together rather than separately, and the chapters take them in turn, beginning with the savings the others draw upon.

Chapter 13 → A System for Saving.text: Compulsory saving directs roughly a third of a worker's gross pay into four earmarked accounts. The money enters untaxed and remains the individual's property, so unspent balances pass to heirs — unlike the American payroll programmes, where unused contributions revert to the state. Before a certain age most of it flows to the account reserved for housing, education and insurance. The author credits that early accumulation with very high home ownership and with workers able to fund retraining.

Chapter 13 → The Security of Savings.text: Balances in the medical account may be spent only on care, for the holder or a family member — insurance premiums, inpatient treatment, selected outpatient courses. Because most people stay healthy for decades the fund accumulates long before it is needed, and the national total grew large enough to finance several years of the country's entire health spending unaided. It grew so large that government capped individual balances, sending the overflow to retirement instead.

items.stem: Flynn opens the chapter by describing the funding system he says works in practice in Singapore. According to the chapter, that system blends which combination of funding sources?
options: Dedicated payroll taxes, employer-sponsored insurance, voluntary charitable donations, and means-tested cash vouchers for the poor
Automatic savings, public and private insurance, a fully endowed safety net, and direct government subsidies for the poor
Voluntary personal savings, private insurance alone, hospital charity care, and refundable tax credits for the poor
General tax revenue, a single national insurer, modest user fees at the point of care, and hardship fee waivers for the poor

items.stem: The chapter introduces three integrated programs at the heart of Singapore's healthcare financing system. According to the chapter, what is MediShield?
options: A very affordable, high-deductible health insurance plan
An insurance plan covering long-term care and assisted living
A mandatory savings program whose proceeds pay for future healthcare expenses
A social safety net that pays the healthcare costs of the indigent

items.stem: According to the chapter, MediSave is a mandatory savings program, and its proceeds are used to pay for future healthcare expenses.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, which statement describes the incentives Singapore's government builds into its healthcare system?
options: It mixes market-based incentives with central-planning incentives, using whatever works in practice.
It relies on central-planning incentives alone, having judged market mechanisms too risky for medicine.
It relies on market-based incentives alone, having removed central planning from healthcare entirely.
It switches between market incentives and central planning as successive governments revise the system.

items.stem: Flynn opens the financing discussion by inviting readers to step back from their presuppositions about the best way to run a healthcare system. According to the chapter, why is that step needed?
options: The chapter concedes that the evidence for Singapore's results is still incomplete, so judgment must be reserved until later chapters supply the data.
Readers' loyalty to the healthcare system of their own country would otherwise lead them to reject any arrangement imported from abroad.
The financing details that follow are technical, and readers without a background in insurance would otherwise misread the chapter's program descriptions.
Singapore's mix of incentives can seem contradictory when judged against a theory, and the chapter's announced test is what actually works in practice.

items.stem: The chapter quotes Yogi Berra: "In theory, there is no difference between theory and practice. In practice, there is." What work does the quotation do in Flynn's opening argument?
options: It concedes that Singapore's blend of incentives has no available theoretical justification, so the chapter must describe rather than analyze.
It reinforces the standard Flynn has announced: theories usually fail in the real world, so judge a system by what works in practice.
It signals that the opening is meant lightly, establishing a humorous tone before the chapter settles into its serious program descriptions.
It cautions that what succeeds in Singapore would remain untested theory elsewhere, so readers should not expect the arrangement to transfer.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the opening exercise treats Singapore's record as the fixed point rather than the thing in question: readers are asked to set aside their presuppositions about what should work in theory, while the fact that Singapore is running the world's best healthcare system in practice is what they are to focus on.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, the wards of Singapore's public hospitals are divided into different classes. What does the chapter say differs from one class of ward to the next?
options: The amenities available, such as internet access and cable TV
The level of medical care delivered to the patients staying there
The insurance program that pays each patient's treatment bills
Which of the hospital's physicians and nurses attend the patients

items.stem: According to the chapter, richer patients in Singapore's public hospitals are encouraged to pay much more than poorer patients pay. What are they paying more for, and what does the chapter say those larger payments do?
options: The services of the hospital's most experienced physicians — payments that fund those senior physicians' higher salaries
A higher class of medical care than the spartan wards receive — payments that let the hospital upgrade its equipment
Their government-set share of the treatment's full cost — payments that repay the direct subsidies granted to the poor
Their accommodations in the fancier wards — payments that help subsidize care for patients in the more spartan wards

items.stem: The chapter reports that a poorer patient's bill for any treatment at a Singapore public hospital comes out much lower than a richer patient's bill. According to the chapter, what holds the poorer patient's bill down?
options: Withdrawals from the poorer patient's MediSave Account, which reimburse most of the bill before it is ever presented
A more basic level of medical treatment in the spartan wards, which costs the public hospitals far less to provide
MediFund, the safety net that steps in to cover the healthcare costs of patients staying in the lower classes of ward
The much larger accommodation payments made by richer patients, plus massive direct subsidies from the government

items.stem: According to the chapter, the Ministry of Health's commitment to 'quality and affordable basic medical services for all' works out in practice to a tiered standard of care: public hospitals divide their wards into classes, and the much higher charges richer patients face in the fancier wards reflect a correspondingly higher grade of medical treatment delivered in those wards.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, balances in a CPF Ordinary Account can be spent on only three kinds of expenses. Which list gives them?
options: Educational expenses, family healthcare costs, and housing rentals
Housing purchases, educational expenses, and insurance premiums
Housing purchases, retirement income, and premiums for long-term care
Inpatient hospital treatments, outpatient chemotherapy, and insurance premiums

items.stem: According to the chapter, money in a MediSave Account can be spent on healthcare for the account holder's family members, not only on the account holder's own care.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter describes both the Special Account and the MediSave Account as savings earmarked for a future purpose. According to the chapter, how do the two differ in when their money can be spent?
options: MediSave can be spent on its earmark at any age; the Special Account cannot be touched before fifty-five
Both are locked until fifty-five, when the two are merged together to form the Retirement Account
The Special Account can be tapped early for family emergencies, while MediSave stays locked until retirement age
MediSave cannot be touched before fifty-five, while the Special Account may pay premiums at any age

items.stem: The chapter notes that CPF balances remain the personal property of the individual. It presumably follows that a worker under fifty-five could draw on his Special Account when a pressing family expense arises.
options: True
False

items.stem: Mei, fifty-seven and still working full-time, wants to pay the fees for a part-time accounting diploma out of her CPF savings. Under the account rules as the chapter describes them, which account can fund it?
options: Her Special Account
Her Retirement Account
Her MediSave Account
Her Ordinary Account

items.stem: Rafael, thirty-eight, is between jobs and asks to pay six months of apartment rent out of his CPF savings until he finds work. Under the account rules as the chapter describes them, what is the outcome?
options: A draw on his Special Account
A draw on his Ordinary Account
No draw: the rules block it
A draw on his MediSave Account

items.stem: Priya, forty-three, has saved so steadily that her MediSave balance has reached the government's ceiling. Under the account rules as the chapter describes them, where does the share of her next contribution that would have gone into MediSave flow instead?
options: Into her Retirement Account
Into her Ordinary Account
Into her Special Account
Back into her paycheck as take-home pay

items.stem: According to the chapter, money in a CPF Ordinary Account can be spent on only certain categories. Which are they?
options: Retirement income, long-term-care coverage, and assisted-living expenses
Anything the account holder chooses, since the balances are personal property
Inpatient hospital treatments, outpatient chemotherapy, and MediShield premiums
Housing purchases, educational expenses, and insurance premiums

items.stem: The chapter credits the Ordinary Account for Singapore's homeownership rate, which it calls the world's highest against an American rate of roughly 65 percent. According to Flynn, what produces that gap?
options: Savings accumulate automatically from early in working life, so nearly every Singaporean can fund a down payment.
Singapore's government builds subsidized public housing and sells it to citizens well below private-market prices.
American housing prices have risen so far relative to incomes that down payments are out of reach for most buyers.
Special government bonds guarantee Ordinary Account balances a return that outpaces any rise in housing prices.

items.stem: Flynn reports that forty percent of Americans cannot cover an unexpected 400-dollar expense. What is this figure doing in the chapter's argument?
options: It shows why America would need a fully endowed safety net like MediFund before trying a mandatory savings program.
It shows that American medical bills have grown large enough to exhaust the emergency funds of a typical household.
It shows that mandatory saving at Singapore's rates would leave many American families unable to meet routine bills.
It shows why displaced American workers must forgo retraining or borrow for it, having no ready savings to draw on.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the same CPF account that lets nearly every Singaporean fund a down payment is also what lets workers pay to retrain when industries die.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, why did Singapore's government impose a ceiling on MediSave Account balances?
options: The guaranteed minimum returns on the special government bonds had become too expensive to honor on ever-larger balances.
The country's collective health savings were becoming excessive relative to its likely future medical expenses.
Medical costs were rising so quickly that balances needed to be held back for the oldest savers first.
Account holders were steadily draining their balances on household expenses that had nothing to do with healthcare.

items.stem: The chapter asks readers to pause in 'bewildered awe' at the fact that Singapore needed to cap MediSave balances. Why does Flynn treat the ceiling as evidence of the system's success rather than as a scaling-back of it?
options: A cap is needed only when savings outgrow likely medical expenses — a worry he claims no other country has ever had.
It confirms that the guaranteed bond returns can grow balances faster than mandatory contributions ever could.
It shows the government adjusting program rules pragmatically, employing whatever works regardless of what the left or the right would prefer.
It demonstrates that redirecting the overflow will leave every saver's Retirement Account large enough to retire on.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the money already in MediSave Accounts could fund Singapore's entire healthcare system for nearly four and a half years without a penny from any other source. What is Flynn's point in setting that fact beside America's Medicare and Medicaid trust funds?
options: A single national health fund is easier to keep solvent than separate programs for the elderly and the poor.
Singapore's guaranteed government bonds earn better returns than the investments backing Medicare and Medicaid.
Singapore has already saved more than it will likely need, while the American programs are massively underfunded.
Americans could close the trust funds' shortfall by saving the same share of income that Singaporeans are required to.

items.stem: The chapter says money 'rapidly accumulates' in most people's MediSave Accounts, giving Singaporeans about three decades of built-up healthcare savings. What explanation does the chapter give?
options: Most people stay quite healthy into their fifties, so contributions pile up for decades while little flows out.
The S$3,000 the government deposits at birth compounds for decades under the guaranteed minimum bond return.
The government's budget-surplus distributions supply most of the money that gradually builds up in the accounts.
Balances cannot be touched for any purpose at all until the accounts are consolidated at age fifty-five.

items.stem: According to the chapter, Singapore's high healthcare quality and low costs are the result of which of the following?
options: The direct subsidies the government grants to poorer patients
The savings citizens have accumulated in their MediSave Accounts
The guaranteed minimum returns paid on special government bonds
The MediFund safety net that pays the healthcare costs of the indigent

items.stem: According to the chapter, what forces the second parties in Singapore's healthcare system (the parties citizens pay for their care) to relentlessly improve quality and reduce costs?
options: MediShield insurers refuse to reimburse any treatment that is priced above the prevailing market average.
Citizens can move their MediSave money to a different provider, so each one must keep earning their business.
The government makes its massive subsidies conditional on providers meeting annual cost-reduction targets.
The Ministry of Health imposes binding price ceilings on every class of ward in the public hospitals it oversees.

items.stem: Flynn argues that money accumulating in individual MediSave Accounts produces high quality and low costs for Singapore's healthcare system as a whole. According to the chapter, how does an individual's balance translate into system-wide results?
options: Large private balances let the government scale back the direct subsidies it must grant to poorer patients.
The pooled balances spread every member's medical risk across millions of accounts, the way insurance premiums do.
The combined national stock of savings stands ready to fund the whole system whenever other sources fall short.
Each citizen can shop around and walk away, so providers must compete on quality and price for every patient.

items.stem: According to the chapter, MediSave balances presumably hold down system-wide costs largely because the government pools the accumulated funds and negotiates lower prices with providers on citizens' behalf.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, why did Singapore's government impose a ceiling on MediSave Account balances?
options: Medical costs were rising faster than the accounts could keep pace with
Too many balances were being drawn down for spending unrelated to healthcare
Collective savings were outgrowing the nation's likely future medical costs
The guaranteed returns on account balances had become too costly to honor

items.stem: According to the chapter, mandatory saving does not stop once a person's MediSave balance reaches the government's ceiling — the money that would have flowed into MediSave is redirected toward the person's retirement instead.
options: True
False

items.stem: Flynn invites readers to sit in 'bewildered awe' at the fact that Singapore needed to impose a cap on MediSave balances at all. According to the chapter, what does the need for such a cap reveal about the system?
options: A tendency to save more for future care than that care is likely to cost
A state that remains the true owner of accounts it calls personal property
A savings mandate set beyond what ordinary households can keep bearing
A government confident enough to trim a benefit no democracy dares touch

items.stem: The chapter calls the money in Singapore's MediSave Accounts 'real security' and sets it against America's Medicare and Medicaid trust funds. According to the chapter, what is that contrast meant to establish?
options: The systems face a shared problem at different scales: both struggle to set aside enough against future care
America's trust funds hold more in total, yet Singapore's accounts carry stronger guarantees against market losses
Both countries cap health balances, but America applies its ceilings to collective funds rather than personal accounts
The systems face opposite problems: one had to restrain over-saving while the other's funds cannot stay filled

items.stem: A conservatory of music requires every department to divert a fixed share of its annual budget into a department-owned instrument reserve, spendable only on replacing instruments. This spring, in the same week it froze hiring and cancelled a hall renovation, the board announced a maximum balance for each reserve, with contributions above it flowing to the department's general operating fund. Faculty denounce the ceiling as one more cut dressed up as housekeeping. Applying the chapter's logic about what makes such a ceiling necessary at all, what does the board's move indicate about the reserves?
options: They had been losing ground against the rising price of instruments
They had been absorbing costs that belonged to the operating fund
They had become too uneven across departments to budget around
They had been growing past what replacements are likely to cost

items.stem: A federation of rowing clubs keeps four reserves. The travel fund collects automatic monthly dues from every member and pays out only toward travel to the world championships, which a typical member qualifies for once or twice in a lifetime. The regatta fund collects the same automatic dues from every member and pays the whole collection out each season to cover that season's entry fees and equipment haulage. The boathouse fund holds the federation's largest balance by far, built from bequests that arrive without pattern, and is drained nearly to zero whenever a dock or boiler finally gives out. The hardship fund collects a small levy the auditors set each year and pays out member grants that have outrun the levy's take in each of the past five seasons. A consultant, reasoning as the chapter does about earmarked savings, tells the board that exactly one of these reserves could ever need a maximum-balance rule. Which one?
options: The boathouse fund
The regatta fund
The hardship fund
The travel fund

items.stem: An archivist is reconstructing the finances of a weavers' guild that dissolved generations ago. The surviving rulebook shows that every member was tithed automatically from each season's sales into a personal loom reserve, spendable only on replacing a loom destroyed by fire or flood. A bylaw added in the guild's fortieth year capped each reserve and sent anything above the cap to the widows' pension. Nothing else about the reserves survives. Judging as the chapter does by what makes such a cap necessary at all, what should the archivist conclude about the reserves in the years before the bylaw?
options: They had grown too unequal from member to member to administer fairly
They had begun the long decline that eventually dissolved the guild
They had been mounting past what loom disasters were ever likely to claim
They had been drained by pension claims faster than tithes could refill them

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.14.1: Identify what the chapter says the original MediShield was — a low-cost catastrophic plan run by the CPF, covering hospitalization and expensive outpatient treatments (dialysis, chemotherapy, radiation) at public facilities, payable from MediSave — and the fact Flynn stresses as the key point: although participation was purely voluntary from the early 1990s until MediShield Life, the vast majority of residents enrolled, most adding paid supplementary coverage on top.
learning_objectives.14.2: Explain how, on the chapter's account, the S$2,000 annual deductible and the Ministry of Health's posted percentile cost data work together to create a competitive healthcare market — first parties spending their own money weigh cost against benefit and judge "Quality v. Price" themselves, so a provider who gets lazy on either loses the business — and why the chapter says that feedback is mostly absent in America, where third-party payment obscures both price and quality.
learning_objectives.14.3: Apply MediShield's cost-sharing structure — everything out of pocket below the annual deductible, then a copay on every dollar above it, shrinking but never reaching zero — to a novel patient situation, determining what share of the next healthcare dollar the patient bears and the incentive the chapter says this creates.
learning_objectives.14.4: Explain how the chapter argues MediShield's administration keeps a lid on prices and wasteful spending: a non-elected CPF bears the actuarial risk and decides coverage without the special-interest lobbying the chapter says plagues US state insurance regulators, while daily, annual and lifetime claims limits discipline providers' pricing and remind patients that MediShield "is not a bottomless common pool."
learning_objectives.14.5: Given a novel supplemental-insurance market design, determine which of the chapter's three Integrated Shield safeguards it preserves or omits and what the chapter's logic says follows — the MediShield-first rule that stops insurers cherry-picking the healthy out of the common pool, near-standardized coverage that forces competition onto premiums, or the cap on the number of plans against consumer information overload.
learning_objectives.14.6: Explain why the chapter calls MediShield "self-reinforcing and self-perpetuating" — high deductibles and meaningful copays create the competition that lowers prices, low prices allow the low premiums that induce mass participation, and mass participation sustains the competition — so that premiums far below the US average are presented as an outcome of the design itself.
learning_objectives.14.7: Given a proposed change to one link in a self-reinforcing insurance design — for instance reducing cost sharing to make a plan more generous — predict the downstream consequence the chapter's logic implies, tracing it through the chain that runs from cost sharing to competition to prices to premiums to participation rather than from generosity straight to take-up.

Chapter 14 → MediShield and the Right In.text: The insurance leg began as a low-cost plan against catastrophe, administered by the same body that holds the compulsory savings and payable from them. It covered hospital stays and a few costly outpatient courses, at public facilities only. The point the author stresses is take-up: enrolment was voluntary for roughly two decades and the great majority joined anyway, most of them buying additional private cover on top.

Chapter 14 → Coverage That Facilitates C.text: Below an annual deductible the patient pays everything, from saved funds or elsewhere, which gives a reason to weigh cost against benefit and creates a market the patient can walk away from. To make comparison possible the health ministry publishes percentile bill sizes for common procedures, so a quotation can be checked against the national spread. A patient may still choose the dearer surgeon with the better reputation; the point is that providers must attend to price and quality together.

Chapter 14 → Keeping Some Skin in the Ga.text: Above the deductible the patient still bears a share of every further dollar. That share shrinks as spending rises but never reaches zero, so the calculation never disappears — unlike plans where sharing stops at a ceiling, after which the insurer bears everything and the reason to shop vanishes. Programmes with little sharing remove it from the first dollar. Patients also pay their own premiums from their own balances, so cover is never mistaken for free.

Chapter 14 → Politically Independent Adm.text: The savings body runs the insurance and carries its actuarial risk, setting the deductible and the sharing thresholds. Unelected, it decides coverage without the lobbying the author attributes to American regulators. Limits by day, year and lifetime cap what may be drawn. Supplementary private plans are governed by three rules: the public plan must be held first, which stops insurers selecting the healthy; cover is near-standardised, so competition falls on premium; and plan numbers are capped against overload.

Chapter 14 → Shockingly Low Premiums.text: The chapter closes on cost, arguing the plan would be pointless if it were ruinous. The author sets the average American individual premium beside the published premiums for the public plan and finds the latter a small fraction of it. He presents this as a product of the design rather than a subsidy: real cost-sharing produces competition, competition lowers prices, low prices permit low premiums, and low premiums bring in nearly everyone, which sustains the competition.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what kind of program was the original MediShield?
options: A low-cost catastrophic plan run by the CPF, covering hospitalization and expensive outpatient treatments at public facilities
A mandatory savings account managed by the CPF, set aside for routine medical expenses rather than for insurance coverage
A comprehensive first-dollar plan run by private insurance companies, covering routine checkups and everyday care at any clinic
A supplementary plan sold by private companies, covering upgraded wards and medical treatments at private hospitals and clinics

items.stem: The chapter makes what it calls a key point about participation in the original MediShield program, before it became MediShield Life. What is that point?
options: Participation stayed low for years until the government finally made enrollment compulsory for every resident
Most residents turned the coverage down, preferring to pay for their healthcare out of their own savings
Enrollment was compulsory from the program's start, which is what produced its high participation rate
Even though enrollment was entirely voluntary, the vast majority of residents signed up for the coverage

items.stem: According to the chapter, most of the people enrolled in the original MediShield also chose to pay extra for supplementary coverage, such as Integrated Shield plans, on top of their basic MediShield policy.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, what cost information does Singapore's Ministry of Health post on the internet so consumers can make informed choices about medical procedures?
options: Quality ratings of individual surgeons compiled from government inspections
The 50th and 90th percentile bill sizes for common hospital procedures
A list of providers disciplined for charging above the national average
A government-approved fee schedule that caps what each provider may charge

items.stem: According to the chapter, the Ministry of Health posts 50th- and 90th-percentile cost data for common procedures. In Flynn's account, how does that posted data help create a competitive healthcare market?
options: It allows the government to identify and penalize providers whose prices run far above the posted percentiles
It replaces the need for out-of-pocket exposure, since informed patients economize even when a third party pays
It steers every patient toward the lowest-priced provider, driving all providers to converge on one price
It lets a patient judge whether a quoted price is competitive, so first parties can take their money elsewhere

items.stem: According to the chapter, why is the competitive feedback of "Quality v. Price" mostly absent in American healthcare?
options: Third-party payment obscures price and quality alike, so providers feel no pressure from the patients they treat
Too few providers compete in most American markets, so patients have no alternative to take their business to
Regulations prevent American providers from advertising their prices, keeping consumers in the dark about costs
American patients lack the expertise to judge clinical quality on their own, no matter who is paying the bill

items.stem: Flynn presents the S$2,000 annual deductible and the Ministry of Health's posted cost data as working together: spending below the deductible comes out of the patient's own pocket, which supplies the motive to shop carefully, while the posted percentile data supplies the information that makes careful shopping possible.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, how does a MediShield policyholder pay for healthcare spending below the annual deductible?
options: Entirely out of pocket, from a MediSave Account or any other personal funds
In full through MediShield, which reimburses the bills once claims are filed
Through government subsidy, with the cost recovered later from payroll taxes
Through a fixed percentage split between the patient and the MediShield fund

items.stem: According to the chapter, a MediShield policyholder who has spent well past the annual deductible still pays a share of every additional dollar of covered spending.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter emphasizes that MediShield's copays shrink as annual spending rises but never disappear. According to the chapter, why is the design built so that no level of spending is ever free to the patient?
options: So patients are steered toward supplementary Integrated Shield plans with fuller coverage
So MediSave balances are drawn down slowly enough to last through a member's retirement
So the fund collects enough patient revenue to keep its premiums from rising over the years
So patients keep weighing costs against benefits however much they have already spent
items.source_anchor: Chapter 14 → Keeping Some Skin in the Game

items.stem: The chapter arguably implies that because MediShield's copay rate shrinks as spending rises, the incentive to spend prudently largely fades away at the highest levels of spending.
options: True
False
