items.stem: The chapter notes that nobody in the favorable studies was assigned to a CDHP at random; everyone volunteered. According to the chapter, why does this undercut the conclusion that the plans' incentives caused the lower spending?
options: The volunteers were never observed before they switched, so there is no record showing whether any single person's spending rose or fell when that person entered a plan.
The kind of person who chose the plans, healthier or better educated or more financially astute, could account for the lower spending instead of the plans themselves.
CDHPs had enrolled only a modest share of American workers, leaving the volunteer samples too small to support a reliable comparison between the competing plan types.
People willing to try an unfamiliar new plan may have known their utilization was being analyzed and adjusted their habits during the study to look like prudent shoppers.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans Change Behavior

items.stem: The first problem the chapter raises with the favorable studies is that nobody followed individuals before and after they entered a CDHP. According to the chapter, what does this gap leave unknown?
options: Whether participants were skipping annual exams and screening tests in order to conserve their account balances.
Whether the lower spending came from using fewer services or from choosing cheaper options within the same care.
Whether a given person's health-spending behavior improves or worsens once that person enters a plan.
Whether the people who enrolled in the plans were healthier or better educated than the people who never joined.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans Change Behavior

items.stem: According to the chapter, the favorable studies it has just reviewed leave the behavioral question unsettled for two reasons: no individual was tracked before and after entering a plan, and participants volunteered rather than being assigned at random, so the lower spending could reflect who chose the plans rather than what the plans changed.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans Change Behavior

items.stem: In 2007, the state of Indiana began offering a Singapore-style CDHP to its employees as one option alongside the traditional plans they had always been able to choose. According to the chapter, the analysis the governor commissioned arrived at its finding that switchers cut spending by 35 percent through which comparison?
options: The state's total outlay on employee healthcare in the years before the CDHP was offered against its outlay in the years after.
Each switching employee's actual spending against an actuarial estimate of what a typical enrollee in that plan would have spent.
Each switching employee's own spending under the traditional plan against that same employee's spending after moving to the CDHP.
The average spending of employees who switched against the average spending of colleagues who stayed in traditional plans that year.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

items.stem: Indiana's CDHP enrollees were volunteers: employees who chose to leave a traditional plan for the new option. According to the chapter, why can the 35 percent drop found in the person-by-person comparisons not be explained by CDHPs attracting a healthier kind of participant?
options: Switchers kept going in for physicals and mammograms as often as before, which shows the group was never unusually health-conscious.
The consultants statistically adjusted every switcher's record for health status, education level, and financial sophistication before comparing the plan years.
A reduction as large as 35 percent is simply too big to be produced by the mix of people who enroll rather than by the plan itself.
Each comparison sets an employee against themselves, so habits, education, and preexisting conditions are the same on both sides of the switch.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

items.stem: Indiana offered its Singapore-style CDHP as one option alongside the traditional plans employees had always had. According to the chapter, because the person-by-person comparisons hold each switcher's habits, education, and preexisting conditions constant, the 35 percent reduction presumably shows that the employees who kept their traditional plans would also cut their spending if they were enrolled.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

items.stem: The chapter closes by granting that the Indiana comparisons demonstrate genuine behavior change, but only among the workers who elected the plan over the traditional options still on offer, and then poses a question it says this evidence cannot settle. According to the chapter, which question is left open, and why?
options: Whether the spending drop will erode in later years, since early savings could be masking deferred medical problems.
Whether employees who never opted in would also cut spending, since everyone in the data joined the plan by choice.
Whether the reductions came from skipping genuinely needed treatment, since spending records alone cannot reveal medical need.
Whether the switchers were an unusually healthy group to begin with, since volunteers often differ from those who decline.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

items.stem: According to the chapter, what does the state of Indiana do each year for an employee who selects the Singapore-style CDHP for their family?
options: It pays the full premium for the family policy and gifts an amount equal to the annual deductible into the employee's HSA.
It pays most of the family premium and matches, dollar for dollar, whatever amount the employee chooses to save in the HSA.
It reimburses the employee at the end of each year for whatever deductible and copay spending the family actually incurred.
It covers half of the family premium and funds the HSA through mandatory payroll deductions from the employee's wages.

items.stem: The chapter claims that under the Indiana plan's design there is no scenario in which a medical catastrophe financially wipes out a family. On the chapter's account, what feature of the design bounds a family's worst-case year?
options: The insurer waives the copay entirely once a family's spending passes the deductible, leaving the deductible as the only sum at risk.
The plan caps what each hospital and physician may charge, so a family's total bills can never outgrow the account's balance.
The state enlarges its HSA gift in any year a family's medical bills run unusually high, topping the account up to what is owed.
The copay applies only to spending between the deductible and a ceiling, and the insurer pays everything above that ceiling.

items.stem: According to the chapter, why can modest saving in an Indiana employee's first years on the plan protect the family through several bad medical years in a row, without touching other income or wealth?
options: Balances grow tax-free, and the chapter counts on that investment growth to compound quickly enough to outpace a run of expensive years.
The state requires additional mandatory contributions out of each paycheck, so the account builds up whether or not the employee chooses to save.
The annual gift arrives at the start of every year regardless of prior spending, and that single deposit covers the plan's worst case by itself.
Unspent balances stay in the account and stack onto each new year's deposit, so light years build a buffer that bounded bad years cannot exhaust.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the HSA balance an Indiana employee accumulates is presumably tied to the job itself: an employee who leaves state employment must largely surrender whatever remains in the account, since the deposits were the state's gifts.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter reports that Indiana's governor commissioned an analysis of state employees' healthcare utilization, which found a large spending drop among employees who switched into the new high-deductible plan. According to the chapter, what feature of that analysis lets the drop be attributed to changed behavior rather than to the plan drawing in a certain type of employee?
options: It set each switcher's spending against the same employee's own record before the switch
Most of the state's workforce eventually chose the plan, making the enrollees representative
The savings appeared across several different categories of care at the same time
The reduction in spending was too large to be explained by chance variation
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

items.stem: According to the chapter, the Indiana comparisons demonstrate that enrolling changed the behavior of the employees who chose the new plan, and the chapter says that learning how everyone else would respond requires randomized groups.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

items.stem: The chapter emphasizes that the Indiana consultants compared each employee's utilization after switching with that employee's utilization before. According to the chapter's reasoning, why does this design defeat the explanation that the new plan merely attracted a certain type of employee?
options: So many employees were compared that individual differences averaged out across the group
The employees who chose the new plan happened to match the rest of the workforce in age and health
The same person's traits do not change at the switch, so who enrolled cannot explain the drop
The consultants statistically adjusted each employee's records to remove differences in health status
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

items.stem: The chapter cites large studies comparing people enrolled in consumer-driven plans with people on traditional plans, and then presents the Indiana analysis of one state's switching employees. According to the chapter, why does the smaller Indiana analysis support a conclusion about the plans' effects that the much larger studies cannot?
options: Indiana's data follow each worker across a switch; the big studies compare separate groups on different plans
The large studies tracked only preventive services, while the Indiana analysis measured spending of every kind
The Indiana consultants worked from more recent and far more complete utilization records than the insurers did
State employees are more typical of ordinary American workers than one insurer's customers are
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans Change Behavior

items.stem: A regional water utility let customers opt into a plan that charges steeply for use beyond a monthly allowance. In its first year only a few hundred of the utility's eighty thousand households enrolled — a sliver of its service area. The utility's analysts pulled each enrolled household's meter readings from the two years before it joined and the two years after, and found its metered use was lower in the years after joining than in the years before. Under the reasoning Flynn's chapter applies to such comparisons, which conclusion do these findings license?
options: Too few households enrolled for the readings to support any conclusion
The pricing would curb use across the utility's whole service area
The lower use may reflect which households chose to enroll
The plan's pricing changed the enrolled households' use
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

items.stem: A national mobile carrier offers a metered data plan alongside its unlimited plans. Its analytics group produced a report drawing on billing records for over two million subscribers across a single year, comparing the data use of customers on the metered plan with that of customers on unlimited plans over the same months. Metered customers used less in every age bracket, every region and every device category the group measured, and the marketing team circulated the report as proof that metered pricing makes subscribers thriftier. Under the reasoning Flynn's chapter applies to such comparisons, which conclusion does the report license?
options: The gap may reflect which subscribers took the metered plan
A single year of records is too short to support any conclusion
Metered pricing reduced its subscribers' data use
Metered pricing would curb use across the whole customer base
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans Change Behavior

items.stem: A school district let teachers trade unlimited ordering through its supply office for a fixed annual stipend they manage themselves. About a fifth of the teachers took the trade. The district's auditors assembled each stipend teacher's order history from the three years before the trade and the two years after — thousands of line items per teacher — and found their ordering costs fell sharply after the trade. Citing the audit, the budget office projected the same reduction across the entire staff if the stipend were made universal. Under the reasoning Flynn's chapter applies to such comparisons, which conclusion does the audit license?
options: The drop may reflect the kind of teacher who took the stipend
The stipend changed the ordering of the teachers who took it
Order histories alone are too narrow to support any conclusion
A universal stipend would cut ordering costs across the staff
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

items.stem: The chapter reports that Indiana employees who switched to the state's Singapore-style plan cut their spending by 35 percent. What evidence does the chapter give for its claim that the reduction is permanent rather than temporary?
options: Switchers' routine physicals, mammograms, and other preventive visits continued at the same rate as before.
Rolled-over HSA balances left most switchers able to absorb several expensive years in a row without out-of-pocket costs.
The consultants kept tracking switchers' spending in later years and found that it never rebounded.
Enrollment in the plan climbed from 2 percent of employees to 70 percent by word of mouth in its second year.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

items.stem: In arguing that the Indiana switchers' 35 percent spending reduction is permanent, the chapter names one future situation that the preventive-care finding lets us stop worrying about. Which situation is it?
options: Savings that reflect healthier-than-average employees choosing the plan rather than any real change in behavior.
Early savings eroding as the enrollee pool ages and its medical needs grow heavier year by year.
Spending that falls today through skipped care, then climbs steeply later as untreated problems worsen.
Health savings accounts running dry and leaving the plan's cost sharing unaffordable in an expensive year.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

items.stem: According to the chapter, why does the Indiana switchers' unchanged preventive-care utilization justify confidence that their spending reduction is permanent?
options: The state's annual HSA gift already covered routine visits, so the reduction never depended on cutting back on them.
Steady preventive visits show the switchers stayed as healthy after the switch as before, proving the lower spending did them no harm.
Skipped screenings surface later as severe, costlier problems; since screenings continued, today's cuts are not borrowed from tomorrow's bills.
Preventive visits make up the largest single share of a typical family's healthcare spending, so holding them steady locks in most of the reduction.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

items.stem: According to the chapter, the steep drops in emergency-room visits and hospital admissions among Indiana switchers presumably show that the high deductible had made them 'pennywise but pound foolish' about their care.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

items.stem: A parcel carrier hands each of two regional depots control of its own vehicle-repair budget, letting each keep whatever it does not spend. A year later the records differ. At the Flint depot, repair spending fell steeply: overnight breakdown call-outs dropped by more than half, tow-ins grew rare, the quarterly schedule of brake and engine servicing was completed at the same rate as before, and two rapid-response repair bays were closed. At the Dover depot, repair spending eased only slightly: overnight breakdown call-outs ran near their old level, tow-ins stayed common, the quarterly schedule of brake and engine servicing was completed at a lower rate than before, and every repair bay stayed open. Applying the reasoning the chapter uses to judge whether a spending drop will last, which verdict follows?
options: Dover's reduction is a lasting saving; Flint's is storing up future repair costs.
Neither reduction is a lasting saving.
Both reductions are lasting savings.
Flint's reduction is a lasting saving; Dover's is storing up future repair costs.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

items.stem: A county switches its four animal shelters to an arrangement under which each shelter manages its own veterinary budget and retains its year-end surplus. After a year, each reports. Harlow's outlays fell by almost half: emergency surgeries dropped steeply, after-hours clinic runs grew rare, vaccination and wellness-exam counts matched last year's, and the shelter ended its on-call veterinary contract. Bellwood's outlays eased modestly: emergency surgeries held near last year's number, after-hours clinic runs stayed common, vaccination and wellness-exam counts came in below last year's, and the shelter kept its on-call veterinary contract. Croft's outlays fell by almost half: emergency surgeries dropped steeply, after-hours clinic runs grew rare, vaccination and wellness-exam counts came in below last year's, and the shelter ended its on-call veterinary contract. Dunmore's outlays eased modestly: emergency surgeries held near last year's number, after-hours clinic runs stayed common, vaccination and wellness-exam counts have not yet been tallied, and the shelter kept its on-call veterinary contract. Applying the chapter's reasoning, which shelter's lower spending reads as a lasting saving?
options: Croft
Bellwood
Dunmore
Harlow
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

items.stem: A software firm moves each product team onto a plan under which the team pays for its own technical support from an annual allowance and keeps any remainder. Within two quarters the firm's support spending has fallen steeply, and at a board meeting one director warns that a drop this abrupt is unlikely to last. The operations chief pulls the year's records: weekend emergency call-outs to the data center are down sharply; help-desk tickets per employee have fallen by nearly half; scheduled monthly server patching and backup checks were completed at the same rate as before; and two outside support contracts were allowed to lapse. On the chapter's reasoning, which record is the test of whether the director's warning holds?
options: The sharp decline in weekend emergency call-outs to the data center
The scheduled patching and backup-check completion rate
The two outside support contracts that were allowed to lapse
The overall depth of the two-quarter fall in support spending
items.source_anchor: Chapter 21 → A/B Testing Consumer-Driven Healthcare Plans

bank_meta.chapter_title: RAND and Oregon: Slashing Spending without Hurting Health

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.22.1: Identify the two studies the chapter presents as the only large-scale, fully randomized examinations in US history of how people behave under different health-insurance schemes, and the headline results it reports from each: the RAND experiment of the 1970s and '80s, in which families randomized into the 95 percent copay spent 30 percent less than families randomized into unlimited free care while health outcomes came out statistically identical across all four Singapore-style plans; and Oregon's 2008 Medicaid lottery, in which enrollees showed no statistically significant improvement in measured physical health while their hospital admissions, outpatient care, emergency-room visits and total spending all rose sharply.
learning_objectives.22.2: Explain how each feature of the RAND design closes off a rival explanation for behaviour differences across the four high-deductible plans: identical comprehensive coverage with only the copay rate varying, so the incentive is the only live difference between groups; compensation for any family assigned a plan less generous than its previous policy — sized to the family's highest possible loss and paid in installments every four weeks irrespective of medical usage — so that spending changes cannot be ascribed to feeling impoverished by the assigned plan; and enrollment closed to anyone sixty-one or older, so that a three-to-five-year stint would be finished before participants could go on Medicare.
learning_objectives.22.3: Explain what the chapter claims randomization buys its argument in both experiments: RAND's 30 percent spending reduction, so similar to Indiana's 35, clears the Indiana result of sample-selection bias; the result holding among randomized Americans eliminates genetics, diet and culture as what lets Singapore pair the world's best outcomes with low spending; equal health across groups whose physician-services usage differed by 37 to 67 percent shows the forgone consumption was not producing health; and Oregon's randomly assigned right to apply turns a budget-capped Medicaid expansion into an experiment whose spending and usage surges can be ascribed to the insurance itself.
learning_objectives.22.4: Explain how the chapter rebuts the reading of the sickly-subset results as proof that high-deductible insurance endangers the most vulnerable: twenty-seven of the thirty health metrics RAND tracked were statistically indistinguishable regardless of income, initial health or assigned group; the corrected-visual-acuity difference was too small to have any effect on patients' lives; the blood-pressure and risk-of-dying differences are what slicing a massively re-analyzed sample into enough subsamples will produce by random chance; and the comparison that governs is the whole sample, where no statistically significant differences could be found at all.
learning_objectives.22.5: Given a novel evaluation reporting a statistically significant effect in a few subgroups of a large study whose full sample shows none, determine what the chapter's subsample logic concludes about that effect — judging by how many slices were examined and by what the entire sample showed, rather than by the vividness or vulnerability of the flagged subgroup.
learning_objectives.22.6: Explain why the chapter refuses to count Oregon enrollees' improved self-reports of depression and financial security as a health benefit of Medicaid: the reports were made after people were enrolled but before they started receiving any benefits, so the improvement can only be a placebo effect or the warm glow of a greater sense of security rather than an effect of care — and any system promising affordable healthcare, a Singapore-style one included, would deliver the same glow, so the result cannot single out Medicaid for praise.
learning_objectives.22.7: Given a novel programme reporting improved self-assessed wellbeing among the people it has accepted, determine what the chapter's logic says that improvement can and cannot evidence — judging by when the assessment was made relative to the delivery of any services, and by whether the gain appears in measured outcomes or only in self-reports, rather than by the size or plausibility of the reported gain.
learning_objectives.22.8: Explain how the chapter answers its own closing question — whether RAND's 30 percent saving falling short of Indiana's 35 means randomization reduced the cost savings — by locating the gap in design differences instead: RAND's incentives were weaker at every point, a 95 rather than 100 percent copay below the deductible and no cost sharing at all above it where Indiana kept a 20 percent copay running through a further band of spending; and RAND had no health-savings component, leaving its participants one reason to economize where Indiana's had two — out-of-pocket exposure plus the desire to preserve their own accumulating savings for a rainy day.

Chapter 22 → RAND and Oregon: Slashing S.text: Only two large American experiments have randomly assigned people to different insurance. In the first, families were put into plans identical in coverage and differing only in the share of early spending they paid. Anyone moved to a thinner plan than before received compensation sized to their worst possible loss, paid on a fixed schedule whatever care they used, so that any change in behaviour could be traced to the price they faced rather than to feeling poorer.

Chapter 22 → Results Unfold.text: Families facing almost all of their early costs spent about a third less than those given care free, and the two groups ended equally healthy — as did every group in between, although the free-care group used far more physician services. Of thirty health measures tracked, twenty-seven showed no difference at any income or starting health. The chapter reads the remaining three as what slicing a much-reanalysed sample yields by chance, and rests on the whole-sample result, which showed nothing.

Chapter 22 → Learning from Oregon.text: Oregon could fund ten thousand more Medicaid places and held a lottery for the right to apply, which made an accidental experiment. Those enrolled showed no measurable gain in physical health, while their admissions, outpatient visits, emergency use and spending all rose. Self-reported mood and sense of security did improve — but the survey came after enrolment and before any care was given, so the chapter reads it as reassurance rather than treatment, obtainable from any credible promise of cover.

Chapter 22 → The Nuts and Bolts of Reduc.text: Why did the randomised trial show a smaller saving than Indiana's scheme? The chapter answers that the trial's incentives were weaker throughout: its most exposed group still paid slightly less than everything below the threshold, and nothing at all above it, where Indiana kept a share running through a further band. The trial also had no savings account, so its participants had one reason to economise — the bill — where Indiana's had two, the bill and a balance they kept.

items.stem: According to the chapter, US history has produced just two large-scale, fully randomized studies of how people respond to different health-insurance arrangements: the RAND experiment of the 1970s and 1980s, and the experiment Oregon created in 2008 by holding a lottery for the chance to apply for roughly ten thousand new Medicaid spots.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 22 → RAND and Oregon: Slashing Spending without Hurting Health

items.stem: The RAND experiment assigned each participating family to one of six health-insurance plans created for the study. According to the chapter, how did the four plans it calls Singapore-style differ from one another?
options: In their copay rates alone, set at 0, 25, 50, and 95 percent, with coverage otherwise identical and comprehensive.
In how care was delivered, with two plans run as HMO-style cooperatives giving free care and two as ordinary insurance policies.
In the breadth of services covered, with the higher-copay plans dropping dental, vision, and mental-health care from the package.
In the length of enrollment, with families on some plans participating for three years and families on others for five.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 22 → RAND and Oregon: Slashing Spending without Hurting Health

items.stem: Which of the following states the headline results the chapter reports from the RAND experiment and from Oregon's Medicaid lottery?
options: In RAND, the highest-copay families cut spending 30 percent below the free-care group but finished the study measurably less healthy; in Oregon, enrollees' usage and spending rose sharply and their measured physical health improved significantly right along with it.

In RAND, families on the 95 percent copay spent 30 percent less than the free-care families and health outcomes were statistically identical across the plans; in Oregon, enrollees' usage and spending rose sharply with no significant gain in measured physical health.

In RAND, spending came out statistically identical across the four plans while the free-care families finished measurably healthier; in Oregon, enrollees' usage and spending held roughly steady while their measured physical health showed no significant change.

In RAND, the free-care families spent the least of any of the four plans because unlimited access let problems be caught and treated early; in Oregon, enrollees' emergency-room visits fell sharply as newly covered patients shifted to routine outpatient care.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what distinguished the four high-deductible RAND plans from one another?
options: The annual deductible level set for families that were not poor
Their copay rates alone; the coverage itself was identical and comprehensive
The set of services each one covered, with dental, vision, and mental health varying by plan
The number of years families stayed enrolled, three under some plans and five under others
items.source_anchor: Chapter 22 → RAND and Oregon: Slashing Spending without Hurting Health

items.stem: RAND compensated any family whose assigned plan was less generous than its old policy, and the payments arrived every four weeks in amounts fixed in advance, whatever care the family used. According to the chapter's design logic, why did the compensation have to stay independent of the family's actual medical spending?
options: Reimbursing actual bills would have duplicated what each family's assigned plan was already paying, covering the same care twice
Payments rising with each bill would have handed back part of the out-of-pocket share, blunting the incentive under study
Unpredictable payment amounts would have disrupted household budgeting, changing spending for reasons unconnected to the plans
Families could then have worked out which plan they had been assigned, and that knowledge would itself have altered their behaviour
items.source_anchor: Chapter 22 → RAND and Oregon: Slashing Spending without Hurting Health

items.stem: RAND enrolled only people younger than sixty-one. According to the chapter, which possible explanation for behaviour differences across the four plan groups did this rule take off the table?
options: That the four groups' plans would differ in which medical services they covered
That participants would reach Medicare partway through and change coverage mid-study
That healthier families would end up concentrated in the plans with higher copay rates
That families assigned stingier plans would spend less out of a sense of being poorer than before
items.source_anchor: Chapter 22 → RAND and Oregon: Slashing Spending without Hurting Health

items.stem: According to the chapter, any family assigned a plan less generous than its previous policy was paid compensation equal to its highest possible loss, so that a drop in the family's medical spending could not be put down to its feeling poorer under the assigned plan.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 22 → RAND and Oregon: Slashing Spending without Hurting Health

items.stem: The chapter reports that RAND participants randomized into the highest copay spent 30 percent less than those randomized into free care, a reduction close to the 35 percent drop among Indiana state employees who chose a consumer-driven plan. What does the chapter say the closeness of those two numbers establishes?
options: That assigning participants to plans at random reduces the savings a high-deductible plan can achieve
That Indiana's reported figure was inflated and the plan's true savings were closer to 30 percent
That Indiana's savings came mainly from its health savings accounts rather than from its cost sharing
That Indiana's savings were not an artifact of disproportionately healthy employees choosing its plan

items.stem: Chapter 22 notes that Singapore delivers the world's best health outcomes while spending far less than the United States. How, according to the chapter, do the RAND results eliminate genetics, diet, and culture as explanations for Singapore's performance?
options: The four experimental plans reproduced MediShield's design so faithfully that cultural differences could not influence the outcome
Lower spending with no loss of health showed up among randomized Americans, so the result cannot require anything Singaporean
Researchers compared Singapore against countries sharing its genetics, diet, and culture and found those countries fared no better
Participants were screened at enrollment so that their diets and family health histories matched typical Singaporean profiles

items.stem: The chapter reports that participants on free care used about 37 percent more physician services than one copay group and about 67 percent more than the highest-copay group, yet every group finished the study equally healthy. What does the chapter conclude from that combination?
options: That the extra services the free-care group consumed were not producing health, so usage can fall without harm
That the free-care group had started out sicker, so its additional services were needed just to reach the same health
That the high-copay groups redirected their care toward preventive services, which kept them as healthy as the heavy users
That the study's health measures were too crude to capture the genuine gains the additional services produced

items.stem: According to the chapter, the Oregon experiment was presumably planned that way from the start: the state deliberately set up a randomized trial to measure what Medicaid coverage does to enrollees' health and spending.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter reports that RAND monitored thirty separate health measures across the experiment. According to the chapter, what did those thirty measures show?
options: On twenty-seven of them, outcomes could not be statistically told apart, whatever a participant's income, starting health, or assigned plan.
Most of them showed modestly worse outcomes under the highest copay rate, though only among families enrolled for the full five years.
All thirty were indistinguishable across the full sample, but a majority of them differed once the sickliest enrollees were examined separately.
They differed consistently by participants' income levels, though not by which of the four plans a family had been randomly assigned to.

items.stem: According to the chapter, since RAND's corrected-visual-acuity difference was statistically detectable, it was presumably also large enough to have a real effect on patients' lives.
options: True
False

items.stem: Within certain subsamples of the RAND data, participants facing the highest copay appeared to fare worse on blood pressure and risk of dying. According to the chapter, why do those findings fail to show that the high-copay plan caused harm?
options: A large sample cut into enough subsamples will include a few that seem to show real effects by sheer chance, and these data were re-analyzed heavily enough to expect that.
The families in those particular subsamples had chosen their own insurance plans, so any differences reflect the kind of people who enrolled rather than anything the plans did.
Those two outcomes were tracked over too short a period, since every family's participation in the experiment ended within five years of its start.
Blood pressure and risk of dying were measured only at enrollment, before the plans' differing financial incentives had had any time to influence participants' behavior.

items.stem: The chapter offers several replies to observers who read the sickly-subset results as evidence that high-deductible coverage endangers the most vulnerable participants. Which reply does it present as the one that ultimately settles the question?
options: Re-analyzing one dataset in hundreds of papers means a few subsamples showing chance-level effects were to be expected.
The whole sample, examined as one group, showed no statistically significant health differences under any of the plans.
On twenty-seven of the thirty tracked health measures, outcomes did not differ regardless of income or starting health.
The one visual-acuity gap that did appear was far too small for any patient to notice in everyday life.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what tends to happen when researchers cut a large study sample into enough separate subsamples?
options: A few of the subsamples will seem to show significant effects that are really products of random chance.
Each subsample yields a more trustworthy estimate than the full sample, because its members are more alike.
The subsamples contradict one another so thoroughly that no conclusion of any kind can be drawn.
Effects that are genuine in the full sample get divided up until they disappear from every subsample.

items.stem: Later analysts flagged a handful of subsample differences in the RAND data. According to the chapter, which fact matters most in deciding what those flagged differences are worth?
options: The flagged subsamples each held too few participants for their health records to carry weight.
The flagged differences surfaced only in later re-analyses, never in the study's own first report.
The flagged differences ran in opposite directions and so largely offset one another.
No statistically significant outcome differences appeared when the entire sample was examined.

items.stem: Some advocates have read a handful of worse subset results in the RAND data as proof that high-deductible insurance endangers the most vulnerable participants. On what grounds does the chapter dismiss the flagged blood-pressure and risk-of-dying differences?
options: The two flagged measures depended on participants' own self-reports rather than on the physical examinations the study administered at both ends.
With so many subsample cuts examined, a few seemingly significant differences were expected by chance, and the entire sample showed none.
The worse results were concentrated among families who dropped out of the experiment before their closing physical examinations could be given.
The affected families had been enrolled for noticeably shorter participation periods than the others, leaving their outcomes too little time to register.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the sheer number of subsamples that researchers examined in the RAND data is itself a reason to expect a few seemingly significant differences to turn up, even if copay rates had no real effect on anyone's health.
options: True
False

items.stem: A five-year randomized trial assigned several thousand farms across one wide growing region to either a low-cost irrigation schedule or the conventional one. Across the full set of farms, yields, farm income, and rates of total crop loss came out statistically indistinguishable between the two schedules. Re-analyses published since have cut the data dozens of ways: by soil class, acreage, crop mix, elevation, and debt load, among others. One cut reported a statistically significant rise in total crop loss on semi-arid land under the low-cost schedule, and campaigners now present that result as proof the schedule ruins the growers least able to survive a failed season. Which reading of the semi-arid result matches the reasoning the chapter applies to findings of this kind?
options: A real difference too small to change any farm's prospects
A chance artifact of the sheer number of cuts examined
Evidence the schedule endangers the most precarious farms
A sign the whole-trial averages concealed offsetting effects

items.stem: A freight carrier randomized its entire driver roster for two years into either a fatigue-management schedule or the existing one. Before any data came in, the study plan named one subgroup comparison, and only one: long-haul drivers. At the close, the full roster showed a statistically significant drop in collisions, and the long-haul comparison showed the same drop. On a second measure, severe injuries, the full roster showed no difference; analysts later combing the records through dozens of segment cuts flagged drivers past their sixtieth year as showing significantly more severe injuries under the new schedule, and a union bulletin now warns that the schedule is wearing down the company's oldest drivers. Under the chapter's reasoning, which pair of verdicts follows?
options: Treat both findings as likely chance from the segment combing
Credit the long-haul finding; treat the age finding as likely chance
Credit the age finding; treat the long-haul finding as likely chance
Credit both findings as genuine effects of the schedule

items.stem: A national lottery randomized eligible applicants into a two-year job-coaching program or a waiting list. Taken across every applicant, employment rates at the end were statistically indistinguishable between the two groups. Because the program was politically contested, follow-up studies multiplied, cutting the records by age, schooling, region, household type, prior work history, and scores of further segments. One cut reported a statistically significant employment gain for single parents with the longest spells out of work, and the program's fundraising letters now feature that result as proof it reaches the people hiring has passed over longest. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what does the flagged gain most likely represent?
options: A chance pattern produced by examining so many segments
A sign the program works only where improvement had most room
Evidence the program lifts the applicants hiring has passed over
A real gain too modest to change any family's prospects

items.stem: According to the chapter, the published results of the Oregon experiment showed a statistically significant improvement for Medicaid enrollees in only one area. Which was it?
options: Their rates of hospital admissions and emergency-room visits
Their risk of dying over the years the researchers tracked the groups
Their measured rates of diabetes, high cholesterol, and high blood pressure
Their self-reported depression rates and feelings of financial security

items.stem: Some commentators read Oregon enrollees' improved self-reports of depression as proof that Medicaid coverage had improved their health. According to the chapter, why can that improvement not have been an effect of the care enrollees received?
options: The surveys were answered after enrollment but before any care had been delivered, so treatment had no chance to act
The gain in reported depression was too small for the researchers to count as statistically significant
Self-reported feelings are too subjective to carry any weight, so the chapter sets them aside without further argument
The researchers demonstrated that the improvement was a placebo effect rather than a genuine change in enrollees' feelings

items.stem: The chapter grants that enrollment gave Oregon's Medicaid recipients a genuine sense of greater security, yet argues the finding is no reason to credit Medicaid in particular. According to Flynn's argument, why does the result fail to single Medicaid out?
options: A sense of financial security is an economic outcome rather than a medical one, so a health experiment cannot credit it to an insurer
Enrollees' usage and spending climbed so steeply that whatever security they gained was cancelled out in the chapter's accounting
Any system that promised affordable coverage would give the poor the same feeling, so it cannot distinguish Medicaid from rivals
The security reports were gathered before any benefits had arrived, so they cannot count as evidence about the program at all

items.stem: According to the chapter, Oregon's Medicaid enrollees genuinely felt better after gaining coverage, and yet they were not actually healthier: on the physical outcomes the researchers measured, they ended up doing no better than people who were not enrolled.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, when the Oregon experiment's health results were published, being randomized into Medicaid had produced a statistically significant improvement in only one area. Which one?
options: Rates of death and of diabetes recorded among enrollees
Enrollees' measured blood pressure and cholesterol readings
How enrollees rated their own depression and financial security
How often enrollees needed hospital stays and emergency-room care

items.stem: The chapter makes a point of when Oregon's newly enrolled answered the surveys that showed lower rates of depression. According to the chapter, those surveys were answered:
options: Before the lottery drawing that decided who could apply
After enrollees had used their new coverage for a full year
Alongside the closing measurements of blood pressure and cholesterol
After enrollment was complete but before any benefits arrived

items.stem: Oregon enrollees reported lower rates of depression on surveys answered after they had been enrolled but before any benefits had reached them. According to the chapter, why does that timing matter for what the improvement can prove?
options: The enrollees had not yet met the income test, so the groups compared were no longer randomly formed
People who know they have won coverage tend to tell surveyors what they think is expected of them
Surveys taken early overstate change, because respondents have not yet adjusted to their new circumstances
No care had yet been given, so the gain can only reflect the reassurance of coverage itself

items.stem: According to the chapter, the statistically significant drop in Oregon enrollees' self-reported depression arguably demonstrates that the medical care Medicaid financed made enrollees healthier.
options: True
False

items.stem: A county hardship fund pays overdue utility bills for households it accepts. Applications far outran the budget, so the fund accepted a share of applicants by drawing names and kept the rest on a waiting list. Acceptance letters went out on March 3; each accepted household's arrears were then confirmed with the utility companies, and the fund issued its first payments on May 2. From April 8 to April 14, a university team had households on both lists answer a questionnaire rating their own sleep, day-to-day mood, and confidence about the months ahead, and accepted households rated themselves markedly better on every question. The fund's director calls the result the clearest sign yet that paying down utility debt improves family life. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what does the questionnaire result show?
options: Discouragement on the waiting list rather than any gain among the accepted
What the promise of relief did, not what the relief did
The fund relieving the household strain it was created to remove
Nothing, since ratings people give their own lives evidence no effect

items.stem: A nonprofit runs evening literacy classes for adults, admitting applicants each autumn and keeping the overflow on a waiting list for the following year. Last year's cohort was admitted in September, attended classes from October through May, and in June the program's funder compared the cohort with the waiting list. Reading assessments scored by outside examiners showed no detectable difference between the groups, and payroll records showed the same mix of jobs and hours in both. On a questionnaire rating their own reading, their ease with everyday paperwork, and their outlook for the coming year, the admitted adults rated themselves markedly higher. The funder must now decide whether the classes have earned another grant. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what does the comparison show?
options: The lingering lift of admission rather than anything the classes taught
Adults who feel better about reading, without reading any better
Nothing at all, since the flat scores discredit the questionnaire too
A program working, with confidence arriving ahead of testable skill

items.stem: A rural trust supplies drip-irrigation equipment to smallholder farms. Demand outran supply, so the trust chose recipients by ballot and left the remaining applicants unassisted. Winning farms were notified in January, installers worked through February and March, and the growing season ran to the October harvest. The trust's evaluation compared recipient farms with ballot losers on three records the local cooperative keeps (weighed harvest deliveries, metered water drawn, and crop rejected at grading) and on a questionnaire in which farmers rated their own prospects and their standing in the village. Recipient farms delivered noticeably heavier harvests on less water with fewer rejections, and their farmers also rated themselves markedly higher. A skeptic on the trust's board argues that the questionnaire is doing the work. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what does the evaluation show?
options: Farmers rating their own standing taints the evaluation beyond use
The program improved the farms' results, whatever the ratings add
Lifted spirits, not the equipment, drove the heavier harvests
A credible promise of help from any source would have shown the same results

items.stem: The chapter closes by asking whether the RAND study's 30 percent spending reduction falling short of Indiana's 35 percent means that randomization reduced the cost savings. According to the chapter, what explains RAND's smaller reduction?
options: Its plans were designed with weaker incentives — lighter cost exposure, and no savings account balance to protect.
Its compensation installments, paid to families assigned less generous plans, blunted the sting of out-of-pocket spending.
Indiana's figure was inflated by the healthier, more cost-aware kind of employee who chose to switch into its plan.
Randomization drew sicker people into its sample than Indiana's workforce, and their unavoidable care narrowed the savings.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 22 → The Nuts and Bolts of Reducing Costs

items.stem: The chapter compares what a participant still owed once annual spending passed a plan's initial threshold. According to the chapter, how did the RAND study's highest-copay plan and Indiana's plan differ at that stage?
options: Indiana's plan took over the full cost beyond its threshold, while the RAND group kept paying most of each bill through an added band of spending.
The RAND group owed nothing once its threshold was met; Indiana's members kept paying a 20 percent share through an added band of spending.
Neither plan charged anything above its threshold; the chapter locates the whole incentive gap in the shares each group paid below it.
Both plans kept a 20 percent share running above their thresholds, but Indiana's threshold sat lower, so its members reached cost sharing sooner.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 22 → The Nuts and Bolts of Reducing Costs

items.stem: The chapter argues that RAND's participants had just one reason to hold their spending down — the share of each bill they paid out of pocket — while Indiana's members had two. According to the chapter, what was the second?
options: The wish to keep their own growing savings for a rainy day, since money they did not spend on care stayed theirs.
A tax penalty: dollars withdrawn from the account for care were taxed as income, so spending cost more than saving.
Price visibility: paying from a personal account put real prices in front of members and set them comparison shopping.
A thrift reward: the state topped up the accounts of members who finished each year having spent little on care.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the RAND study's plans gave participants weaker financial reasons to economize than Indiana's plan gave its members.
options: True
False

bank_meta.chapter_title: Why Healthcare Spending Can Decline without Hurting Health Outcomes

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.23.1: Identify the three categories of factors the chapter says produce the large majority of health outcomes — public health measures (clean drinking water, immunization programs), economic factors (access to nutritious food, whether a person can get a job), and social factors (the popularity of smoking, literacy, supportive social networks) — and the attribution it leads with: of the thirty years by which US life expectancy rose over the twentieth century, twenty-five were due to public health improvements.
learning_objectives.23.2: Explain how the chapter's historical evidence is built to establish that prevention, not medicine, produced the modern mortality decline and did so cheaply: New York City's death rate falling to roughly a third of its 1900 level even as the population more than doubled, the leading killers shifting from communicable diseases striking every age to the chronic diseases of old age, and every remedy on the chapter's list being a public-health measure that prevents disease before anyone gets sick — while medicine, which comes into play only after somebody is sick, contributed just one major advance, antibiotics; with clean water and vaccinations carrying the heaviest load at trivial cost.
learning_objectives.23.3: Explain the salience argument on which the chapter's title claim rests: dramatic, easily remembered events have high salience, while public health's engineers and garbage collectors go unremembered; salience is not the same as effectiveness, yet the healthcare debate has been hijacked by the high salience of modern medicine — so high-salience, low-impact medical spending can be cut dramatically without harming outcomes, because the real drivers are low-salience, high-impact activities too boring to remember.
learning_objectives.23.4: Explain the end-of-life margin as the chapter draws it: costly medical interventions have only a modest effect on life expectancy because they go to middle-aged or elderly patients, where public health's huge gains come from preventing infant and child deaths — the extreme case being the quarter of annual Medicare spending that goes to patients in their last year of life — and the one policy difference the chapter says re-aims incentives at that margin: Singapore's elderly can bequeath unspent MediSave balances to their loved ones, where older Americans have, from age sixty-five, grown used to Medicare paying most of their costs.
learning_objectives.23.5: Explain why, on the chapter's account, most types of preventive care do not reduce costs even when they work — prevention is not free: many people must be screened to identify each one who needs treatment, the collective cost of those screenings in most cases equals or exceeds the future costs saved by early treatment, and false diagnoses of the perfectly healthy add unnecessary costs of their own — and what the twenty-services analysis is deployed to show: applying twenty expert-recommended preventive services to 90 percent of the US population would cut total healthcare spending by just 0.2 percent, with a single service supplying the great bulk of both the life-expectancy gain and the savings, while the other nineteen together increase spending in exchange for about two months of added life expectancy.
learning_objectives.23.6: Explain how the chapter builds its case that general checkups are a net loss for society, and the screening policy it credits Singapore with drawing from that logic: a meta-analysis of fourteen randomized studies found general health checks reduced neither morbidity nor mortality, while those checked received up to 20 percent more diagnoses over the following six years — more treatment and more spending for no health gain, with a routine-scan cascade as the personal cost — so Singapore's health ministry encourages only screenings with clear net benefits, leaving the rest available but out-of-pocket, which gives doctors and patients alike a financial incentive to screen sparingly and only where the likelihood of net good is significant.
learning_objectives.23.7: Given a proposed budget reallocation in a novel city or health system — programs to be cut, protected, or expanded — determine whether the chapter's logic predicts its health outcomes will suffer, judging by whether the change touches the quiet drivers of outcomes (sanitation, immunization, food safety, housing, jobs, literacy, social networks) rather than by the visibility or drama of the services affected.
learning_objectives.23.8: Given a novel screening or checkup proposal, predict the direction of its net effect on total healthcare spending on the chapter's account — equivalently, whether a Singapore-style policy would subsidize it or leave it out-of-pocket — judging by the screen-many-to-treat-few arithmetic and the treatment cascades that follow extra diagnoses, rather than by the intuition that catching illness early must save money.

Chapter 23 → Why Healthcare Spending Can.text: Most health outcomes come not from medicine but from public health, economic and social conditions — clean water, immunisation, food, work, literacy, social ties. Of the thirty years American life expectancy gained last century, twenty-five trace to public health. New York shows it: the population more than doubled while deaths fell, and the great killers shifted from infections striking all ages to the diseases of old age. Medicine acts only after sickness; what we remember is not what works.

Chapter 23 → The Quiet Power of Public H.text: Clean water is credited with nearly half the fall in city death rates and most of the fall among infants and children, at pennies a person each day; vaccination comes second, for a few cents a year. Treating one measles case costs hundreds of times what preventing it does. Medical procedures run to hundreds of thousands and move life expectancy far less, because prevention saves the very young while treatment mostly reaches the middle-aged and old.

Chapter 23 → Spending on the Very Old.text: A quarter of yearly Medicare spending goes to patients in their last year of life, where added years are fewest and costs highest. Singapore's arrangement changes what that choice costs a family: whatever an elderly person leaves unspent in their medical savings account passes to their heirs, so a costly late intervention has a visible personal price. Americans covered from sixty-five face no such trade-off, having grown used to the programme meeting most of the bill.

Chapter 23 → Prudence and Prevention.text: Most clinical prevention does not pay for itself: many must be screened to find one to treat, the screening often costs more than the early treatment saves, and healthy people are wrongly diagnosed and then treated. Pooled trials found routine check-ups improved neither illness nor death while producing more diagnoses. Of twenty recommended services applied widely, one — childhood immunisation — carries most of the benefit; without it the rest raise spending. Singapore subsidises only screens with clear net benefit.

Public health improvements accounted for twenty-five of the thirty years.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what separates the public-health measures it credits with the twentieth century's mortality decline from healthcare and medicine?
options: Public health is funded through taxes, while medicine is paid for privately by patients and their insurers.
Public health works through dramatic, memorable rescues, while medicine's benefits go largely unnoticed and unsung.
Public health prevents disease before anyone falls sick, while medicine acts only once illness has struck.
Public health targets the chronic diseases of old age, while medicine fights communicable infections.

items.stem: The chapter reports that New York City's leading causes of death changed from pneumonia, tuberculosis, and diarrhea in 1900 to chronic conditions like heart disease and cancer today. In the chapter's argument, what does this change show?
options: That prevention so weakened the communicable killers of every age group that most people now live long enough to die of the diseases of old age.
That breakthroughs in curative medicine eliminated the infectious killers, leaving behind only those conditions that medicine cannot yet cure.
That chronic diseases became steadily more lethal across the century, offsetting much of the ground gained against infectious disease.
That the city's population simply grew older across the century, shifting which diseases residents faced regardless of any progress against infection.

items.stem: The chapter translates its two leading causes of rising life expectancy into daily costs: clean water at roughly fifty cents per person per day, and childhood immunizations at about five cents per day. What do these translations accomplish in the chapter's argument?
options: They show that prevention looks inexpensive day by day but accumulates into a substantial burden over a whole lifetime.
They show that the biggest contributors to longer lives cost almost nothing, so strong outcomes do not depend on heavy spending.
They show that households already carry these costs privately, so expanding the programs would require no new public money.
They show that prevention pays for itself by heading off costly treatment later, so screening more people lowers total spending.

items.stem: The chapter's New York City evidence arguably shows that advances in medical treatment drove the modern decline in mortality, with preventive public-health measures playing a supporting role.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter sorts health-promoting activities along two dimensions: salience (how dramatic and memorable an activity is) and impact (how much it actually reduces mortality and morbidity). According to the chapter, where do public health and medicine each fall?
options: Public health is low-salience and low-impact; healthcare and medicine are high-salience and high-impact.
Public health and medicine are both high-impact; they differ only in that medicine is far more salient.
Public health is low-salience but high-impact; healthcare and medicine are high-salience but low-impact.
Public health is high-salience but low-impact; healthcare and medicine are low-salience but high-impact.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the belief that healthcare and medicine are the major drivers of health outcomes is mistaken but understandable. What, on the chapter's account, produces the mistake?
options: Elapsed time: the great sanitation and clean-water victories are so distant that no one alive saw what they prevented.
Deliberate preference: people knowingly favor spending they can watch working over spending that stays out of sight.
Skewed memory: a dramatic cure is unforgettable, while the quiet work that prevents disease is too dull to register.
Missing information: the public has simply never been shown the outcome data, and seeing it would correct the mistake.

items.stem: The chapter's title claims that healthcare spending can decline without hurting health outcomes. According to the chapter, why would outcomes hold up even under sharp cuts to spending on healthcare and medicine?
options: Because medical care contributes essentially nothing to health outcomes, so even deep cuts would sacrifice nothing that keeps people alive.
Because the money saved would be redirected into public health budgets, and the added prevention would offset whatever treatment was lost.
Because the cuts land on conspicuous care that only modestly moves outcomes, while the quiet activities that mainly drive health go untouched.
Because most healthcare spending goes to administration and paperwork, which can be trimmed deeply without touching any actual patient care.

About a quarter
About half
About a tenth

items.stem: The chapter claims that public health measures have a huge effect on life expectancy, while costly medical interventions, though they too save lives, have only a modest one. How does the chapter explain the gap?
options: Public health programs reach entire populations at once rather than one patient at a time, so they avert many more deaths in total, even though each averted death preserves a similar span of years.
Medical care begins only after a person has already fallen ill, and by that point even a successful treatment can rarely return the patient to full health and a normal span of years.
Public health mostly averts infant and child deaths, each of which preserves decades of life, while costly interventions mostly go to patients in middle or old age, with fewer years at stake.
Costly medical interventions fail more often than they succeed, so most of the money spent on them delivers no benefit at all to the patients who actually receive the care.

items.stem: The chapter argues that older Singaporeans and older Americans weigh costly end-of-life treatment under different financial incentives. Which policy difference does the chapter identify as the source of that contrast?
options: Singapore's elderly can bequeath unspent MediSave balances to their families, while older Americans have grown used to Medicare paying most of their costs from age sixty-five.
Singapore's elderly need their family's consent before drawing MediSave down for a costly treatment, while older Americans can commit Medicare funds without consulting anyone.
Singapore's policy-makers direct national healthcare resources toward public health and prevention, while American policy-makers concentrate theirs on high-cost hospital medicine.
Singapore's public coverage stops paying for treatment once a patient is judged to be in the final year of life, while Medicare keeps paying at every age and stage of illness.

items.stem: Because the chapter stresses that a quarter of annual Medicare spending goes to elderly patients in their final year, Flynn's argument presumably amounts to a recommendation that costly care for the very old be rationed or withheld.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter cites a study of twenty preventive services recommended by expert panels, which asked what would happen if each service were delivered to 90 percent of the US population. What does the chapter report the study projected for total US healthcare spending?
options: It would rise outright, because each of the twenty services costs more to deliver than its early treatments save.
It would fall, but only by about two-tenths of one percent — a saving the chapter treats as strikingly small.
It would stay essentially flat, with the savings from early treatment exactly offset by the added cost of the screenings.
It would fall by roughly a fifth, with most of the savings coming from hospital stays avoided through early treatment.

items.stem: Suppose a screening program performs exactly as intended: every diagnosis it produces is accurate, and treating each condition it finds early costs less than treating that same condition late would have. According to the chapter, why can such a program still increase total healthcare spending rather than reduce it?
options: Patients treated early go on to live longer, and the extra care they consume over those added years ends up costing the system more than their early treatment saved.
Each case found means screening many people who needed nothing, and together those screenings usually cost as much as or more than the early treatments save.
Providers respond to the guaranteed stream of screening patients by raising their prices until whatever the early treatments save has been absorbed back into fees.
The screenings have to be repeated year after year, so their costs recur indefinitely, while each case the program catches produces its saving only a single time.

items.stem: The chapter reports a projection that delivering twenty expert-recommended preventive services to 90 percent of the US population would trim total healthcare spending by about 0.2 percent — and it argues that a closer look makes the cost picture worse, not better. According to the chapter, what does the closer look reveal?
options: Most of the projected benefit comes from one service, raising childhood immunization rates; without it, the other nineteen together raise spending in exchange for about two months of added life.
The services that do save money achieve it chiefly by shifting treatment costs onto patients' own pockets, so the projected saving changes who pays without reducing what the system spends.
The twenty services overlap heavily in the populations they screen, and the expense of all the duplicated screenings would consume the entire projected saving before any of it was realized.
The projection leaves out the cost of treating people falsely diagnosed as sick, and once those added treatment costs are counted, all twenty services together raise spending instead of trimming it.

items.stem: According to the chapter, most forms of preventive care do not lower overall healthcare spending — and this holds even for services that work, catching real conditions early and extending life expectancy.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, what is the evidence behind Flynn's claim that general health checks do nothing for health?
options: A national patient survey in which most of those given annual checkups reported no change in their own health
A six-year study at one hospital in which patients given checkups fared worse than patients given none
A comparison of national death rates across countries that promote annual checkups and countries that do not
Pooled results from fourteen randomized studies, finding no drop in morbidity or mortality among the checked

items.stem: The chapter's policy verdict is that general checkups leave society worse off. According to the chapter, what turns them from merely useless into an outright loss?
options: Every dollar spent on checkups is a dollar unavailable for the public-health work that drives most outcomes
Those checked collect extra diagnoses, hence extra treatment and spending, with no reduction in sickness or death
The examinations themselves injure enough healthy patients to cancel out the few conditions they catch early
Finding one treatable case means screening so many healthy people that the bill exceeds what early treatment saves

items.stem: Flynn writes that Singapore's arrangement leads doctors and patients alike to screen sparingly. According to the chapter, what is the arrangement that produces this restraint?
options: Doctors whose ordered screenings too often come back clear face reduced reimbursement, which discourages speculative testing
The ministry covers half of every screening's price, leaving a copay sized to make patients think twice about marginal tests
Screenings off the encouraged list come out of the patient's own pocket, so doctor and patient weigh cost against benefit
Each public clinic receives an annual allotment of screening slots, so doctors must ration the tests across their patient lists

options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, what produces the large majority of health outcomes, including how long and how well people live?
options: The level of per-person spending a nation devotes to its healthcare and medical system each year
Breakthrough treatments such as antibiotics, open-heart surgery, and cancer therapy delivered in modern hospitals
Public health measures plus economic and social factors, from clean water and immunization to jobs and literacy
Healthcare and medical services, whose curative power takes effect only once a person has already fallen sick

options: True

items.stem: According to the chapter, why can a nation's healthcare and medical spending be cut dramatically without its health outcomes suffering?
options: Because competition among hospitals and doctors for patients who pay their own bills pushes prices down until the same services cost far less to deliver
Because outcomes are produced mainly by quiet, inexpensive conditions, from clean water and safe food to jobs and literacy, that medical budgets barely touch
Because wider screening would catch disease early, when treatment is cheap, saving enough in late-stage hospital care to offset whatever is cut elsewhere

items.stem: The chapter counts childhood immunization among the century's main sources of health gains yet calls general annual checkups a net loss for society. According to the chapter, what grounds that difference?
options: Checkups cost more per visit than vaccines per dose, though the chapter accepts both will cut death rates once their reach is wide
Immunization protects children, and the chapter holds that health spending directed at anyone past childhood is spending wasted
Immunization buys big life-expectancy gains at low cost, while the trials cited found checkups improved neither illness nor death rates
Immunization is publicly funded while checkups are privately sold, and the chapter trusts public programmes further than profit-driven medicine

items.stem: The river city of Valmera must close a budget shortfall, and its council has approved four cuts of roughly equal size. It will suspend the replacement of its corroded drinking-water mains and the overdue repair of its sewer outfalls. It will end the contract for the helicopter service that flies crash and stroke victims from outlying villages to the regional hospital. It will discontinue the vouchers that pay for every symptom-free adult to receive a complete medical examination each year. It will close the ward that gives intensive hospital treatment to residents in the final months of terminal illness. Judged by the chapter's reasoning, which cut is most likely to worsen the city's illness and death rates in the years ahead?
options: The terminal ward
The examination vouchers
The waterworks suspension
The helicopter contract

items.stem: Four districts of the province of Keldova must each cut the same share from their health budgets this year, and each has filed its plan. Darvel saves by trimming its transplant surgery unit and ending yearly full examinations for its symptom-free adults, while sparing its waterworks and housing-repair crews. Arlow saves by postponing water-main renewal and sewer repairs for a decade, while sparing its mountain rescue teams and its yearly examination scheme. Brennis saves by dismissing the inspectors of its food markets, dairies, and street kitchens, while expanding its yearly examination scheme as the plan's centrepiece. Corvand saves by trimming its transplant surgery unit and halting repairs to its damp, unventilated housing blocks, while sparing its yearly examination scheme. Judged by the chapter's reasoning, which district can deliver its savings without its health outcomes deteriorating?
options: Brennis
Darvel
Arlow
Corvand
items.source_anchor: Chapter 23 → Why Healthcare Spending Can Decline without Hurting Health Outcomes

items.stem: Two highland tea companies, Rosmere and Kintal, each run townships for several thousand workers, and three years ago both halved their township medical budgets in the same way: fewer clinic hours, fewer beds, longer waits for a doctor. Since then, illness and deaths among Rosmere's workers have climbed while Kintal's figures have held steady. Four other changes separate the two. Rosmere dismissed the stewards who inspected its market stalls and canteen kitchens; Kintal kept them. Rosmere closed the small operating theatre at its clinic; Kintal kept a surgeon on call. Rosmere ended the full medical examination required of every worker each year; Kintal kept the requirement. Rosmere stopped subsidising workers' visits to specialists in the valley town; Kintal kept the subsidy. Judged by the chapter's reasoning, which difference most plausibly explains the divergence?
options: The market stewards
The operating theatre
The yearly examinations
The specialist subsidy
