items.stem: The chapter says Singapore's policy-makers understand a crucial problem about preventive care. According to the chapter, what is that problem?
options: Most of it is priced beyond the poor without subsidies, so the people likeliest to carry undetected conditions are the least likely to be tested.
Most of it does not cut costs: screening enough people to find one treatable case usually costs as much as, or more than, the early treatment saves.
Most of it goes unused: patients avoid screenings they must arrange themselves, so conditions keep surfacing only after symptoms have appeared.
Most of it depends on patients changing their habits afterward, and the spending is wasted on the many who never act on the advice they are given.

items.stem: According to the chapter, which preventive screenings does Singapore's Ministry of Health encourage and help pay for — and what happens with the rest?
options: Screenings that are the cheapest offered for each condition; costlier versions stay available to patients who carry supplemental private insurance.
Screenings whose net benefit is clear, such as those for breast and cervical cancer; the rest stay available, but patients pay for them themselves.
Screenings that a patient's family history makes advisable; tests without that backing are removed from clinic menus as wasteful public spending.
Screenings a physician orders in response to symptoms; tests sought by people who feel well are treated as elective and booked through private clinics.

items.stem: Given the study of twenty recommended preventive services reported in the chapter, a preventive service that fails to cut healthcare spending presumably fails to lengthen life expectancy as well.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter reports a meta-analysis in which people assigned at random to receive general health exams went on to collect up to 20 percent more diagnoses than people who were not, while their rates of illness and death improved not at all. On the chapter's reading, why does that finding make such exams a net loss rather than a harmless extra?
options: The diagnostic step is the most expensive part of modern care, so more diagnoses means the testing budget swells faster than any other part of spending.
Conditions found before symptoms appear are found too soon for medicine to act on, so the extra diagnoses represent care postponed rather than care delivered.
Exams that produce diagnoses without producing health must be misdiagnosing, so the finding shows the exams mostly label healthy people with conditions they do not have.
Each diagnosis tends to invite treatment, so the extra findings become extra spending and added medical risk for people who end up no healthier.

items.stem: A dairy cooperative pays every testing and treatment bill for its member herds out of one shared fund, and four screening programs are before its board. The infected-herds program would test cows only in herds where the udder infection has struck before and remains common; its pen-side test is cheap and returns a firm yes or no, and a short, inexpensive course of treatment clears the infection dependably when it is found. The every-season program would test every cow in every herd each season for a wasting disease, devastating wherever it lands but found in only a few herds region-wide; its test costs pennies per animal, first results often needing confirmation, and it spots the disease long before a farmer would. The newborn-calf program would test every newborn calf for an inherited blood disorder vanishingly rare in the region's breeds; its lab test is modestly priced and clear enough, and the few farmers who have caught it early on their own tell every meeting about the animals testing saved them. The oldest-cows program would test only the oldest cows in each herd for a joint condition common at their age; its scan is costly and often cannot tell the condition from ordinary wear, and the lengthy treatment that follows a positive makes little difference at those ages. Weighing the four as the chapter weighs preventive care, which program should the board expect to lower the fund's total outlays?
options: The oldest-cows program
The infected-herds program
The every-season program
The newborn-calf program

items.stem: A city utility owns the water lines running to every house, most of them replaced within recent decades. After one aging line burst and flooded a block — an episode still in the local news — the utility proposes sending acoustic sensors through every residential line on a rolling schedule; any line whose readings mark it as deteriorating would be dug up and replaced at the utility's expense, and on a sensor trace, harmless mineral scale is not always distinguishable from wear. The plan's champions point to a pilot in which one street's line was replaced before it could fail, and the homeowners there have campaigned for the program ever since. If the proposal is weighed the way the chapter weighs screening, what should the utility's board expect from adopting it?
options: Few lines marked for replacement, and total spending higher
Few lines marked for replacement, and total spending lower
Many lines marked for replacement, and total spending higher
Many lines marked for replacement, and total spending lower

items.stem: A vendor brings Singapore's Ministry of Health a new saliva test for a serious nerve disorder of mid-life. The disorder is uncommon outside families it has already touched; a positive result takes months of follow-up examinations to confirm; and the treatment that early detection makes possible is long and demanding, begun years before any symptom would appear. The vendor's launch events feature people whose disorder the test found early, each crediting it with the preparation time it gave them, and a patients' association has petitioned for the test to be offered nationwide. Judging from the chapter's description of how that ministry handles preventive screening, what would it most likely decide?
options: Let clinics offer it, with patients who want it paying themselves
Add it to the subsidized screening list for every adult in the country
Subsidize it for several years while its effect on spending is studied
Keep it out of clinics until its benefit to patients is established

bank_meta.chapter_title: P, Q, and Big Savings for You

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.24.1: Identify the accounting identity the chapter builds its whole argument on: total expenditure on any good or service equals price times quantity (E = PQ), US healthcare expenditures approaching $4 trillion a year conceptualized as high prices multiplied by a lot of quantity consumed, and the implication the chapter draws from the algebra — the only way to reduce total healthcare expenditure is to reduce the price per treatment, the number of treatments, or both.
learning_objectives.24.2: Explain why, on the chapter's account, the Indiana and RAND results stopped at 30-to-35-percent reductions while Singapore manages about 75 percent from similar policies: their small participant groups could reduce only Q, because prices respond only when a substantial fraction of consumers cuts back enough to move overall market demand — the contrast between one shopper boycotting Walmart unnoticed and everybody cutting back until prices must fall — so Indiana's thirty thousand employees, about 1 percent of the state's labour force, left P untouched.
learning_objectives.24.3: Explain how the multiplication inside E = PQ gives simultaneous declines in P and Q their synergistic effect — each variable's fall cuts expenditure directly and also shrinks the base on which the other variable's fall operates — and why that synergy means Singapore-scale savings do not require equally large price declines.
learning_objectives.24.4: Explain how the chapter assembles its case that large price declines are attainable: administrative costs put far above Canada's share with a largely cash-and-carry system claimed to beat a single-payer's paperwork; elective equipment falling in price once buyers pay from their own pockets; the Indiana per-prescription generics saving scaled to the national prescription count; non-emergency care shifted from emergency rooms to urgent-care and convenient-care clinics at a small fraction of the cost, with far shorter waits; and the medical-tourism price gaps on major surgeries.
learning_objectives.24.5: Explain how the chapter answers who absorbs the hit of far lower healthcare spending: not doctors, whose lower median pre-tax earnings are, on its account, offset by a much lower top income tax rate so that after-tax pay is basically on par — but insurance companies needing fewer employees with less paper to push, pharmaceutical companies losing brand-name revenue to generics, and device makers selling fewer units at lower prices, companies not directly providing medical services — with the cuts described as targeted: overhead and low-value items weeded out while beneficial services remain.
learning_objectives.24.6: Explain how each further Singapore practice in the chapter's closing inventory is meant to cut spending without relying on price and quantity alone: fixed annual salaries for public-sector doctors, removing the financial incentive to raise income by ordering more tests or recommending more procedures; public hospitals run as independent non-profits that must compete for clients while keeping their own budgetary and management rights; and the separation of quality care from cushy accommodations, getting the rich to pay more voluntarily and using that money to subsidize healthcare for the poor.
learning_objectives.24.7: Given a novel program, employer or region reporting that participants cut their healthcare consumption, determine whether the chapter's E = PQ reasoning expects prices to fall as well or expenditures to fall through quantity alone — judging by whether the participants' combined cutback is an appreciable share of overall demand in the relevant market, never by the size of each participant's individual savings or how dramatic the behaviour change sounds.
learning_objectives.24.8: Given a novel cross-setting price comparison offered as evidence that large price reductions are achievable at home, determine which comparison case the chapter's reasoning treats as probative — the case that shares the home setting's high wages and costs, so the price gap cannot be explained away by cheap inputs — rather than the case with the biggest gap or the lowest price.

Chapter 24 → P, Q, and Big Savings for Y.text: Spending equals price times quantity, so cutting it means cutting one or the other. Indiana and RAND cut only quantity: their enrolled groups were too small a share of the market to move prices, which shift only on broad changes in demand. Enrol everyone and both fall together, and because they multiply, the saving exceeds either alone — so a given cut in spending needs a smaller cut in price. Flynn expects cheaper paperwork, generics and surgery to supply it.

Chapter 24 → Reducing ER Visits and Cost.text: For complaints like bronchitis, sore throat, back pain or an ear infection, an emergency room charges several hundred dollars where an urgent-care centre charges around a hundred — roughly a fifth to a sixth as much, by the insurer data Flynn cites. Waits differ as sharply: minutes at an urgent-care centre against hours at an emergency room, which is usually further away. A high deductible, he argues, would move routine cases there and leave emergency staff to emergencies.

Their plans tied weaker financial incentives to spending than Singapore's plans do, so enrollees never changed their habits deeply enough.

items.stem: Flynn argues that the Indiana and RAND experiments could not have pulled medical prices down. On his account, why were prices beyond their reach?
options: American medical prices are set by insurers and government payers, so nothing patients themselves do can move what providers charge.
Providers recovered the revenue lost on enrollees by charging other patients more, neutralizing whatever downward pressure the experiments created.
Providers price against overall market demand, and the enrollees were too small a share of all consumers for their cutbacks to register.
The experiments' incentives were too mild to produce the deep, sustained cutbacks that force providers to respond with lower prices.

items.stem: The chapter works through Indiana's situation in detail: about thirty thousand state employees, roughly 1 percent of the state's labor force, most of them enrolled and cutting their healthcare spending by about a third. According to the chapter, what does this walk-through establish?
options: Thirty thousand people are too small a sample to show whether the spending reductions were real or statistical noise.
State employees consume healthcare unusually, so their savings rate cannot be projected onto the rest of the population.
The plan enrolled too small a share of the eligible workforce for its reported quantity savings to be trusted.
Even deep cutbacks by the enrolled group barely changed statewide demand, giving providers no reason to lower prices.

items.stem: The chapter builds its scale argument on the equation E = PQ. According to the chapter, what happens to total healthcare expenditure when the price of care and the quantity consumed fall at the same time?
options: It falls only if the price decline is at least as large as the quantity decline.
It falls by the same percentage as the larger of the two individual declines.
It falls by less than either individual decline, because the two partly offset.
It falls by a larger percentage than either variable's own decline.

items.stem: In the chapter's walk-through, a 35 percent drop in the quantity of care and a 20 percent drop in its price together cut total spending by nearly half. According to Flynn, why does the combined fall come out larger than either variable's own decline?
options: Fewer treatments mean fewer bills to process, so administrative overhead falls and supplies a third source of savings beside the two declines.
Each decline cuts spending on its own and also shrinks the base the other decline works on, since the two variables are multiplied.
The two percentage declines simply add together, and expenditure falls by their combined sum rather than by either figure alone.
A fall in prices induces people to consume still less care, so the price decline keeps producing further quantity declines beyond the original one.

items.stem: Flynn argues the United States could cut total health spending by about 75 percent — the Singapore-scale target — without healthcare prices having to fall by that full amount. On the chapter's algebra, what makes a smaller price decline sufficient?
options: Medical-tourism prices show most of the gap is already closed abroad, so savings from treatment overseas supply what prices here do not.
Enrolling everyone in the plans multiplies the quantity reductions across the population until they alone add up to the full target.
Each point of quantity decline substitutes one for one for a point of price decline, shrinking what prices must contribute to the difference.
Quantity also falls, and since price multiplies against that smaller quantity, a price cut well short of the target completes it.

Caps on hospital charges, nationally negotiated drug prices, limits on equipment purchases, and fixed budgets for each provider

items.stem: The chapter reports that administrative costs take a far larger share of US healthcare spending than of Canada's, yet it argues a Singapore-style system should beat even Canada on administration. How does it make that argument?
options: Singapore pays its healthcare administrators far less than North American systems do, so even a similar volume of paperwork costs much less to process
Singapore has digitized its records and billing systems, eliminating the paper claim forms that Canada's provincial plans still generate and process by hand
One national payer processes claims more cheaply than many competing private insurers, and Singapore concentrates that efficiency in a single government fund
Most treatments are paid cash and carry, with no third party billed, so the paperwork a single-payer system generates on every claim never has to be produced

items.stem: The chapter claims a high-deductible plan would move minor ailments like earaches and sprained ankles out of emergency rooms, and it tests the savings with a condition-by-condition cost comparison. According to the chapter, what did that comparison show?

Treatment for each of several common conditions ran roughly 80 to 85 percent less at an urgent care center than at an emergency room
Urgent care saved money on some of the conditions compared but cost more on others, so the gains depend on steering only the right cases out of the ER

items.stem: The chapter argues that someone must be absorbing most of the financial hit of Singapore's far lower healthcare spending. Who, on its account, takes that hit?

A lower cost of living in Singapore stretches the smaller salaries further, matching US doctors' real purchasing power.
Public-sector doctors are placed on fixed annual salaries set high enough to equal what their US colleagues earn.
A far lighter income tax burden makes up the difference, leaving after-tax pay roughly on par with US colleagues'.

Regulators cap what manufacturers may charge for any equipment they classify as elective rather than essential.

items.stem: In its closing paragraph, the chapter draws one lesson from its inventory of further Singapore practices: salaried public-sector doctors, public hospitals run as independent non-profits, and the separation of quality care from cushy accommodations. According to Flynn, what is that lesson?
options: Cutting health spending by Singapore's margin first requires enrolling every American in a Singapore-style plan, and until then the further practices add nothing.
Cutting health spending need not rest on P and Q falling alone; competition, choice, and sensible payment policies offer other ways to reduce it.

items.stem: An association representing most of the independent bakeries in one state rolls out a dough-handling method that lets a bakery turn out its usual breads while buying noticeably less flour. On the chapter's E = PQ reasoning, what outcome should the members expect for their flour costs?

Members' flour bills stay roughly level, because mills raise prices to recover lost sales
Members' flour bills fall because they buy less, at prices that stay where they were

items.stem: A city's twelve independent theatre companies adopt a shared scheduling platform that trims the rehearsal hours each company books but never uses. A trade-paper columnist totals the results, calls the program a tidy housekeeping exercise, and notes that no company saves more than a few thousand dollars a season. What does the chapter's E = PQ reasoning predict for the companies' rehearsal-space spending?
options: It barely changes, because the halls raise hourly rates on the bookings that remain
It falls only for the companies that cut their own booked hours most sharply
It falls through both fewer booked hours and lower hourly rates

items.stem: Four organizations adopt cost-cutting programs.
