items.stem: Corvia's transit authority is preparing a report arguing that the price of building light rail in Corvia, where construction wages are among the continent's highest, could fall substantially, and it has gathered per-kilometre costs from four countries. Dalmore certifies its civil engineers under the same licensing compact as Corvia; its newest line cost about a third of Corvia's figure, and its construction crews are paid well below Corvian rates. Keslin built its newest line for about half of Corvia's figure, in a market where building trades earn slightly more than Corvia's and urban land runs dearer, though the line opened late after a contractor dispute. Tyrene matches Corvia's metro area almost rider for rider in population and network size; its line cost about a quarter of Corvia's figure, with crews paid a small fraction of Corvian wages. Omber, the one other country where Corvian is the working language on its building sites, built for about a sixth of Corvia's figure — the steepest saving gathered — with labour costs among its region's lowest. The authority's planning chief has circulated Omber's numbers at every public hearing as proof of what disciplined procurement can deliver. On the reasoning the chapter models with its cross-country price comparisons, which country's figure does the most to show that light-rail prices could fall in Corvia?
options: Omber
Tyrene
Keslin
Dalmore
items.source_anchor: Chapter 24 → P, Q, and Big Savings for You

items.stem: Maren's consumer-affairs office is drafting a submission arguing that the price of a licensed heavy-vehicle driving course in Maren, a province with high pay for certified instructors, could fall considerably, and it cites four other provinces. Ostwick's schools are accredited by the same examiners' board that accredits Maren's; a standard course there runs about half of Maren's typical fee, taught by instructors paid well below Maren rates. Rhyle matches Maren almost exactly in licensed schools and annual candidates; its courses cost about a quarter of Maren's fee, its instructors earn far below Maren pay, and its prices have drawn national coverage. Quarrow charges about two-thirds of Maren's fee for a standard course, in a market where instructors earn above Maren rates and practice-yard rents run higher still, though its schools book out weeks in advance. Selhurst teaches from the identical written curriculum Maren uses, examination for examination; a course there costs about nine-tenths of Maren's fee, with instructors paid somewhat below the going Maren rates. The national examiners' council has twice commended Ostwick's accreditation standards as indistinguishable from Maren's own. On the reasoning the chapter models with its price comparisons, which province's fee does the most to show that course prices could fall in Maren?
options: Rhyle
Quarrow
Ostwick
Selhurst
items.source_anchor: Chapter 24 → P, Q, and Big Savings for You

items.stem: A homebuyers' association in Veska is preparing a bulletin arguing that the fee for a standard property transfer in Veska could fall substantially. Its researcher has ranked four foreign comparisons by the size of the saving, largest first. Larkmoor shares Veska's civil-law code down to the deed forms; a transfer there runs about a fifth of Veska's fee, its conveyancers paid far below Veska salaries — the researcher's standout case. Norvale charges about two-fifths of Veska's fee, in a market where conveyancers earn on a par with Veska's and office rents run higher, though transfers there take longer to complete than Veska's. Hartswood drafts its transfers in Veska's own official language, clause for clause; a transfer there costs about half of Veska's fee, with its conveyancers earning noticeably below Veska salaries. Imbry's property registry handles about as many transfers each year as Veska's does; a transfer there costs about four-fifths of Veska's fee, with conveyancers paid modestly below Veska salaries. The association's board, wary of comparing unlike markets, has reminded the editor that Imbry's property market is the one most like Veska's in size. On the reasoning the chapter models with its price comparisons, which country's figure should anchor the bulletin's claim that transfer fees could fall in Veska?
options: Larkmoor
Imbry
Hartswood
Norvale
items.source_anchor: Chapter 24 → P, Q, and Big Savings for You

bank_meta.chapter_title: You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.25.1: Identify the chapter's prescription -- that people must in one way or another be compelled to save for future healthcare expenses, because left to their own devices they will not save enough -- and the two routes it says the necessary savings can be obtained: overtly, as with Singapore's open and explicit requirement that money go into MediSave Accounts, or covertly, by employers depositing money into employees' health savings accounts, as the chapter says Whole Foods Market, the state of Indiana, and roughly seven in ten firms offering consumer-directed healthcare plans do.
learning_objectives.25.2: Explain why the chapter counts employer HSA deposits as compulsory saving even though workers experience them as an extra perk: in a competitive labor market, any money a firm puts into a health savings account would otherwise have flowed to those same workers, as higher take-home pay or as other fringe benefits such as day care or life insurance -- so routing it into a health account forces them to save for future health expenses instead of leaving them free to spend what is really their own compensation.
learning_objectives.25.3: Explain how decision-making myopia -- the behavioral economists' term the chapter adopts for focusing on short-term options to the detriment of longer-term opportunities -- defeats purely voluntary consumer-directed plans: nearly everyone favors now over later and so under-saves, as in the college-fund example where each month's planned deposit loses out to purchases with immediate payoffs, so most people on a voluntary high-deductible-plus-HSA arrangement never accumulate enough to cover the deductible and copays, and when the expenses arrive they must beg or borrow, sell or hock assets, or forgo treatment.
learning_objectives.25.4: Explain the political cascade the chapter predicts from putting people into consumer-directed plans without ensuring they can pay the cost-sharing: a medically underserved group blames the system rather than its own myopia, concludes the arrangement is costly, unfair and inefficient, and demands traditional insurance with negligible out-of-pocket costs, locking in third-party payment and perhaps favoring single-payer options; and why the chapter calls that demand ironic -- the same myopia makes the no-out-of-pocket short-run option attractive while discounting the superior long-run option of lower spending, lower taxes and longer lives.
learning_objectives.25.5: Explain how Singapore's design compensates for myopia and the sufficiency criterion the chapter extracts from its experience: money flows automatically into MediSave Accounts, building a nest egg that covers MediShield's premiums, deductibles and copays for the vast majority of savers, so participants end up neither short of money nor resentful of their high-deductible plan -- the teaching being that the automatic savings, whether overt or covert, must be large enough to cover the system's cost-sharing, with an institution like MediFund taking over in catastrophic spending or deep poverty, after which agitation for lower deductibles, copays or first-dollar coverage stays modest.
learning_objectives.25.6: Given a novel consumer-directed plan design, predict on the chapter's account whether it will produce a resentful, medically underserved group demanding first-dollar coverage or a population content to stay on a high-deductible plan -- judging by whether savings accumulate automatically in amounts matched to the plan's cost-sharing, rather than by how coercive the funding mechanism looks or how generous its sponsor appears.
learning_objectives.25.7: Given a novel employer benefit arrangement, determine whose money the chapter's competitive-labor-market reasoning says is funding it -- compensation the workers would otherwise have received, rather than a gift at the employer's expense -- and therefore whether the arrangement constitutes compulsory saving in the chapter's sense.

Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's H.text: Because people favour the present, they will not save enough for future care on their own, so the saving must be compelled — overtly, as with Singapore's required MediSave deposits, or covertly, through employer HSA deposits. Purely voluntary high-deductible plans therefore leave most enrollees short, and the resentment becomes a demand for first-dollar coverage. Singapore's lesson: automatic savings must be large enough to cover the system's cost-sharing, with a backstop for catastrophe and deep poverty.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what must happen for people to end up holding enough savings to meet their future healthcare expenses, and why?
options: Their care must be financed from general taxation, so that no household has to accumulate medical savings of its own.
Their deductibles and copayments must be cut low enough that routine care no longer calls for any meaningful household saving.
They must one way or another be made to save, because a short-term focus keeps them from setting enough aside on their own.
They can be counted on to save enough by themselves once a high-deductible plan makes the true cost of their care visible.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: According to the chapter, the savings people need for future healthcare expenses can be put in place by either of two routes: overtly, as when Singapore openly and explicitly requires deposits into MediSave Accounts, or covertly, as when employers place money in their workers' health savings accounts.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: The chapter says the needed savings can arrive covertly, through employers depositing money into workers' health savings accounts. Which of the following does it name as doing exactly that?
options: Canada, the United Kingdom, and employers that provide fringe benefits such as day care or life insurance.
The state of Indiana, enrollees in Affordable Care Act plans, and the researchers behind a Commonwealth Fund study.
The state of Indiana, Whole Foods Market, and roughly seven in ten firms offering consumer-directed healthcare plans.
Whole Foods Market, Singapore's MediSave program, and most firms still offering traditional insurance with low deductibles.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: According to the chapter, the money a firm deposits into its employees' health savings accounts is presumably a pure gain for those workers -- compensation they would not have received in any other form had the employer chosen not to make the deposits.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: Workers at a firm that deposits money into employee health savings accounts typically read the deposits as a perk -- extra money on top of the pay they would otherwise get. According to the chapter, why is that reading mistaken?
options: The firm recovers the cost of the deposits by charging workers more for the underlying insurance coverage, so whatever lands in the account is clawed back through premium contributions deducted from their paychecks.

The deposits are rarely large enough to cover a high-deductible plan's deductible and copays, so workers who treat them as a windfall are still left exposed to heavy out-of-pocket costs when they need care.
The deposited amounts are taxed just as ordinary wages would be, so once taxes are taken out the accounts leave workers no better off than an equivalent raise would have left them.

In a competitive labor market the money would have reached those same workers anyway, as higher take-home pay or as other fringe benefits, so the deposits redirect compensation instead of enlarging it.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: The chapter concludes that an employer's deposits into workers' health savings accounts are not a gift but the workers' own compensation in a redirected form. Which assumption does the chapter's argument depend on to reach that conclusion?
options: That the amounts firms choose to deposit are large enough to cover the entire annual deductible and all of the copays of the health plan that accompanies the account.
That the labor market is competitive, so pay a firm holds back from one channel must surface in another -- the money could not simply have stayed with the firm.
That the accounts' own rules prevent workers from ever withdrawing any of the deposited money for any purpose other than the qualified medical spending the plan itself recognizes.
That workers, given the choice by their employer, would rather have deposits into a health account than a raise of exactly equal size showing up in their regular paychecks.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: The chapter notes that the saving Singapore collects openly through MediSave accounts can also be obtained covertly, with employers depositing money into workers' health savings accounts. On the chapter's account, in what sense are the workers at such firms being made to save?
options: Rules modeled on retirement accounts bar any withdrawals until a set age, so the deposits accumulate for decades regardless of what the workers themselves might have preferred to do with the money.
Money that would otherwise have been theirs to spend freely -- coming as higher pay or as other fringe benefits -- is committed to future health costs without their ever choosing to set it aside.
Workers remain free to take the money as cash instead, but short-term thinking is expected to keep nearly all of them from completing the opt-out, so the deposits stay put through inertia.
Enrollment in such a plan obliges each worker to match the employer's deposits with automatic payroll deductions, so part of every paycheck is diverted into the account whether they like it or not.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: The chapter borrows a term from behavioral economists: 'decision-making myopia.' According to the chapter, what does the term describe?
options: A tendency to freeze when a decision offers too many choices, settling for whatever is familiar
A tendency to copy the spending and saving habits of coworkers, neighbors, and relatives
A tendency to weight options paying off now over opportunities whose benefits arrive later
A tendency to underestimate the likelihood of ever facing a large and unplanned medical expense
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: According to the chapter, why do most people on a purely voluntary consumer-directed arrangement — a high-deductible plan paired with a health savings account that each person funds on their own — fail to accumulate enough to cover the deductible and copays?
options: Because the deductibles on such plans sit beyond what a typical household could put aside within a single plan year, however disciplined its saving
Because people favor now over later — both under-saving and overspending — each month's deposit loses out to a purchase with an immediate payoff
Because enrollees assume routine care is the insurer's to pay, and learn how much the deductible leaves with them only after treatment has been billed
Because without an employer's contribution the account grows too slowly for even a steady depositor to reach the deductible before a large bill arrives
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: In arguing that purely voluntary saving for future health expenses fails, the chapter dismisses the hope that some other member of the household will be the better planner and saver: nearly everyone, it holds, tends to favor now over later.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: An enrollee on a purely voluntary arrangement — a high-deductible plan plus a health savings account holding only what the enrollee chose to deposit — has, like most people in the chapter's telling, saved too little for the deductible and copays. According to the chapter, what does such a person face when the medical expenses arrive?
options: Seeing the insurer pay the shortfall and recover it later through a surcharge on the next year's premiums
Having to beg or borrow the money, sell or pawn possessions, or go without the treatment
Receiving the care anyway, with the unpaid balance trailing them afterward as medical debt in collections
Switching at the next enrollment to a plan with lower deductibles, absorbing the higher premiums it carries
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: According to the chapter, people left unable to pay the deductibles and copays of their consumer-directed plans will presumably respond by blaming their own failure to save enough.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: On the chapter's account, people placed into consumer-directed plans without any assurance that they can meet the deductibles and copays become a medically underserved group. Why does the chapter predict that this group will press for traditional insurance with low out-of-pocket costs rather than for better-funded savings accounts?
options: It expects them to blame their own failure to save and, no longer trusting themselves to manage a savings account, to prefer coverage that asks no saving of them at all.
It argues that their verdict would be accurate: consumer-directed plans genuinely deliver less care at greater cost than conventional insurance arrangements do.
It expects them to fault the arrangement rather than their own under-saving — judging it costly, unfair and inefficient — and so to want out of cost-sharing entirely.
It holds that traditional insurance really would leave them better off over the long run than any savings-funded arrangement could ever manage to do.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: Why does the chapter describe the predicted demand for traditional insurance with minimal out-of-pocket costs as ironic?
options: If the demand were met, it would lock in the third-party-payment arrangement that the chapter's entire reform program has been designed from the outset to displace.
The group ends up demanding a return to the very consumer-directed arrangement that left it medically underserved and resentful in the first place.
The demand runs on the same decision-making myopia that produced the under-saving: no out-of-pocket spending appeals now, while the better long-run option is discounted.
The group aims its resentment at the arrangement it was enrolled in even though, on the chapter's own account, the shortfall traces back to its earlier failure to save.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: The chapter predicts that, to the dissatisfied enrollees, an arrangement with no out-of-pocket spending will look like the obviously attractive choice. On its account, what does their decision-making myopia lead them to discount?
options: A single financial gain: the long-run fall in what the enrollees themselves would eventually spend on their own medical care.
The catastrophic healthcare expenses that even well-funded savings accounts would still leave to a separate backstop.
Their own part in creating the shortfall — the earlier under-saving that the chapter predicts they will decline to blame.
The option the chapter rates superior in the long run: lower national healthcare spending, lower taxes, and longer lives.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: According to the chapter, money flows into Singaporeans' MediSave Accounts automatically through required saving, and the nest egg this builds is big enough that the vast majority of savers can meet MediShield's premiums, deductibles, and copays from it.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: According to the chapter, Singapore's experience teaches a general lesson about how to make a consumer-directed healthcare system both workable and palatable. Which statement best captures that lesson?
options: Savings must reach enrollees' accounts automatically and be large enough to meet the plan's premiums, deductibles, and copays, with a backstop for catastrophic spending or deep poverty.
Contributions must be collected openly under a named public program rather than through employer deposits, because enrollees who can see the saving requirement come to trust and defend the plan.
Enrollees must keep the freedom to spend their account balances on other goals, because people whose money is locked away for a single purpose grow resentful of the entire arrangement.
Deductibles and copays must be scaled down to the amounts enrollees typically manage to put aside on their own, so that no participant ever faces a bill beyond what unaided saving has covered.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: The chapter describes two routes by which money can get into people's health savings accounts: Singapore's open, legally required MediSave contributions, and the deposits that employers such as Whole Foods Market, the state of Indiana, and most firms offering consumer-directed plans make on workers' behalf. According to the chapter, how much weight does the choice between these two routes carry?
options: A great deal: the chapter argues the open route works better, since workers who know the saving is required cannot mistake the deposits for a disposable fringe perk.
A great deal: the chapter argues the employer route works better, since deposits that feel like a fringe benefit arrive without the resentment an open mandate stirs up.
Very little: the chapter treats both routes as insufficient by themselves, holding that accounts of the needed size can only be funded out of general tax revenue.
Very little: the chapter treats the route as secondary, so long as what flows in automatically is large enough to cover the plan's premiums, deductibles, and copays.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: According to the chapter, once a consumer-directed system's automatic savings are large enough to cover its premiums, deductibles, and copays, what does Flynn predict about subsequent political pressure to cut cost-sharing or to replace the system outright?
options: He predicts it will stay modest, since participants who are neither short of money nor resentful of a high-deductible plan have little reason to press for first-dollar coverage.
He predicts it will change target, with participants campaigning for the safety-net institution to extend its reach from catastrophic cases and deep poverty to routine bills.
He predicts it will continue at full strength, because decision-making myopia leads even well-funded participants to prefer the short-run appeal of no out-of-pocket spending.
He predicts it will disappear altogether, with no funded participant ever again drawn toward traditional insurance or toward single-payer financing of any kind.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: According to the chapter, what is the lesson of Singapore's experience for anyone designing a consumer-directed healthcare plan?
options: Deductibles and copays must be scaled down until a typical household can meet them out of ordinary income even in a financially difficult year
Money flowing into people's accounts on its own must be enough for the plan's premiums, deductibles, and copays, with catastrophe and deep poverty handled separately
Enrollees must first be taught to recognize their own decision-making myopia, so that saving on their own initiative becomes dependable over time
The savings requirement must be imposed openly by legislation, as Singapore's is, rather than arranged quietly through deposits made by employers into workers' accounts
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: According to the chapter, whether compulsory savings are collected openly by a government program or deposited quietly by employers is presumably the decisive factor in whether a consumer-directed plan wins acceptance.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: The chapter calls the human tendency to under-save 'lethal' for purely voluntary consumer-directed plans. According to the chapter, why is it lethal?
options: Employers contribute far less to the accounts under voluntary plans than they would under a plan all of their workers were required to join
Most people, left alone, never put by what the cost-sharing requires, and expenses leave them borrowing, pawning, or going untreated
Account holders invest their balances too cautiously for the money to keep pace with the steadily rising price of the covered services
Voluntary plans mainly attract enrollees who already expect heavy use, which pushes the plans' premiums past what ordinary savers can manage
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: The chapter says the needed savings can be obtained overtly, as in Singapore, or covertly, through employer deposits that workers read as a perk. According to the chapter, why does the choice between the two routes matter so little?
options: Employers deposit roughly what legislation would have demanded of them anyway, so the same sums end up moving under either arrangement
Both routes put money aside without waiting on the saver, and the outcome turns on whether enough builds up, not on which route it took
Workers eventually learn that employer deposits come out of their own pay, so the two routes come to feel identical to the people inside them
Both routes keep the deduction inconspicuous enough that nobody resents it, and that low visibility is what keeps complaints from forming
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: A touring musicians' guild runs an instrument-protection plan: after any damage claim, the member pays a sizable excess, plus a fixed charge for each visit to an approved repair shop. To help members meet those outlays, a cultural foundation offers a two-for-one match — every dollar a member sends in during the spring contribution window is joined by two from the foundation, all held in a repair account in the member's name; the foundation deposits nothing on its own. The plan's excess and shop charges are reviewed by the guild's trustees and have held steady for years. The foundation's two-for-one rate is the richest benefit the guild has ever negotiated, and trade-press coverage of the program has been admiring. On the chapter's reasoning about how plans like this must be funded, what should be predicted for the membership over the coming years?
options: A membership broadly content to stay with the plan as the foundation's match continues
A campaign to push the foundation's match above two-for-one so balances build faster
A steady drift of members out of the plan and into repair cover bought independently
A growing bloc demanding cover that pays repair bills in full from the first dollar
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: A grain growers' cooperative enrolls every member in a machinery-breakdown plan carrying a large per-claim excess and a charge for each service call. The funding was never put to a vote: the co-op withholds a levy out of each member's harvest settlement and banks it in a repair reserve kept in that member's name. The levy is refigured each season by the plan's actuary against the excesses and service charges members actually bore the season before. At rollout, a petition demanding a member vote on the levy collected signatures from a third of the membership, and two directors resigned over the manner of its imposition. On the chapter's reasoning about how plans like this must be funded, what should be predicted for the members a few seasons on?
options: Members content with the plan only after the levy is converted to a voluntary contribution
A sustained drive to repeal the levy while keeping the breakdown plan itself in place
Members largely settled on the plan, the levy fight dwindling into occasional grumbling
Members pressing the co-op to drop the excess and pay claims in full from the first dollar
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: A state association of self-employed land surveyors places its members under an instrument plan: when a total station or scanner is lost or wrecked, the plan replaces it once the member has paid a substantial share of the loss, plus a handling charge per claim. A benefactors' fund tied to the association wires each member a monthly stipend, set by the plan's administrators from the cost-sharing a typical member bears over time; the wire goes out whether or not the member does anything. The stipend lands in the member's ordinary bank account, usable for any purpose, under a cover note commending it to future instrument costs. The fund's trustees have said publicly that they would sooner enlarge the stipend than see a member caught short. On the chapter's reasoning about how plans like this must be funded, what should be predicted for the membership?
options: Members banking the stipend untouched once early claims show what the cost-sharing runs
Members increasingly demanding a plan that pays losses in full from the first dollar
A membership petitioning the fund year after year to enlarge the monthly stipend it pays
Members broadly content on the plan as the monthly wires continue arriving on schedule
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: According to the chapter, how do workers typically regard the money their employers deposit into their health savings accounts?
options: As an added perk from their employer, over and above their pay
As an advance on future wages that they will eventually have to pay back
As a government benefit that their employer merely passes along to them
As part of their own compensation that has been redirected into saving
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: According to the chapter, in a competitive labor market, money that an employer deposits into workers' health savings accounts is money the workers would have received anyway, as higher pay or as other benefits.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: According to the chapter, why do employer deposits into workers' health savings accounts count as a form of compulsory saving, even though workers tend to see them as an added perk?
options: The money is really part of the workers' own pay, and once deposited they are no longer free to spend it as they choose
The deposits are withheld directly from each worker's paycheck before taxes are applied, so workers never handle the money
Employers offering such plans are required by government regulators to fund every account at a set minimum level each year
The accounts lock the money away until retirement age, so workers are forced to defer spending all of it for decades
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: A firm announces it will begin depositing money into every employee's health savings account. According to the chapter's competitive-labor-market reasoning, what happens to the workers' total compensation?
options: It depends mainly on whether the firm's profits that year can absorb the cost of funding the accounts
It rises by roughly the amount deposited, since the accounts are funded on top of existing pay and benefits
It falls over time, because firms use such programs to justify holding wages below the going market rate
It stays about the same: the deposits displace pay or other benefits the workers would have gotten instead
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: A trade bulletin surveys employee programs at four firms in the Aldern Valley, which hire from the same seasonal workforce. Garnet Excursion Railway funds restricted certification-fee accounts for its crews entirely from a rail-heritage trust's annual grant, which must be used this way or be returned; the owner is toasted for the program every season. Marden Seed Company pays a fixed monthly sum from its own revenues into an account for each worker, spendable only on future course fees at approved schools; its enrollment paperwork draws steady complaints. Hollis Print Works pays the premiums, from its ordinary funds, on a group life-insurance policy that covers every employee on its rolls; the coverage goes mostly unmentioned until a claim arises. Brightwater Timber adds a flat sum it calls a 'future-needs supplement' to every paycheck from its own funds, which employees may spend however they like; most of it goes to current bills. On the chapter's reasoning, which firm's arrangement amounts to compulsory saving in its sense?
options: Marden Seed Company
Garnet Excursion Railway
Hollis Print Works
Brightwater Timber
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: Ketter & Sons, a furniture maker, runs one workshop on Harrow Lane and another on Mill Street, hiring joiners from the same regional trade pool. At each workshop, every joiner holds an account that receives a set sum each month and may be spent only on future guild-license and examination fees. At Harrow Lane, the deposits are paid entirely from a craft foundation's grant, which the foundation releases for these deposits and for nothing else. At Mill Street, the deposits are paid from the firm's own revenues, as they have been since that workshop opened. Joiners at both workshops talk about the accounts the same way: as a gift from the owning family. On the chapter's reasoning, which of the programs is compulsory saving in its sense?
options: The Mill Street program
Both programs
The Harrow Lane program
Neither program
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

items.stem: Four fishing companies work out of the same harbor, and deckhands move freely among them between seasons. At Corrow Fisheries, deckhands may choose to put part of their pay into a gear account, and the company adds half again to whatever each volunteer puts in; takers are indifferent to it. At Pelham & Dray, the company pays a set share of its own funds into a locked gear account for every deckhand; crews praise the owners, though statements arrive late and confuse some. At Searle Brothers, every deckhand gets a cash 'gear allowance' with each settlement, spendable on anything at all, alongside leaflets urging crews to bank it; most spend it straightaway, quite cheerfully. At Nankervis Boats, a harbor-improvement fund pays into locked gear accounts for every deckhand, on terms that allow no other use; crews grumble that money of theirs is being tied up. On the chapter's reasoning, at which company is compulsory saving in its sense taking place?
options: Pelham & Dray
Nankervis Boats
Corrow Fisheries
Searle Brothers
items.source_anchor: Chapter 25 → You Have to Fund People's HSAs for Them

bank_meta.chapter_title: We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

source.title: The Cure That Works: How to Have the World’s Best Healthcare — at a Quarter of the Price

learning_objectives.26.1: Identify the findings the chapter assembles against Medicaid, matched to the comparison each study ran: the Oregon recap (people randomized into Medicaid did no better on measured health outcomes while spending 36 percent more); the cancer-mortality study in which Medicaid patients and the completely uninsured were both about 50 percent more likely to die than the privately insured; and the three studies in which Medicaid patients did worse than the uninsured — after surgery, after angioplasty, and after lung transplant.
learning_objectives.26.2: Explain how the chapter's sequence of studies is built to escalate its claim — it first voices the reading it wants to destroy ("they at least were not harmed"), then moves from no measured benefit at higher cost, to no better than being uninsured, to worse than being uninsured — so that Medicaid is repositioned from wasteful-but-harmless to actively harmful, which is what makes retiring it rather than funding it better the chapter's pro-poor move.
learning_objectives.26.3: Given a novel set of outcome comparisons across coverage groups, determine which comparison the chapter's reasoning treats as capable of showing that the program itself causes harm — the one whose design rules out that enrollees were sicker, poorer-situated or more burdened to begin with, as the chapter says its cited studies did by controlling for demographics, initial health status, location and comorbidities — rather than the comparison with the largest gap, the largest sample or the most alarming outcome.
learning_objectives.26.4: Explain how the chapter connects what Medicaid pays to what its enrollees can get: reimbursement far below private rates leaves Medicaid patients losing the competition for the limited supply of medical services, which the chapter evidences with nearly one-third of primary care doctors refusing new Medicaid-only patients and the Chicago secret-shopper survey, where callers whose children had public insurance were six times as likely to be denied an appointment and waited more than twice as long when they got one.
learning_objectives.26.5: Given a novel program whose eligibility rules, funding and payment rates are described, predict where the chapter's spread-more-thinly mechanism expects access problems to appear — judging by whether coverage has been extended faster than the money behind it, which forces per-service payment below what providers can get elsewhere — rather than by how generous or restrictive the program's eligibility looks.
learning_objectives.26.6: Explain how, on the chapter's account, each announced criticism of health-savings accounts for the poor was met by a Healthy Indiana Plan design feature: no money for preventive care answered by first-dollar preventive coverage; inability to afford the deductible answered by the state's contribution sized to the would-be deductible; and personal responsibility enforced by a small mandatory income-scaled monthly contribution with a grace period and a twelve-month lockout for missing it — with unspent balances rolling over only when specified preventive care has been obtained.
learning_objectives.26.7: Explain what the chapter takes the Healthy Indiana Plan's reported results to establish: that low-income people spend their own money as capably as anyone else — preventive-care participation rising from 39 to 59 percent within a year, most enrollees keeping up their contributions, consumer behavior shifting toward fewer emergency-room visits, generic drugs and second opinions, balances accumulating — and that the program achieved this without employers dumping workers onto it, because eligibility required six months without insurance.
learning_objectives.26.8: Explain why the chapter offers the Healthy Indiana Plan as its proof that Singapore-style plans work for America's poor and still refuses to recommend what that plan literally is — a separate plan for the poor: on its account a system serving only the poor is inherently susceptible to underfunding and neglect by politicians who pay lip service to quality care for the needy, so the remedy is one system for rich and poor alike, as Singapore uses MediShield, and never two.

Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor fro.text: On the chapter's reading, its cited studies show Medicaid patients faring no better than the uninsured, and in several worse, and it blames reimbursement far below private rates: paying too little, Medicaid leaves enrollees losing a competition for limited medical services, as refusals and long waits show. Indiana's savings-account plan for the poor is its proof the Singapore approach serves them — yet a system serving only the poor invites underfunding, so it wants one system for rich and poor.

items.stem: As background for its case, the chapter recaps the Oregon experiment, in which some applicants were randomly selected into Medicaid. According to the chapter, how did the people selected into Medicaid compare with those who were not?
options: They did no better on the measured health outcomes but spent about the same amount.
They did no better on the measured health outcomes but spent about a third more.
They did modestly better on the measured health outcomes but spent about a third more.
They did noticeably worse on the measured health outcomes but spent about a third more.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: According to the chapter, the cancer-mortality study it cites found that Medicaid patients and people with no health insurance at all were both about 50 percent more likely to die than privately insured patients.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: One study the chapter cites tracked how often patients died after surgery, and found Medicaid enrollees dying at nearly double the rate of the privately insured. According to the chapter, how did those Medicaid enrollees compare with the completely uninsured in the same study?
options: Neither more nor less likely to die
About one-eighth more likely to die
About twice as likely to die
Modestly less likely to die
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: According to the chapter, the studies it gathers on Medicaid point to a program that is presumably wasteful -- costing more while delivering no measured health benefit -- but one that at least leaves its enrollees unharmed.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: Just after recapping the Oregon results -- enrollees spent more and did no better on measured outcomes -- the chapter pauses to spell out a thought it expects the reader to have: that the enrollees 'at least were not harmed' by the program. What is that sentence doing in the chapter's argument?
options: It raises the most generous reading the Oregon results leave open, precisely so the studies that follow can take it away step by step.
It plants a position the chapter will later attribute to the program's defenders, storing up a quotation to be turned against them in the closing pages.
It concedes the limit of what the Oregon experiment can show, a moment of candor the chapter offers before moving to evidence it finds more conclusive.
It marks the chapter's real complaint as financial, telling the reader that what follows will be an accounting of cost rather than a claim about health.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter lines up its evidence in a fixed order: the Oregon recap, where enrollees spent more without doing better on measured outcomes; then a cancer study in which Medicaid patients and people with no insurance were equally likely to die; then surgery, angioplasty, and lung-transplant studies in which Medicaid patients fared worse than the uninsured. Within the chapter's argument, what does presenting the studies in this order accomplish?
options: The procedures grow graver as the list advances, letting the reader watch the program's shortfall widen as the medical stakes of each study rise.
The chapter rests its weight on the randomized Oregon experiment and arranges the rest as echoes, so the strongest research design is what the reader meets first.
The chapter opens with the result most favorable to the program as a show of even-handedness, buying credibility before the critical findings arrive.
Each study removes a fallback defense the previous one left standing, so the wasteful-but-harmless reading is gone by the end of the sequence.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter closes by urging that Medicaid be retired and its enrollees brought into one system serving rich and poor alike. Suppose it had offered only the Oregon recap -- higher spending, no better measured outcomes -- before making that recommendation. Within the chapter's own argument, why would the case for retiring the program then be weaker?
options: A no-benefit result might still be explained by enrollees who were sicker to begin with, and only the statistical controls of the later studies could close that explanation off for good.
The Oregon recap says nothing about whether physicians will accept Medicaid patients, and the chapter treats the appointment-refusal evidence as what finally clinches its closing recommendation.
A merely wasteful program still invites repair -- spend smarter, pay providers more -- and only the harm the chapter reads in its studies makes removal, not repair, the way to help the poor.
A single randomized experiment in one state could not carry a nationwide recommendation, and the chapter needs the added studies chiefly to show that the Oregon pattern holds in other places.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter pauses, after laying out the Medicaid outcome studies it cites, to note something about how each study was conducted. According to the chapter, what did the researchers in each of those studies do?
options: Followed all patients for an identical number of years and dropped any who changed coverage midway.
Controlled statistically for demographic factors, initial health status, location, and comorbidities.
Assigned patients at random to Medicaid, private insurance, or no coverage before tracking outcomes.
Drew all of their patients from a single hospital so that quality of care was the same for every group.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter argues that, because the researchers in its cited studies took factors like initial health status into account, the studies' worse results for Medicaid patients cannot be explained as those patients having been sicker from the start.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: A reader grants that the studies the chapter cites found Medicaid patients doing worse, but objects that people on Medicaid are poorer and in worse health when they enroll, so their outcomes would lag no matter what the program did. According to the chapter, what about the studies' design already answers this objection?
options: The reported gaps are so wide that differences in starting health alone could never plausibly account for them.
Each study set Medicaid patients only against uninsured people, whose incomes and circumstances are comparably hard.
Each study adjusted for demographics, starting health, location, and comorbidities before comparing the groups' outcomes.
The same pattern recurs across several independent studies, which differences among enrollees could not produce every time.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter could have reported simply that Medicaid patients' outcomes trail those of other coverage groups. Instead it writes that the studies show Medicaid 'actually hurts' the poor. According to the chapter, what licenses the stronger, causal reading?
options: The sheer width of the mortality gaps, which the chapter treats as beyond what any benign account of the program could produce.
The random assignment of coverage in every study it cites, which guaranteed the compared groups were identical at the outset.
The studies' adjustments for baseline differences, which the chapter says rule out enrollees having simply started out worse off.
The standing of the medical journals that carried the findings, which the chapter presents as the profession's endorsement of them.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The province of Askerton runs FieldStart, a voluntary scheme that supplies small farms with subsidized seed and an assigned crop adviser, and four bodies have examined how farms under it fare. The grain board set the results of every member farm beside those of every non-member on the provincial roll, thousands of farms in all, and reported members going under at nearly triple the non-member rate. The cooperative bank paired member farms with non-members alike in operator age, yields before entry, district, and outstanding debt, and found members' yields trailing modestly; its review ran only in the bank's annual. The agronomy institute charted provincial farm failures across the eight years before the scheme opened and the eight years since, weighting for the changing share of smallholdings, and found failures running a fifth higher in the later period. The scheme's own office set farms that stayed a full five years beside farms that left within their first, alike in acreage, and found the stayers finishing slightly behind across the same seasons. In the provincial press, the grain board's triple figure is the one every account leads with. Under the reasoning the chapter applies to its cited outcome studies, which comparison is capable of showing that FieldStart itself harms the farms in it?
options: The grain board's comparison
The agronomy institute's comparison
The cooperative bank's comparison
The scheme office's comparison
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: A town's education trust runs Evenstudy, a free after-school homework centre open to any pupil who registers, and the trust's board, told that registered pupils end the year further behind, will commission one evaluation. A polling firm proposes to survey every family the programme has ever enrolled, above nine thousand, gathering pupils' own accounts of the centres including whatever complaints they hold; it is the costliest plan of the four. A retired examiner proposes to set registered pupils beside unregistered pupils of the same age, prior-year marks, catchment school, and duties at home, comparing end-of-year marks; her report would not arrive until a second year had run. A statistics lecturer proposes to chart the town's promotion rates across the six years before the centres opened and the six years since, weighted for class sizes, though the earliest records are thin. A teachers' panel proposes to match registered with unregistered pupils on the footing the examiner would use, measuring how often families attend, how long pupils stay each evening, and how they rate the centres. Among board members the panel's design has drawn the widest support. Which proposal, under the reasoning the chapter applies to its cited outcome studies, could produce a result capable of showing that Evenstudy itself sets its pupils back?
options: The teachers' panel's proposal
The polling firm's proposal
The statistics lecturer's proposal
The retired examiner's proposal
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: A regional crafts guild runs Benchline, a scheme offering new furniture workshops subsidized tenancy in guild buildings, and a trade paper has carried a long exchange over whether the scheme damages the workshops in it, with four comparisons cited. A craft magazine set the scheme's whole membership against the national closure average for small workshops, drawn from the register's full roll and compiled in a single week, finding members shutting at four times that rate. A chamber of commerce paired member workshops with non-members alike in founding capital, trade, and town, and found the members outlasting their matches, a result its authors have restated twice in the exchange. An accountancy firm paired members with non-members alike in founding capital, years at the bench, town, and sideline work carried, and found members closing somewhat more often; its study sits in a little-read annual. The guild's own office set workshops that renewed membership beside workshops that let it lapse, alike in age of business, and found the renewers finishing slightly behind over the same span. It is the magazine's four-fold figure that heads nearly every letter the paper prints. Under the reasoning the chapter applies to its cited outcome studies, which comparison can carry the claim that Benchline itself damages the workshops in it?
options: The craft magazine's comparison
The guild office's comparison
The accountancy firm's comparison
The chamber of commerce's comparison
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: According to the chapter, once a family qualifies for Medicaid its children can presumably get doctors' appointments on largely the same terms as children with private insurance, since both kinds of coverage pay for the same care.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter reports that state Medicaid programs reimburse primary care at well below private rates — 55 cents on the private dollar in Texas, 38 in California, 29 in New York. According to the chapter, why does paying so little leave enrollees unable to turn their coverage into actual care?
options: The low rates push doctors out of medicine altogether, shrinking the overall supply of care until patients of every insurance type face the same shortage.
States stretch the low rates by narrowing the list of services Medicaid covers, so enrollees discover that many routine treatments are simply no longer covered benefits.
Enrollees are expected to pay providers the difference between Medicaid's rate and the private rate out of pocket, and few poor families can afford the balance.
Services are in limited supply, and providers filling a schedule prefer patients whose insurers pay full private rates, so Medicaid enrollees lose that competition.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter treats one nationwide statistic about primary care doctors as the unsurprising consequence of Medicaid paying far below private rates. Which statement matches the chapter's report?
options: Nearly a third of them admit to dropping longtime patients who moved from private coverage onto Medicaid.
Nearly a third of them admit to refusing to take on new patients whose only form of insurance is Medicaid.
Nearly a third of them admit to closing their practices to new patients of every kind as reimbursements have tightened across insurers.
Nearly a third of them admit to turning away every Medicaid patient, including those who carry private insurance alongside it.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter reports a survey of Chicago specialty clinics in which children with public insurance were denied appointments six times as often as privately insured children, and waited over twice as long when they got one. How, according to the chapter, was that evidence gathered?
options: Researchers mailed questionnaires to mothers of young children, asking how long they had waited for appointments and whether any clinic had turned a child away.
Researchers pulled the clinics' own scheduling records and compared the recorded waits for publicly and privately insured children who were treated across the same months.
Researchers sent matched pairs of families to visit clinics in person, identical except that one child in each pair carried public and the other private coverage.
Researchers posing as mothers phoned clinics for children's appointments, noting what schedulers asked first — usually the insurance type — and what they were offered.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter compares state Medicaid programs using a reimbursement ratio, reporting Texas at 0.55, California at 0.38, and New York at 0.29. According to the chapter, what do these ratios measure?
options: How much of each state's Medicaid spending is contributed by the federal government rather than by the state
How much Medicaid pays providers for primary care relative to what private insurers pay for identical services
How much of each state's budget goes to Medicaid relative to what its legislature originally appropriated
How much Medicaid enrollees pay out of pocket for care relative to what privately insured patients pay
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: According to the chapter, Medicaid is funded jointly by the federal government and the states, and each state decides for itself who qualifies and how generous its coverage is.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter reports that state reimbursement ratios vary widely, from 55 cents on the private dollar in Texas down to 29 cents in New York. What explanation does the chapter give for why some states' ratios sit so much lower than others'?
options: Some states qualify as many people as they can without more money behind the program, so each service gets paid at a thinner rate
The federal government contributes a smaller share of the program's costs in some states, leaving those states less to pass through to providers
Some states steer more of their program budgets toward hospital and specialty care, leaving a smaller share for the primary care the ratio tracks
Private insurers in some states pay providers far more for identical services, which drags the ratio down even where Medicaid's own payments are typical
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: According to the chapter, a low reimbursement ratio like Texas's 0.55 signals difficulty for the patients the program covers. On the chapter's account, how does a low ratio turn into that difficulty?
options: Providers can earn more treating the privately insured, so Medicaid patients lose the competition for a limited supply of services
The state responds by trimming what its coverage includes, so patients' benefits shrink even though their eligibility is unchanged
So many people qualify in low-ratio states that clinics cannot see them all, no matter what any insurer pays
Patients are left owing providers the difference between what Medicaid reimburses and what a private insurer would have paid
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: Four counties run childcare-assistance programs that pay independent childcare providers directly when an approved family places a child, and providers in all four counties also serve ordinary fee-paying families. Dunmore's program accepts only families in deep poverty, pays providers their posted rates, and is picketed each budget season by parents' groups demanding looser rules. Callis's program takes any family under a moderate income line, and a statute enlarges its appropriation whenever its caseload grows; auditors grumble that its budget line keeps climbing. Harwick's program qualifies a wider share of working families than any neighbouring county's, operates within its founding appropriation, and draws editorials calling it over-generous to middle-income households. Verone's program pays providers their posted rates but admits a new family only when an enrolled one leaves, and spring applications routinely outnumber the places that open. Judging by the chapter's spread-more-thinly reasoning, families already enrolled in which program should have the most trouble finding a provider willing to take their subsidy?
options: Dunmore's
Callis's
Verone's
Harwick's
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: A province pays private attorneys a flat per-matter fee to represent qualifying residents in housing and benefits disputes, and the same attorneys are free to fill their calendars with ordinary paying clients instead. The fee schedule is recalculated each year from the program's fund and its expected caseload. The legislature has twice widened who qualifies, first to all tenants facing eviction and then to anyone under a moderate income line, and each widening statute carried a matching enlargement of the fund. The caseload is now the largest of any provincial program, attorneys grumble about its filing portal, and a newspaper campaign argues that a program grown this large must soon be turning the needy away. Judging by the chapter's spread-more-thinly reasoning, what lies ahead for residents who qualify?
options: Cases wait unassigned in a growing queue
Per-matter fees sink below what paying work yields
Attorneys keep taking their cases
Attorneys drift toward paying clients only
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: A city trust arranges home repairs for low-income elderly homeowners, drawing on the same licensed contractors who work the private market. Its endowment has not grown in a decade, and its rolls have not grown in years either, though inquiries arrive steadily; the few openings each year go to names from a long-standing intake list. Each job the trust commissions is paid at the contractor's own standard bid price and invoiced like any private order. At a council hearing, a grants officer warns that with money this tight, contractors will soon stop answering the trust's calls. Judging by the chapter's spread-more-thinly reasoning, what should the households already on the trust's rolls expect?
options: They are rotated off the rolls to make room
Contractors keep taking their jobs
Their repairs get shaved down to patchwork
Contractors quietly drop them for private work
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: On the chapter's account of the Healthy Indiana Plan, members were presumably left to cover the plan's would-be deductible out of their own pockets, building it up through their required monthly payments into the POWER account.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter quotes Seema Verma, the Healthy Indiana Plan's architect, recounting that the designers studied the announced criticisms of health savings accounts for the poor and built a feature to answer each one. One criticism held that poor people would have no money for preventive care. On her account as the chapter gives it, which feature answered that criticism?
options: Preventive services were taken out of the deductible and covered from the first dollar.
The state deposited an amount corresponding to the would-be deductible into each member's account.
Unspent year-end balances could be carried forward into the next year's contribution requirements.
Monthly payments into each member's account were scaled to income, between 2 and 5 percent.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter quotes the Healthy Indiana Plan's architect presenting the required monthly payment into each member's POWER account -- scaled between 2 and 5 percent of income, with a 60-day grace period -- as the design's personal responsibility mechanism. On that account, what gives the requirement its force?
options: Missing a payment past the grace period is covered out of the state's deposit, shrinking the next year's account.
Missing a payment past the grace period puts the member out of the program for the next twelve months.
Missing a payment past the grace period cancels the member's right to carry unspent year-end balances forward.
Missing a payment past the grace period forfeits the member's accumulated balance, though coverage itself continues.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The Forbes piece the chapter quotes describes what can happen to money remaining in a member's POWER account at the end of the year: the member can put that balance toward the next year's required payments. On the account as quoted, what determines whether a member gets this rollover?
options: Whether the member has made every required monthly payment on time during the year.
Whether the member has obtained a specified set of preventive services during the year.
Whether the member has stayed enrolled in the program continuously for the full twelve months.
Whether the member has avoided non-urgent use of emergency rooms during the year.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: According to the chapter's account of the Healthy Indiana Plan, enrollees shifted toward consumer-like behavior -- fewer emergency-room visits, more generic drugs, requests for second opinions -- and balances began building up in their health savings accounts.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter relays a set of reported results from the Healthy Indiana Plan: preventive-care participation climbed sharply, most enrollees kept up their required monthly contributions, emergency-room use fell, and account balances grew. Within the chapter's argument, what are these results offered as evidence for?
options: That low-income people handle their own money as capably as anyone else, so a savings-based plan is a workable remedy for the poor and not only for the well-off.
That the main obstacle to insuring the poor is affordability, so a program succeeds once the state fully funds the deductible and covers preventive care from the first dollar.
That high-deductible coverage holds spending down chiefly by making enrollees think twice before seeking any care at all, preventive visits included.
That capping enrollment is what keeps a public program's costs predictable, so cost control in programs for the poor comes down to limiting how many people may join.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The Forbes piece the chapter quotes reports a Mathematica Policy Research finding that the Healthy Indiana Plan dramatically raised preventive-care participation, citing figures of 39 percent and 59 percent. What do those two figures compare, on the chapter's account?
options: Participation among enrollees who met the rollover requirement against participation among those who forfeited the state's contributions.
Participation among the program's enrollees against the rate the piece reports for the privately insured population.
Participation among Healthy Indiana enrollees against participation among Indiana residents who stayed on traditional Medicaid.
Enrollees' participation during their first six months in the program against their participation after a full year.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter reports that the Healthy Indiana Plan grew without employers dropping coverage and pushing their insured workers onto it. According to the account the chapter quotes, which feature of the program blocked that move?
options: Enrollment was capped, so by the time an employer dropped coverage there were no remaining places for its workers to claim.
The required monthly contributions were scaled to income, making membership costlier for workers than staying on an employer's plan.
Applicants had to have gone six months without insurance, so an employer's just-dropped workers were not eligible.
Members who missed a monthly contribution were removed from the program for twelve months, making it an unreliable place to send workers.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: According to the chapter, the Healthy Indiana Plan's success presumably settles what the country should do next: extend that kind of plan -- a separate, Singapore-style program serving only the poor -- nationwide.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter closes by offering the Healthy Indiana Plan as proof that Singapore-style plans can work for America's poor -- and then declines to recommend the very design that plan embodies: a separate plan serving only the poor. According to the chapter, why?
options: The chapter judges that most poor households outside Indiana could not keep up the plan's required monthly contributions, so a savings-based design would in practice reach only families with steady earnings.

A program serving the poor alone invites underfunding and neglect -- politicians can champion the needy's care in speeches while thinning its budget -- so the chapter would put rich and poor in one system, never two.

The plan's capped enrollment and its waiting list in the tens of thousands persuaded the chapter that a savings-based design, whatever it does for current enrollees, could never be stretched to cover every poor American.

A nationwide version would, like Indiana's plan, have to operate inside the Medicaid machinery it is meant to replace, and the chapter will not endorse anything that keeps the program it wants retired alive.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: Earlier in the chapter, Flynn traces Medicaid patients' trouble getting care to how little the program pays: state Medicaid systems reimburse providers at a fraction of what private insurers pay for identical services. How does that account bear, within the chapter's argument, on its closing refusal to recommend a separate plan for the poor?
options: It gives the warning its evidence: Medicaid is itself a program for the poor alone, and its thin payment rates are the fate the chapter predicts for any such program -- what one shared system is meant to prevent.

It generalizes the problem to public payers of every kind: wherever a government writes the checks, rates get squeezed, so the poor would be better carried by private coverage than by any publicly run program.
It reverses the benchmark: private insurers are overpaying for identical services, and one combined system would let everyone's prices be pulled down toward what Medicaid already pays.

It locates the fault in the worst-funded states: where a legislature pays providers decently the access gap closes, so the real target is the handful of low-paying states rather than the separate-program design itself.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid

items.stem: The chapter's account of the Healthy Indiana Plan -- drawn largely from a Forbes piece it quotes at length -- reports enrollees obtaining preventive care at sharply higher rates, keeping up their monthly contributions, and rating the program highly. The chapter then states plainly that it does not advocate a separate Singapore-style system for the rich and another for the poor. What work, within the chapter's argument, is the Indiana story doing?
options: It stands in for the Singapore evidence -- a concession that results from so distant and different a country cannot, on their own, carry the chapter's case with American readers.

It shows that state capitals rather than Washington should design the new system, since a state built and ran a successful plan in the very years when the programs drawing the chapter's criticism were federal creations.
It answers the doubt that a Singapore-style plan could work for poor Americans at all; whether to run one plan or two is a separate question, which the chapter settles on political grounds.

It shows that a program for the poor alone can escape neglect when its enrollment is capped and its costs made predictable, so the chapter's warning is aimed at open-ended programs rather than at the two-system design.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 26 → We Must Rescue the Poor from Medicaid
